It is not a general amiability, not a desire to be liked, and not a strategy for avoiding conflict — and a man who adapts himself endlessly and never gets round to the gospel is not doing what Paul did; he is doing the opposite of it, using Paul’s words as cover.

The second is the modesty of “some”. Paul does not say he became all things to all people in order to save everybody. He has adapted himself in every direction he can think of, at real cost, and his stated expectation is some. That is a realistic sentence, and it protects two kinds of people: the evangelist who is discouraged because the response is small, and the one who is tempted to think that if he only got the presentation right, everybody would come. Neither is how it works. You spend yourself, and God gives the growth (3:6), and some are saved.

And there is a caution here for our own time that runs the opposite way to the usual one. Yes, this passage is misused to justify a Christianity that has quietly stopped saying anything difficult. But the commoner failure in conservative churches is the reverse: treating our own inherited cultural form — the music, the vocabulary, the dress, the assumptions about what a serious person is like — as though it were the gospel itself, and regarding anyone who does not fit it as not really interested.

Paul dismantled his own preferences in every direction for the sake of people he wanted to reach. The question is not whether we are willing to compromise the gospel. It is whether we are willing to be inconvenienced for it (cf. Gal. 6:2; Rom. 15:1–3).

verseByVerse.quote: I do it all for the sake of the gospel, that I may share with them in its blessings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I do it all for the sake of the gospel, that I may share with them in its blessings.”

The little word with is doing a great deal of work, and it changes the picture of the apostle entirely.

Paul is not standing outside the gospel handing it to other people. He is inside it with them, receiving the same thing he is offering, dependent on the same mercy, sustained by the same promises. The man who has just described himself as under compulsion, enslaved to all, going hungry and preaching for nothing, is not a functionary distributing a benefit he does not need. He is a beneficiary who has been given the job of telling others where he found it.

Which is a necessary corrective to something that happens to nearly everyone who works with the things of God for long enough.

It happens to ministers most visibly: the Bible becomes raw material for Sunday, prayer becomes something conducted publicly on behalf of others, and a man can go months handling the gospel professionally without once being addressed by it. But it is not confined to the paid. It happens to the Sunday school teacher who only ever reads to prepare, to the parent whose faith has become entirely a matter of transmitting something to the children, to the long-standing member who has heard every sermon in the building as an assessment of the preacher rather than a word to himself.

The tell is a subtle change in how you hear things. You listen to a sermon and think, that would help so-and-so. You read a passage and immediately consider who needs it. And in itself that is a good instinct — it is love, and it is what a teacher should do. The danger is when it becomes the only way you receive anything, and the thought this is about me stops arriving altogether.

Paul will not have it. The blessings are his too, and he says so — and it is the reason his preaching had weight. A man who is visibly living on what he is describing preaches differently from a man who is describing it accurately from outside.

So a test, and it can be run this Sunday. During the next sermon you hear, notice how many times you think about somebody else and how many times you think about yourself. And when you next open the Bible outside your preparation — if you open it outside your preparation at all — notice whether you are reading for material or for food.

The apostle to the Gentiles, in the middle of listing everything he had given up for other people, stopped to say that he was in it for himself as well. There is no other honest way to do this work (cf. 1 Tim. 4:16; Ps. 34:8).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–27 — The Discipline of the Athlete
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chapter closes with the athletic metaphor that grounds the principle of self-discipline in the logic of purposeful effort. The Isthmian Games, held near Corinth every two years, were the second-most prestigious games in the ancient world; the image of the runner and the boxer would have been immediately vivid to the Corinthian reader. Paul uses the image to describe the kind of disciplined self-denial that purposeful Christian living requires — not the harsh asceticism of the body-hating Gnostic but the focused self-management of the athlete who wants to win.

The force of the passage is partly eschatological: the athlete’s crown is perishable (a wreath of celery or laurel that wilted within days); the Christian’s crown is imperishable. And partly it is deeply personal: “I discipline my body and keep it under control, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified” (v. 27). Paul is not claiming security in his own self-discipline; he is claiming that genuine discipleship requires disciplined effort. The apostle who preaches freedom is also the apostle who runs hard, boxes purposefully, and keeps his body under control — because the prize is real, and the possibility of disqualification is real.
verseByVerse.theology:
Assurance and Effort: The Perseverance of the Saints

The warning of v. 27 — “lest I myself should be disqualified” — has been debated in relation to the doctrine of perseverance. Reformed theology does not take this as a threat to genuine believers’ final security but as the description of the means by which that security is maintained: the God who sovereignly keeps his people does so through their own disciplined effort, not instead of it. The warning is the mechanism of perseverance: those who are genuinely elect will take the warning seriously, run hard, and thereby demonstrate and maintain their calling.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians lived in the shadow of the Isthmian Games and would have immediately understood the competitive imagery. Paul makes the comparison in order to shame them slightly: the athletes prepare with greater earnestness for a temporary prize than the Corinthians apply to an eternal one. Now: The contemporary church has, in many quarters, lost the language of spiritual discipline entirely — afraid that any emphasis on effort sounds like works-righteousness. Paul’s athletic imagery corrects this: grace produces effort; the free gift of the gospel generates the runner’s willingness to run hard.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that in a race all the runners run, but only one receives the prize? So run that you may obtain it. Every athlete exercises self-control in all things. They do it to receive a perishable wreath, but we an imperishable.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Do you not know that in a race all the runners run, but only one receives the prize?”

The image would have needed no explanation at Corinth. The Isthmian Games were held a few miles outside the city every two years, second in prestige only to the Olympics, and Corinth hosted them. Everyone reading this letter had seen the athletes train, had watched the races, and knew exactly what the prize looked like.

“So run that you may obtain it.” And a guard is needed at once, because the analogy has a limit Paul plainly does not intend. He is not saying only one Christian will be saved — that would contradict everything in the letter. The point of comparison is the manner of running, not the number of winners. Run like a man who means to win, rather than like someone jogging round because attendance is expected.

“Every athlete exercises self-control in all things.” The word is enkrateuetai — the same root as the self-control of the fruit of the Spirit. And Paul’s readers knew what it involved: competitors at the Isthmian Games were required to swear they had trained for ten months, on a controlled diet, under supervision. Nobody turned up on the day.

What strikes Paul is the disproportion between the effort and the prize. “They do it to receive a perishable wreath, but we an imperishable.”

The Isthmian crown was made of wild celery, or in some periods of pine. Ten months of denial, and the reward was a handful of leaves that browned within a week and was thrown out. Men gave years to that.

And the comparison is not primarily a rebuke of athletes; it is a rebuke of us. Paul’s point is that people will discipline themselves ferociously for something they know is temporary, and Christians will not discipline themselves at all for something that is not.

Which is easy to verify. Consider what people you know are prepared to give up for a marathon, a qualification, a business, a physique, a musical instrument — the early mornings, the diet, the years. All of it for something that will be forgotten, or lost with age, or superseded. Then consider what the same people find impossible for prayer or Scripture, and notice that the difference is not availability of time.

And there is a word here for a Christian who has grown suspicious of effort. Some are so anxious not to fall into works-righteousness that any talk of discipline sounds to them like a threat to grace. That is a misunderstanding, and this passage settles it. Nobody supposes an athlete’s training earns him the right to enter the stadium. The training is what a man does because he is in the race, not in order to be admitted to it.

So the question is simply whether you are training for anything. Not whether you feel spiritual, and not whether you are trying hard in some vague and continuous way — but whether there is any actual, deliberate, scheduled practice in your life aimed at godliness, of the kind an athlete would recognise as training (cf. 1 Tim. 4:7–8; Heb. 12:1–2).

verseByVerse.quote: So I do not run aimlessly; I do not box as one beating the air. But I discipline my body and keep it under control, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“So I do not run aimlessly; I do not box as one beating the air.” Two negatives, and both describe activity without contact — the runner with no finish line in view, the boxer throwing punches at nothing. Effort is being expended; nothing is happening.

Which is a fair description of a good deal of religious life. It is entirely possible to be busy in a church for thirty years, to attend everything, to be tired from it — and to be shadow-boxing. Paul’s alternative is not more energy. It is aim.

“But I discipline my body and keep it under control.” The verb is startling and translations soften it: hypōpiazō means to strike under the eye, to give a black eye. Paul says he punches himself in the face — and the second phrase means to lead away as a slave. Having just called himself a servant to all (v. 19), he now makes a servant of his own body.

That must not be misread as contempt for the body; this is the same apostle who has just called it a temple of the Holy Spirit and insisted that the Lord is for it (6:13, 19). He is not describing the self-punishment of a man who thinks flesh is evil. He is describing an athlete’s relation to his own appetites: the body is a magnificent servant and a ruinous master, and the training consists in keeping it in the right position.

Then the reason, and it is the most sobering sentence in the chapter: “lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified.”

The word is adokimos — failing the test, not standing up to examination, rejected as counterfeit. And Paul applies it to himself.

Readers ask immediately whether this means a true believer can be lost, and the question deserves a straight answer rather than a hurried one. Scripture elsewhere is emphatic that those whom God justifies he also glorifies (Rom. 8:30), that no one can snatch Christ’s sheep from his hand (John 10:28), and this letter itself grounds the Corinthians’ security in the faithfulness of God (1:8–9). Paul is not contradicting that here.

What he is describing is the means by which God keeps his people. The warning is not idle machinery; it is one of the instruments, and it works precisely by being taken seriously. A man who reads this and thinks that could not happen to me has misunderstood it. A man who reads it and disciplines himself is the very man the warning was written to preserve. The fence at the cliff edge is not useless because nobody has gone over.

And notice the exact danger Paul names, because it is specific and it is his own: after preaching to others. The peril of the herald is that he handles the truth so constantly that he stops being handled by it — that he can describe repentance without repenting, and warn against sins he is quietly committing, and do it competently for years.

So the chapter that began with a man defending his rights ends with him afraid of himself. He had seen the risen Christ, planted churches across the empire, and written Scripture, and he still thought it necessary to keep his body under and his aim clear.

Which is not anxiety, and it should not produce any. It is what a man looks like who takes both the prize and the race seriously — who knows that the crown is imperishable and that the running is real, and who intends, having called others to the line, to be found on his feet at the end (cf. Phil. 3:12–14; 2 Tim. 4:7–8; Heb. 12:1).

10.title: Israel’s Warning, the Lord’s Table, and the Glory of God
10.overview:
Chapter 10 deploys Israel’s wilderness history as a theological warning against the Corinthian assumption that spiritual privilege guarantees spiritual safety. Israel had extraordinary covenant advantages — cloud, sea, spiritual food and drink, the presence of Christ — and they still fell. Four catastrophic failures are cited: idolatry, sexual immorality, testing Christ, and grumbling. These are not ancient curiosities; they are “written down for our instruction, on whom the end of the ages has come” (v. 11). The Corinthians who were confident they could attend temple meals without danger were flattering themselves into disaster.

Paul then draws the sharpest line in the letter about idol worship: the cup of blessing and the bread of the Lord’s Supper are participations in the blood and body of Christ; the cup of demons and the table of demons are genuine spiritual participations in the demonic. You cannot be at the Lord’s table and the demons’ table simultaneously. The chapter closes with the most comprehensive positive principle in Paul’s ethics: “So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.” Every act of ordinary life is capable of being an act of worship.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The “for” that opens chapter 10 links back to Paul’s warning about disqualification in 9:27: the Corinthians need to take the possibility of spiritual failure seriously, and Israel’s wilderness history provides the case study. The parallel Paul draws is deliberate and pointed. Israel was baptised in the cloud and the sea — immersed in the presence and power of God. They ate supernatural food and drank supernatural drink — the manna and the water from the rock. And the rock that followed them, providing spiritual drink, was Christ himself (v. 4). This is not a typological embellishment; it is Paul’s claim that the pre-incarnate Son was the mediator of God’s sustaining grace in the wilderness.

Yet Israel fell. Despite their spiritual advantages, despite their sacramental participation, despite their proximity to the divine glory — they were struck down in the wilderness because of idolatry, sexual immorality, testing Christ, and grumbling. Paul’s point to the Corinthians is precise: you have spiritual advantages too — baptism, the Lord’s Supper, the indwelling Spirit. These are not security guarantees. They are resources for running the race; they do not exempt anyone from the possibility of disqualification.

Verse 13 is one of the great pastoral promises in the NT: “No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.” The promise is not that temptations will be light but that they will be manageable — that divine faithfulness will always supply a path through that the believer is genuinely capable of taking.

Between the four failures and the promise stand two verses that carry the weight of the section. Verse 11 says the wilderness record was written down for our instruction, on whom the end of the ages has come — the Old Testament was composed with later readers in view, and we read it standing nearer the end than Israel ever stood. Verse 12 then turns the whole history into a single sentence aimed at the confident: let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall. The warning is not addressed to the struggling believer who already fears himself. It is addressed to the one who has stopped fearing. And far from being the opposite of God’s keeping of his people, a warning like this is one of the ways he keeps them — the alarm that gets a household out of a burning house is not the failure of the rescue but the means of it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Pre-Existent Christ and the Typology of the Wilderness

Paul’s identification of the rock in the wilderness as Christ (v. 4) is a claim that the Son of God was the agent of God’s sustaining grace before the incarnation — the “Angel of the LORD” tradition of the OT now understood christologically. This is christological pre-existence applied to redemptive history: the same Christ who died on the cross was present and active in the wilderness, providing the spiritual sustenance that Israel squandered. Reformed typology has always read the OT this way: Christ is not absent from the old covenant; he is present as promise, type, and mediator.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians who were attending temple meals — eating idol food in an actual pagan temple — needed to hear that spiritual confidence is not the same as spiritual safety. Israel had more obvious privileges than any of them and still fell. Now: The sacramental Christian who trusts in regular communion and baptism as automatic guarantees of spiritual health — without the disciplined effort, the watchful sobriety, the dependency on God that Paul describes — is making exactly the Israelite mistake. The sacraments are genuine means of grace, not magic shields.

verseByVerse.quote: For I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul has just described himself in the language of an athlete who could still bedisqualified (9:27). Now he turns and says, in effect: this is not a nightmare I invented.It happened. And it happened to the most privileged generation that ever lived.

I do not want you to be unaware, brothers. That is a gentle sentence with a hardedge. The Corinthians prided themselves on being aware — on knowledge (8:1), oninsight, on having worked out that an idol is nothing. Paul does not attack theirknowledge. He tells them there is a piece of history they have not factored in.

Then count the word all. It comes five times in four verses. All under thecloud. All passed through the sea. All baptised into Moses. All ate. All drank. Paul isnot describing a spiritual elite; he is describing every last person in the camp,including the ones who would be dead within the year.

Stand there for a moment. The pillar of cloud is overhead — not a metaphor, avisible column of the presence of God, close enough to shade the whole column of march(Ex 13:21). Ahead, the sea has stood up on both sides. They walk out on the seabed on dryground, and the water that drowned the Egyptian army does not touch them. Cloud above,water on either hand: they are, says Paul, surrounded — and he uses the word forbaptism to say so.

Baptised into Moses is a striking phrase, and it needs unpacking, because it isnot water baptism. To be baptised into someone is to be bound to that person, sothat his deliverance becomes your deliverance and his story becomes the story you liveinside. Israel came out of that sea belonging to Moses in a way they had not belonged tohim when they went in. They had a mediator, a rescue, a covenant sign, and a visible God.If church membership, the font and the table could save anyone, that generation was safe.

Which is exactly the point Paul is setting up. Everything in these two verses isgenuine. None of it is criticised. The cloud was real, the sea was real, the belonging wasreal — and the word nevertheless is coming in verse 5 (cf. Ex 14:21–22;Rom 6:3).

It is worth saying at the outset who this passage is for, because it is easy to file itunder other people. It is for the man who was baptised as a baby and has the certificate ina drawer. It is for the woman who was dipped in a river at seventeen in front of a weepingcongregation. It is for the family that has not missed a Sunday in a decade, whose childrenknow the songs, who take the bread and the cup every month without fail. Paul’s pointis not that these things are worthless — he is about to call them spiritual food andspiritual drink. His point is that Israel had the equivalent of every one of them, in a morespectacular form than any church has ever seen, and it was possible to have the lot andperish anyway.

The cloud did not make anyone love God. It only made him impossible to ignore.

verseByVerse.quote: and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The privileges keep coming, and now they are edible. All ate the same spiritualfood, and all drank the same spiritual drink.

Spiritual here does not mean immaterial. The manna could be gathered in a jarand it went bad if you hoarded it. The water from the rock was wet. The word meanssupplied by the Spirit — food and drink that no farmer grew and no wellyielded, arriving because God sent them. For forty years an entire nation woke up in adesert that grows nothing and found breakfast on the ground. Not once. Every morning,about fourteen thousand mornings, minus the Sabbaths, until the day they ate the produce ofCanaan and it stopped (Josh 5:12).

Then Paul says something that would be reckless if it were not true: they drank fromthe spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ.

Two questions come up here, and both deserve straight answers. First, is Paul repeatinga Jewish legend? There was a rabbinic tradition that the rock of Exodus 17 literally rolledalong behind Israel, a boulder on tour. Paul is not endorsing that. He is reaching for whatthe tradition was clumsily reaching for. Water came from a rock at Rephidim near thebeginning of the journey (Ex 17:6) and again at Meribah near the end of it, forty yearslater (Num 20:11). The rocks were different rocks in different places. What followed themwas not a stone; it was the One who gave the water, and he was there at both ends of thewilderness and every dry mile in between.

Second, why call him the Rock at all? Because that is God’s own name in thesong Moses sang over this very generation: The Rock, his work is perfect; youwere unmindful of the Rock that bore you (Deut 32:4, 18). Paul takes a divine title outof the Old Testament, a title reserved for the LORD, and lays it on Jesus of Nazarethwithout a word of apology. This is not the New Testament borrowing an image. It is the NewTestament identifying a person.

Before there was a manger, there was a rock in a desert. The Son of God stood in awaterless place beside a people who had already decided he was not worth trusting, andopened a spring for them. He would do it again on a hill outside Jerusalem, where the rockstruck was himself, and what came out was not water only (Jn 19:34). He fed the men whowould grumble at him by evening. He gave drink to the throats that would curse him bynightfall. There has never been a season of the world’s history in which he was notdoing this.

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, with most of them God was not pleased, for they were overthrown in the wilderness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything turns on one word. Nevertheless.

With most of them God was not pleased, for they were overthrown in thewilderness. Paul says most, and the word is almost a mercy, because thearithmetic is worse than it sounds. Of the adults who came out of Egypt, two entered theland: Caleb and Joshua. Two. Out of a fighting-age muster of six hundred thousand men(Num 1:46; 14:29–30).

The verb translated overthrown is a picture word: katestrōthēsan,strewn, scattered, laid out flat — bodies spread across a desert floor. Put a figureon it. Something like forty funerals a day, every day, for thirty-eight years. There wasnever a week in that generation’s life without a burial party going out at dusk. Thechildren who came into Canaan had grown up hearing that sound.

And every one of those people had been under the cloud. Every one had walked through thesea on dry ground. Every one had eaten the bread of heaven that morning. Whatever thesacraments do, they did not do this.

This is the sentence the confident Corinthians needed and did not want. They hadconcluded that spiritual privilege was a kind of insulation — that a man who had beenbaptised, who ate at the Lord’s table, who had the Spirit and could speak in tongues,was in a category where serious spiritual danger no longer applied. Paul answers with agraveyard. He does not deny that the privileges were real. He denies that they werearmour.

One clarification is needed before the reader draws too much from the wordoverthrown, and it should be given rather than left to worry him. Paul is notsaying that every Israelite who died in the desert is in hell. Moses died in the wildernessunder God’s displeasure, and Moses is on the mountain of transfiguration(Deut 34:5; Lk 9:30). Miriam and Aaron died there too. To be shut out of Canaan was a realand terrible judgment, but Canaan is not a picture of heaven in any simple way, and Paul isnot conducting an inquest into individual souls. He is making one point, and it is enoughon its own: God’s manifest favour to a group is no guarantee about any particularperson in it.

Note also the restrained phrase God was not pleased. It is a mild-soundingverb for a fearful outcome, and the mildness is deliberate. God does not rage. He is simplynot pleased — and a generation ends. The displeasure of God is quiet, and it is heavierthan anything else in the world.

verseByVerse.quote: Now these things took place as examples for us, that we might not desire evil as they did.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now these things took place as examples for us. The word is typoi— the mark a die leaves when it stamps a coin. The wilderness was not merely a badpatch of history that happens to be instructive. God shaped those events so that thepattern pressed into them would still be legible centuries later, to people who would neversee a desert. The Old Testament is not raw material we are cleverly applying. It was struckthis way on purpose.

And notice what the stamp says: that we might not desire evil as they did.

Paul reaches past the four sins he is about to list and names the thing underneath them.It was not, first of all, that Israel worshipped a calf or slept with Moabites. It was thatthey craved. The Greek is epithymētas kakōn — cravers ofbad things. The first great collapse in the wilderness was a food riot. They wanted fish,cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions and garlic (Num 11:5) — and they wanted them so badlythat they said out loud they had been better off as slaves. God gave them quail until itcame out of their nostrils, and the place was named the Graves of Craving (Num 11:34).

Here is the test, and it is uncomfortable because it is easy to run. Think back over thelast week and ask: what did I want that I would have been embarrassed to pray for out loud?Not what did I do — what did I want. That is the question this verse isasking, and it is asking it before any sin has been committed, while the whole thing isstill only an appetite in a decent-looking person.

Every sin in the rest of this chapter began there. So did every sin in Corinth. So doesevery sin in the reader (cf. Jas 1:14–15).

A word of caution about how to use this. Saying the Old Testament was typed forus does not license treating every detail as a code to be cracked — the scarlet cord,the number of the pillars, the colours of the curtain. That kind of reading turns Scriptureinto a puzzle and the interpreter into a genius, and it produces sermons that could not havebeen preached by Moses. Paul’s typology is disciplined and it is moral: here is apeople with advantages, here is what they did with them, here is what happened, and you aremade of the same material. The pattern is not hidden. It is the plain sense of the story,pressed on a later generation.

And the reason it presses is not that history repeats itself but that human hearts do.The desert is gone. The craving is not.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be idolaters as some of them were; as it is written, “The people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first of the four wilderness failures, and Paul picks the one everybody knows.Do not be idolaters as some of them were; as it is written, “The people sat downto eat and drink and rose up to play.”

He is quoting Exodus 32:6, the golden calf, and he quotes the line about the meal becausethe Corinthians are arguing about meals. But look closely at what the golden calf actuallywas, because almost everyone gets it wrong. Israel did not decide to swap the LORD for aCanaanite deity. Aaron built the calf and then announced, Tomorrow shall be a feast tothe LORD (Ex 32:5). They kept the name. They kept the God. What they changed was theterms: they would have him visible, manageable, on their own schedule, in a form they hadchosen. That is idolatry, and it is a religious sin, committed in a worship service, bypeople who would have described themselves as devout.

The last verb is worth a moment. Rose up to play is the polite translation of aHebrew word that covers dancing, revelry, and what happens after the dancing. Exodus notesdrily that they had broken loose (Ex 32:25). The pattern is fixed and Paul will repeat it inthe next verse: worship on your own terms first, and the bed follows.

Which is why the modern reader should not relax here. Nobody in the reader’s streetis casting bullocks out of earrings. But an idol, as Keller has put it, is a good thing thathas become an ultimate thing — anything you look to for what only God can give.Here is a way to find yours, and it is quicker than introspection. Finish this sentencehonestly: if I lost ______, life would not be worth living. Whatever fills thatblank is receiving worship. It may be a wholly good thing — a marriage, a child, areputation, a ministry. Good things make the strongest idols, because nobody thinks tosuspect them.

If that test feels too dramatic, here is a duller one that catches more people. An idolis not usually discovered by asking what you believe; it is discovered by looking at wherethe money goes when it is not needed elsewhere, where the free hours go when nobody iswatching, and what you think about in the ten minutes before sleep. A person’stheology is on his lips. His worship is in his diary and his bank statement.

And notice the mercy in the way Paul frames it. He does not tell the Corinthians tomanufacture a stronger devotion to God. He tells them to stop feeding a rival. Nobody hasever loved God more by trying harder to feel it; hearts warm to God when the thing that wasabsorbing the heat is set down. That is why the command in verse 14 will be flee— a thing you can actually do on a Monday — and not feel differently,which you cannot (cf. Ex 32:5; 1 Jn 5:21).

verseByVerse.quote: We must not indulge in sexual immorality as some of them did, and twenty-three thousand fell in a single day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We must not indulge in sexual immorality as some of them did, and twenty-threethousand fell in a single day.

The episode is Numbers 25, at Baal of Peor, and Paul chose it deliberately, because it isthis chapter’s exact problem in Old Testament dress. Read how it starts: the Moabitewomen invited the people to the sacrifices of their gods, and the people ate and boweddown to their gods (Num 25:2). It began with an invitation to dinner. The meal camefirst; the immorality came second; the idolatry was in both. A Corinthian believer acceptinga temple invitation would have said he was only eating. Israel said the same, andtwenty-four thousand of them were buried.

Twenty-four thousand — and there is the difficulty, because Paul writestwenty-three. It is a small thing and it deserves a straight answer rather than a cough,because a thoughtful reader will notice it and wonder whether anyone was going to mentionit.

First, notice that the two texts are not making the same claim. Numbers gives a total forthe whole judgment: those who died by the plague were twenty-four thousand(Num 25:9). Paul adds three words Numbers does not have — in a single day.The plague was not the only killing in that chapter; the chiefs of the people were executedby judicial sentence as well (Num 25:4–5), and the plague itself ran until Phinehasstopped it. A day’s toll inside a larger total is not a contradiction of the total;it is a smaller number inside it, which is what one would expect.

Second, both figures are round. Nobody counted twenty-three thousand nine hundred andeighty-one corpses. Ancient reporting rounds, and rounding to the nearer or the lowerthousand is not error, any more than saying a stadium held forty thousand is a lie becausethe turnstiles read 40,412.

And third, notice what Paul does not do. He does not harmonise. He had the scroll ofNumbers; he could have copied the number and nobody would ever have known. A manmanufacturing a religion smooths his sources. Paul, writing to a hostile and clever churchthat would have loved to catch him out, leaves the rough edge standing. Small discrepancieslike this one are not the crack in Scripture’s credibility; they are the fingerprintson it — evidence of real writers handling real records, rather than a committeetidying after the fact.

What must not be lost in the arithmetic is the warning. Twenty-three thousand peoplewere alive at breakfast and dead by dark, and it started with an invitation they saw noharm in accepting.

verseByVerse.quote: We must not put Christ to the test, as some of them did and were destroyed by serpents,
verseByVerse.commentary:
We must not put Christ to the test, as some of them did and were destroyed byserpents.

Some manuscripts read the Lord here, and a few read God; the ESVfollows the reading with the strongest early support, and it is also the reading no scribewould have invented. A copyist might soften Christ to the Lord becausethe sentence startled him; nobody sharpens the Lord into Christ in anaccount of Israel in the desert. So the startling reading is almost certainly what Paulwrote — and it says the same thing verse 4 said: the one they were provoking inNumbers 21 was the Son of God.

The incident is worth having in front of you. Israel is on a detour around Edom, the roadis long, and they say the thing that people say on long roads: Why have you brought usup out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? For there is no food and no water, and we loathethis worthless food (Num 21:5). The worthless food is the manna. They are complainingabout the miracle. Snakes come into the camp, people die, and the remedy God gives is abronze serpent on a pole: look at it and live. Jesus took that image and applied it tohimself — as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Manbe lifted up (Jn 3:14).

So what is it to put Christ to the test? It is not doubt, and it is not asking hardquestions; God is patient with both. Testing is what you do when you want to find out howfar he can be pushed. It is treating his patience as a margin you are entitled to spend.Israel had watched him split a sea and they were probing to see whether he would reallyfollow through on his threats.

Which gives a test the reader can run on himself, and it is a searching one. Have youever done something while quietly counting on being forgiven for it — the forgivenessfactored in beforehand, part of the calculation, the cross treated as an allowance? That isnot weakness. Weakness falls and is horrified. This is the sin of the confident, which iswhy it is in a chapter written for people who thought their knowledge kept them safe.

It has a second form, quieter and commoner: the demand for one more sign. If Godwould just make this unmistakable, I would obey. Israel had a pillar of fire and askedfor evidence. More proof has never yet produced obedience in anybody, because the problemwas never the quantity of evidence. Jesus met this exact request in the wilderness with theexact answer — You shall not put the Lord your God to the test (Matt 4:7) —and it is striking that where Israel failed the test in the desert, the true Son passed it inone.

Which is the comfort buried in a frightening verse. The Christ these people provoked inNumbers 21 went into a wilderness of his own, hungry and alone, and would not provoke hisFather even once. The obedience the reader has not managed has already been managed, and bythe very person who was being tested in the desert (cf. Num 21:8–9; Jn 3:14).

verseByVerse.quote: nor grumble, as some of them did and were destroyed by the Destroyer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nor grumble, as some of them did and were destroyed by the Destroyer.

Of the four sins, this is the one that looks out of place. Idolatry, immorality, testingGod — and complaining. One of these is not like the others, or so it seems, until younotice that grumbling is the sin that killed more of that generation than any other. It wasgrumbling at the report of the spies that shut the door on the whole nation(Num 14:1–4, 29). It was grumbling behind Korah that opened the ground(Num 16:41–49), and fourteen thousand seven hundred died in the plague that followed.The Destroyer is the destroying angel, the same figure who passed through Egypt onthe night of the Passover — now walking through Israel’s own camp.

Why does God take it so seriously? Because grumbling is never really about the food. Itis a verdict. Every complaint carries an unspoken clause: this arrangement is wrong,and I would have arranged it better. The manna was on the ground that morning. Thecomplaint was not that God had failed to provide; it was that his provision was beneaththem. Grumbling is the sound a heart makes when it has reviewed God’s management andfound it wanting.

It is also the most respectable sin in the list. No church discipline case has ever beenopened over it. A man can grumble his way through forty years of Sundays, about the music,the temperature, the preacher, the roster, the young people, the old people, and be thoughta pillar. Israel grumbled their way to a desert grave and never once thought of themselvesas rebels.

Here is the test, and it takes about a minute. Replay yesterday’s conversations andcount the sentences that were, at bottom, a review of God’s arrangements — theweather, the body, the salary, the family you were given, the church you are in. Then setthat number against the number of sentences that were thanks. The ratio is a fair reading ofwhere the heart is (cf. Phil 2:14–15).

But one distinction has to be made here, or this verse will wound the wrong people. Thereis a world of difference between grumbling and lament. A third of the Psalms are complaints,and some of them are savage: How long, O LORD? Will you forget me for ever?(Ps 13:1). God did not merely tolerate those words; he put them in the hymn book andcommanded his people to sing them. So the difference is not the presence of pain in thesentence, and it is not the volume.

The difference is direction and address. Lament is spoken to God, and it staysin the room with him; it argues, weeps, and will not leave. Grumbling is spokenabout God, to everyone except him. Israel in Numbers 11 did not pray. They stood intheir tent doorways and talked to each other. The tell is simple and it is worth knowing:when something is wrong, who hears about it first? If the answer is God, that is asufferer. If the answer is anyone else, that is a grumbler — and the way out is not tosuppress the complaint but to redirect it, which is what the Psalms are for.

verseByVerse.quote: Now these things happened to them as an example, but they were written down for our instruction, on whom the end of the ages has come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These things happened to them as an example, but they were written down for ourinstruction, on whom the end of the ages has come.

Two claims sit in that sentence, and both are large.

The first is about the Old Testament. It was written down for our instruction.Not merely preserved, not merely available — written with us in view. When Moses setdown the account of the quail, the calf, the serpents and the plague, God intended theparagraph to be read by a Gentile believer in a port city four hundred years later, and bywhoever is reading it now. That settles the question of whether the Old Testament is stillthe Christian’s book. Paul is arguing a live pastoral crisis in a Greek church out ofthe book of Numbers, and he expects it to land (cf. Rom 15:4; 2 Tim 3:16).

The second claim is about where we are standing. On whom the end of the ages hascome — literally, the ends of the ages have arrived at us. The old ageand the age to come are not separated by a tidy line in front of us; they overlap, and weare living in the overlap. The decisive act has happened: the Rock has been struck, thePassover Lamb has been killed, the tomb is empty. And the world is manifestly not yet putright — the wilderness is still a wilderness, the funerals still go out at dusk, andnobody is asked to pretend otherwise.

But this is what makes the warnings weightier rather than lighter. Israel had the shadowand fell. We have the substance. They had a rock in the desert; we have the crucified andrisen Son and his Spirit living in us. Greater light is a greater privilege and a greateraccountability, in that order and always together.

There is a practical consequence for how the Old Testament gets read, and it is worthstating because so many Christians have quietly given up on three-quarters of their Bible.Numbers is not a museum. A reader who works through the wilderness narratives askingwhat does this tell me about people like me, dealing with a God like this isreading it the way an apostle read it. He does not need a technique. He needs to believeverse 11: it was written down for him.

And there is a comfort in the timing. If the ends of the ages have arrived, then nobodyis waiting for the interesting part of history to begin. Whatever the reader’s weeklooks like — and it may look like nothing at all — it is being lived after thedecisive event and before the final one, in the short overlap where the outcome is settledand the fighting is still going on (cf. Heb 9:26; 1 Pet 1:12).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall.

This is the sentence the whole history has been building towards, and it is aimed withprecision. Not at the struggling. Not at the man who knows he is weak and comes to churchfrightened of himself. It is aimed at the one who thinks that he stands — theverb means supposes, presumes, takes it as settled. In Corinth that was the confidentbeliever with the correct doctrine of idols, sitting down to dinner in a temple and quitesure the theology covered him.

Now the question a Reformed reader will feel immediately, and it should be answeredrather than dodged: does this mean a true Christian can finally be lost? If Christ saysno one will snatch them out of my hand (Jn 10:28), why the warning?

The answer is that the warning is not an alternative to being kept. It is one of the waysGod keeps his people. He does not preserve his own by making them immune to danger whilethey sleep through it; he preserves them by waking them up. Paul writes work out yourown salvation with fear and trembling and then, in the same breath, for it is Godwho works in you (Phil 2:12–13). Both halves are true and they are not intension. The alarm that gets a family out of a burning house is not evidence that the firebrigade failed; it is how they were saved. This verse is an alarm, and God has been using itto keep people on their feet for two thousand years.

Which yields a strange and rather comforting test. If this verse frightens you, it isalready doing its work, and you are not the person it is warning. The one in danger is theone who reads it and feels nothing — who assumes at once that it is about somebodyelse in the congregation. The man most likely to fall down the stairs is the one who says hecould walk them in the dark.

So take heed. Not by working up anxiety about your standing, which helps nobody, but bydoing the ordinary things a person does who knows he could fall: stay near the means ofgrace, keep short accounts, tell someone the truth about yourself, and stop rehearsing thesins you have decided you are no longer capable of (cf. 1 Cor 9:27; Rom 11:20).

And be careful of the particular kind of confidence Paul is naming, because it is notusually loud. It rarely says I could never fall. It says smaller things. It saysthat a certain sin is simply not in one’s temperament. It says that a friendship whichwould look questionable in someone else is fine here, because the people involved aremature. It says that a habit which flattened another Christian is manageable in a personwith better theology. Every one of those sentences is the sentence of a man walking a wall inthe dark, telling himself he knows where the edge is.

verseByVerse.quote: No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then, immediately, the promise. Paul has spent twelve verses making a Christianafraid of himself, and he will not leave him there for a single sentence longer.

No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. The word isanthrōpinos — human-sized, the sort of thing human beings get. This isthe first mercy of the verse, and it goes straight to an ache most people carry in private:the conviction that mine is different. That whatever else is common, thisparticular pull, at this particular hour, with this particular history behind it, is afreakish thing that would horrify anyone I told. It is not. It has a name, other people haveit, and some of them are sitting in your row. The loneliness is a lie, and it is the liethat keeps the sin fed, because a thing you believe is unique is a thing you will never sayout loud.

Then the ground of the promise, and notice that it is not you. God is faithful.It is the same phrase that closed the opening thanksgiving of this letter (1:9), and it putsthe weight of the sentence entirely on his character. Check the verb, too, because it is notthe verb people remember: he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability. Thatis not a description of your strength. It is a limit God imposes and polices. He stands atthe gate of every trial that comes at you and decides how much of it gets through.

Two things need saying plainly here, because this verse is misquoted more than almost anyother.

The first is a correction that has brought real relief to crushed people. This verse isabout temptation, not about suffering. The saying it has spawned — God willnever give you more than you can handle — is not in the Bible, and Paul himselfflatly denies it about affliction: we were so utterly burdened beyond our strength thatwe despaired of life itself (2 Cor 1:8). God does give his children more grief thanthey can carry. That is often the point of it, because the next line is to make us relynot on ourselves but on God who raises the dead. So if you are reading this with adiagnosis in your hand or an empty chair at your table, this verse is not telling you thatyour load has been measured to fit your shoulders. It is telling you something about thepull toward sin, which is a different thing.

The second is harder, and it is the objection an honest reader raises at once: ifthere was always a way out, then every time I sinned I could have not sinned — andthat only makes me guiltier. Yes. That is exactly what the verse says, and pretendingotherwise would be no kindness. There was a door. But look at who is standing beside it.The same sentence that removes the excuse names God as faithful, and a God faithful enoughto have built the door is faithful enough to forgive the man who walked past it. The versetakes away the alibi and hands over the Father in the same breath.

And where is the door, in practice? Ekbasis is a way out of a defile — thepass that lets an army get clear of a valley it should never have marched into. It isusually further back than people look for it. Nobody is given a supernatural exit at thelast second; the escape is nearly always upstream. It is the second drink, not the twelfth.It is the reply typed at eleven at night, not the affair eighteen months later. It is thedecision about what the laptop does after everyone else is asleep, not the moment oflooking. Track any fall backwards and you will find the door standing open at a point thatfelt utterly harmless at the time.

So the practical form of this promise is a question to ask while you are still calm: forthe temptation I know is coming this week, where is the pass out of the valley, and whatwould I have to decide today to be standing in it? God has promised the way of escape. Hehas not promised to carry you through a door you refuse to look for.

Note the last clause, too, because it is not the one we would have written: that youmay be able to endure it. Not that you may be able to avoid it. Sometimes the escapeGod provides is a road out, and sometimes it is the strength to stand in the fire withoutbowing. Both are the way of escape. Both come from the same faithful God(cf. Heb 2:18; 2 Pet 2:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–22 — The Lord’s Table and the Demons’ Table
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry” — the same verb used in 6:18 for sexual immorality: not engage, not manage, not negotiate. Flee. The reason Paul now gives is the most theologically serious argument in the three-chapter discussion of idol food. Eating at the Lord’s table is a genuine participation (koinōnia) in the blood and body of Christ. The cup of blessing is not merely a symbol; it is a sharing in Christ’s own death. And eating at a pagan temple feast is not merely a neutral social act: it is a participation in what the sacrifice is offered to — not to the idol (which is nothing) but to the demonic powers behind the idol.

The argument does not depend on the idol having genuine divine existence; it depends on the demonic powers having genuine existence. Paul believes in demons (cf. Eph 6:12; 1 Tim 4:1); he believes that pagan worship, whatever its conscious intent, operates in a sphere of spiritual reality that the strong Corinthians, with their confident monotheism, are underestimating. You cannot share in the Lord’s table and the demons’ table — not because the idol is real but because the demons are real, and fellowship with them is incompatible with fellowship with Christ.

Two features of the section frame it. Paul opens by inviting scrutiny — I speak as to sensible people; judge for yourselves what I say (v. 15) — refusing to settle the matter by apostolic authority alone when he can settle it by argument. And he closes with two questions that he does not answer, because they answer themselves: Shall we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he? (v. 22). God’s jealousy is not the vice of an insecure man but the proper possessiveness of a husband who has paid everything for his bride, and the second question is asked by an apostle who has just filled twelve verses with graves.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord’s Supper as Participation

Paul’s use of koinōnia in vv. 16–17 — the cup of blessing is a koinōnia in the blood of Christ; the bread is a koinōnia in the body of Christ — is the most precise language of eucharistic participation in the NT. It does not specify the mode of Christ’s presence, but it insists on its reality: something genuinely happens in the Supper that is a real sharing in what Christ accomplished. Reformed eucharistic theology (following Calvin rather than Zwingli) has insisted on this real spiritual presence: Christ is truly present in the Supper, giving himself to be received by faith.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Attending a civic dinner at a Corinthian temple was not optional for many members of the social elite; it was part of the patronage network on which their livelihood depended. Paul’s “flee idolatry” would have carried genuine social cost. Now: The situations where Christian participation in cultural or civic life involves implicit participation in what is spiritually incompatible are multiple and not always obvious. Paul’s principle — you cannot share in the Lord’s table and the demons’ table — is the test: what are you actually participating in when you participate in this?

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry. I speak as to sensible people; judge for yourselves what I say.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry.

Take the address first. My beloved — from a man who has just spentthirteen verses on graves in the desert. He is not a prosecutor. He is a father, and thesternness and the tenderness come from the same place; only someone who loves you tells youthe graveyard story.

Then the command, and it is worth noticing everything Paul does not say. Notstudy idolatry. Not manage it. Not develop a mature theology of it, which is precisely whatthe strong Corinthians had done. Flee. The verb is a present imperative —keep on running, make it your standing policy — and it is the same verb he used in6:18 about sexual immorality. Those are the only two things in this letter that Paul tellsthe church to run away from, and it is not an accident that they are the two thatCorinth’s temple culture served up in the same room.

Christians are told to stand and fight almost everywhere else: resist the devil, put onthe armour, endure hardship. Here, no. Here the brave thing and the stupid thing are thesame thing. Joseph did not reason with Potiphar’s wife or explain his convictions; heleft his coat in her hand and got out of the house (Gen 39:12). There is no medal for howlong you stayed in the room.

I speak as to sensible people; judge for yourselves what I say. Having given aflat command, Paul now hands them the argument and invites them to check his working. Thatis a remarkable thing for an apostle to do, and it is a model for anyone who teaches: hedoes not want compliance without conviction. He is about to lay out the reasoning in theverses that follow, and he expects thinking people to follow it and agree.

So what does fleeing look like when the temple is gone? It looks like the boring,unspiritual, entirely practical measures that people are embarrassed to admit they need.Deleting the thing rather than resolving to use it better. Taking the other road home. Notbeing alone in that house. Telling one person the truth so that the secret has a witness.Handing over the card, the password, the key. None of that is glamorous, and all of it worksin a way that resolutions do not, because it removes the opportunity instead of relying onthe will — and the will is exactly the thing that has already proved unreliable.

The objection comes quickly: is that not avoidance rather than victory? Should a matureChristian not be able to stand in the room? But that question has the shape of theCorinthian error, which was to treat strength as something to be demonstrated. Scripturenever asks anyone to prove he can stand beside an idol. The mature response to a fire is notto practise standing in it. Fleeing is the victory; it is simply a victory thatgives nobody a story to tell.

verseByVerse.quote: The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ? Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ?The bread that we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ?

Both are rhetorical questions expecting the answer yes, and Paul needs that yes, becausehis whole argument about temple meals depends on a prior conviction: that eating anddrinking at a table can be a real sharing in what the table represents. If the Lord’sSupper is only a memory exercise, then a temple dinner is only a dinner, and the strongCorinthians are right.

The word he uses is koinōnia — participation, sharing, havingsomething in common with. The English word fellowship has been worn down until itmeans coffee after the service; the Greek word means a genuine joint holding, the waybusiness partners hold a firm. Paul says the cup is a joint holding in the blood of Christ.The cup of blessing is a phrase lifted straight from the Passover table — thethird cup of the meal, the cup over which the blessing was said. That is the cup the Lordtook in his hands in the upper room, on the night the last Passover became the firstSupper.

So what actually happens at the table? It is worth answering carefully, because a readerhas probably heard three answers and been told the differences are enormous.

Some have said the bread and wine become the body and blood, ceasing to be bread andwine. Scripture will not carry that: Paul goes on calling it bread in the very next verse,and the Christ who is present is a risen and ascended Christ who is not brought back downto be re-offered, because the offering was made once for all (Heb 10:12). Others, reacting,have said the Supper is nothing but a memorial — a moving reminder of something absentand long past. But Paul does not say the cup reminds us of the blood of Christ. Hesays it is a participation in it, and a reminder is not a participation.

The older Reformed answer holds both without flinching. The bread stays bread. Christ istruly given and truly received — not down in the elements but by his Spirit, who doesnot drag Christ down to the table so much as lift the believer up to Christ. Calvin wascontent to say he experienced the thing more surely than he could explain it. What thatmeans at the rail is not nothing and not magic: it means that when you eat, you are notperforming a memory. You are receiving, by faith, the Christ who died, and he is givinghimself to you as certainly as the bread is in your hand.

Then verse 17, which is the sentence a divided church needs most. Because there isone bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread. One loaf,torn, and everyone eats from the same torn loaf. That is a hard image to hold whilemaintaining that you are of Paul and he is of Apollos (1:12). The bread on the table is thestanding argument against every faction in the room. You cannot eat from one loaf withsomeone all month and claim to have nothing to do with him.

And under it all, the thing itself. A cup of ordinary wine, in the hands of ordinarypeople, in a rented room in a Greek port — and what is being handed round is the deathof the Son of God, given away as freely as bread at a family meal. He did not hoard it. Hedid not ration it. He took what it cost him to purchase and made it the most common thing onthe table, so that the poorest believer in Corinth could hold it in his hand on a Sundayevening and know it was his (cf. Matt 26:27–28; Jn 6:53–56).

verseByVerse.quote: Consider the people of Israel: are not those who eat the sacrifices participants in the altar? What do I imply then? That food offered to idols is anything, or that an idol is anything?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Consider the people of Israel: are not those who eat the sacrifices participants inthe altar?

Paul is building a case with three tables on it, and this is the second. He has done theLord’s table; now Israel’s; then the demons’. The principle he wantsestablished is that eating from a sacrifice puts you in league with the altar it came from.

The Old Testament practice behind this is the peace offering, and it is worth knowing,because most modern readers assume every sacrifice was burnt whole. It was not. In the peaceoffering, part went up on the fire to God, part went to the priest, and the rest was eatenby the worshipper and his household in a meal on the spot (Lev 7:15–16). It was ashared dinner with God as host. Nobody in Israel thought of it as a snack with religiousdecoration. To eat there was to be counted in.

Then Paul steps in front of an objection before it is raised. What do I imply then?That food offered to idols is anything, or that an idol is anything? He knows exactlywhat the clever ones in Corinth will say: you told us in chapter 8 that an idol has noreal existence and there is no God but one, and now you are treating idol meat as though itwere charged with something.

His answer, coming in the next verse, is not a retreat. He is not about to concede thatthe idol is real after all. He is about to say that the Corinthians drew the wrongconclusion from a true premise — and the gap between those two things is where a greatdeal of confident Christian foolishness lives.

It is worth pausing on that gap, because it is the intellectual habit this whole letteris correcting. A true statement is not a finished argument. An idol is nothing istrue. Therefore I may eat in its temple does not follow, and no amount ofinsisting on the first sentence will make it follow. The Corinthians had learned to reasonfrom a doctrine straight to a permission, without ever asking what else was true in the room.That is not knowledge; it is one piece of knowledge used as a lever.

And notice the tenderness of the word consider. Paul does not scold. He asksthem to look at something they already know from the Scriptures and draw the obviousconclusion themselves. He is treating them, as he said in verse 15, like sensible people— even while telling them their sense has failed them.

verseByVerse.quote: No, I imply that what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God. I do not want you to be participants with demons. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No, I imply that what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God. I do notwant you to be participants with demons.

Here is the correction, and it is precise. The strong Corinthians reasoned: the idol isnothing, therefore there is nothing at the altar, therefore the meal is empty of spiritualcontent. Every step of that but the last is right. Nothing at the altar is not the same asnobody at the altar. The statue is a block of stone with no more divinity in it than thequarry it came from — and something is nevertheless being transacted, becausesomebody is receiving what is offered, and it is not God.

Paul is not inventing this. He is quoting the same song of Moses he drew on in verse 4:They sacrificed to demons that were no gods, to gods they had never known(Deut 32:17). The Old Testament had already said both halves — no gods, and demons— and held them together without embarrassment.

Which raises the question a modern reader will have, and it should not be left hanging:is any of this still live? The temples are museums now. But the impulse to reach past Godfor power or knowledge on terms he has not authorised has never gone out of fashion, and itis currently doing extremely well. The card reading booked as a laugh, the app that givesthe daily horoscope, the ancestor shrine kept in the corner because the family expects it,the ceremony entered into on holiday because it seemed rude to decline. In every case thereasoning is the Corinthian reasoning: it is nonsense, so it is harmless. Paul’sanswer is that the first clause does not deliver the second.

This is not a call to see a devil behind every hedge; that is a different error and itmakes for a frightened, superstitious Christian who has forgotten that Christ has alreadydisarmed the powers and made a public spectacle of them (Col 2:15). It is a call to stopbeing naive.

Then comes the sharpest pair of sentences in the chapter. You cannot drink the cup ofthe Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table ofdemons. Notice: not may not. Cannot. Paul is not laying down a rulethat could in principle be broken discreetly. He is describing an impossibility, the way aman cannot be married to two women in one house and call it a marriage. The attempt does notproduce a double portion. It produces the loss of the first.

verseByVerse.quote: Shall we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shall we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?

Two short questions, and Paul asks them and walks away without answering, which is howyou ask a question that has already answered itself.

The first is another line from the song of Moses, and from the same paragraph:They stirred him to jealousy with strange gods (Deut 32:16, 21). It needsexplaining, because jealousy is a word we now use only for a vice, and applying itto God sounds like an accusation. But there are two jealousies. One is envy — wantingwhat belongs to somebody else. That is never in God, and never can be, since everything isalready his. The other is the jealousy of a husband for his own wife, and it is not a defectin him but the proof that the marriage is real. A man who watched his wife leave withanother man and felt nothing at all would not be admirably calm; he would have stoppedloving her some time ago. God’s jealousy is of that second kind. He has bound himselfto a people at the cost of his Son’s life, and he will not be treated as one optionamong several.

The second question is flatter and more frightening. Are we stronger than he?Paul has just filled twelve verses with corpses in the wilderness, so the reader knows whatthe question is doing. It asks a congregation of the confident whether they have thoughtabout who it is they are provoking. There is a way of using Christian freedom that is notreally freedom at all but a small experiment in whether God will actually do anything.

And there is a good and warm way to hear this too. The God who is jealous over you is notindifferent to you. To be loved by someone who will not share you is a fearful thing and asafe thing at once. Cold gods let you drift. This one comes after his own (cf. Ex 34:14;Jas 4:5).

Test it against the alternative. Suppose God were not jealous. Suppose he watched hispeople give their evenings, their money and their affections to whatever caught them, andfelt nothing about it at all — benign, unbothered, endlessly accommodating. That Godwould be easier to live with, and he would be worth nothing, because his tolerance would bethe measure of his indifference. Nobody has ever been comforted at a graveside by a deitywho did not much mind.

So the two questions of this verse turn out to be one question asked twice. Is hestrong? Yes — look at the wilderness. Does he care? Yes — look at the jealousy.A god who was strong and did not care would be a terror. A god who cared and was not strongwould be a tragedy. Israel had neither, and neither has anyone since.

He is jealous because the cost of getting his people was his own Son, and a man does notshrug about what he has bled for.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–33 — Do All to the Glory of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chapter closes with a nuanced set of practical guidelines for the specific situations the Corinthians face: buying meat in the market (eat freely, ask no questions), dining at a non-believer’s house (eat what is served, ask no questions), being told the food was offered to idols (don’t eat, for the sake of the one who told you). The practical wisdom is shaped by two principles: freedom from unnecessary scruples in ordinary life, and sensitivity to conscience — both the weak person’s conscience and the unbeliever’s perception.

The governing positive principle — “do all to the glory of God” (v. 31) — is the comprehensive positive statement of Christian ethics that underlies everything in chapters 8–10. It applies to eating and drinking; it applies to everything else. Every ordinary act of human life is capable of being an act of glorification when performed in dependence on God, in gratitude for his gifts, and in awareness of his presence. This is the Reformed vision of the sanctified life: not the withdrawal from ordinary life into monasticism but the consecration of ordinary life to the glory of God.

The section is often quoted for its high point and stopped there, but two stretches at either end of it do essential work. In vv. 29–30 Paul guards the freedom he has just declined to use: he gives up the exercise of his liberty for his neighbour’s sake, and refuses to hand over the liberty itself, which protects the church from being governed by whoever is most easily offended. And in vv. 32–33 he names the three groups — Jews, Greeks, the church of God — and states his own motive without disguise: not seeking my own advantage, but that of many, that they may be saved. That clause is what distinguishes his accommodation from the man-pleasing he condemns in Galatians 1:10. The question is never whether one is accommodating people, but who the accommodation is for.
verseByVerse.theology:
Soli Deo Gloria Applied to Ordinary Life

The Reformation’s fifth great watchword — soli Deo gloria, to God alone be glory — finds its Pauline root in v. 31. Every meal, every conversation, every commercial transaction, every athletic effort is capable of being an act of worship when performed in the right spirit and with the right orientation. Calvin’s “all of life is worship” is the systematic development of this verse. The “sacred/secular divide” is not merely unhelpful; by Paul’s logic it is theologically incoherent: all of life, including the most mundane, is lived before the face of God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The practical guidelines of vv. 25–28 gave the Corinthians actionable wisdom for the specific daily situations they faced. The principle of “ask no questions” at the market protected them from unnecessary scrupulosity; the principle of sensitivity at the dinner table protected the weak and the unbeliever. Both together are shaped by the glory of God, not by personal preference. Now: “Do all to the glory of God” is not a cliché but a practice — a habit of asking, in any situation: how can this moment, this act, this conversation, be a participation in the glorification of God?

verseByVerse.quote: “All things are lawful,” but not all things are helpful. “All things are lawful,” but not all things build up. Let no one seek his own good, but the good of his neighbor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“All things are lawful,” but not all things are helpful. “Allthings are lawful,” but not all things build up.

The slogan is back. It was quoted first at 6:12, and it is almost certainly theCorinthians’ own line — the sort of thing a church says when it has learnedgrace and is enjoying it. Paul does not delete it. He puts a comma after it. Twice.

The two tests he attaches are not is it permitted but something else entirely.Is it helpful — does it get anyone anywhere? And does it build up— a construction word, the same root as edification; does anyone end up strongerbecause you did it? Notice that both questions have someone else in them. The lawfulnessquestion can be answered alone in a room. These cannot.

Then the sentence that governs everything from chapter 8 to chapter 11, and it is ninewords long: Let no one seek his own good, but the good of his neighbor. That is thewhole ethic of the idol-meat discussion boiled down, and it is more radical than the wayChristians usually apply it. The usual version is: enjoy your freedom, but be considerate.Paul’s version puts the neighbour’s good in the driving seat, not the passengerseat.

Here is the test, and it works on any decision. Take the last time you defended somethingyou were free to do. Play back the argument you made in your head. Whose flourishing wasactually in view — his, or yours? Being right about your liberty and wrong about yourneighbour is the exact position Paul has been dismantling for three chapters, and it ispossible to hold it while quoting this very verse’s first half (cf. Rom 15:1–2;Phil 2:4).

It is worth being clear about what Paul is not doing, because this verse is sometimesread as a general demand that Christians never consider themselves at all, which is neitherpossible nor commanded. Paul has just spent a chapter telling the Corinthians to look aftertheir own souls with great care — take heed lest you fall, flee idolatry, watch whatyou are participating in. Self-neglect is not the goal. What is forbidden is making your owngood the deciding factor when someone else’s good is also on the table.

And note the word build up. Paul could have said not all things are safeor not all things are wise. He chose a builder’s word, and he uses it allthrough this letter. The picture is of a congregation as a structure going up, course bycourse, where the question about any action is not merely whether it damages anyone butwhether it adds a stone. A great deal of Christian liberty is defended on the grounds thatit hurts no one. That is a lower bar than the one in this verse.

verseByVerse.quote: Eat whatever is sold in the meat market without raising any question on the ground of conscience. For “the earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eat whatever is sold in the meat market without raising any question on the ground ofconscience.

After all that solemnity, a surprisingly relaxed instruction — and it is deliberate,because Paul is as concerned to protect the over-scrupulous as the over-confident.

The word is makellon, the covered market; excavators at Corinth have turned up aninscription naming one. Much of the meat on those slabs had come from a temple, sincesacrifices produced more carcasses than the priests could eat and the surplus was sold on.A conscientious believer could therefore spend his whole life anxious about his dinner,interrogating butchers, tracing provenance, going hungry on principle. Paul’s rulingis: do not ask. Not ask, and then decide. Do not ask.

And he gives the reason from a psalm: the earth is the Lord’s, and the fullnessthereof (Ps 24:1). This is the answer to a fear that runs deeper than meat. The idoldoes not get to change the ownership of a cow. A false priest can mutter over a carcass allafternoon and he has not transferred the title; the beast belonged to God when it was born,belonged to God on the altar, and belongs to God on the slab. Nothing in the world has beensuccessfully stolen from its Maker.

That is worth a great deal to the anxious reader, who is more common in the church thanthe arrogant one. It is the reader who wonders about the yoga class, the label on thepackage, the greeting the neighbour used, the second-hand furniture, the doorway that feltwrong. Paul’s rule for ordinary life is freedom without an investigation. Creation isGod’s and it is good, and a Christian may eat it with thanks and stop performingbackground checks on his groceries.

One guard is needed, though, or this freedom will be stretched into something Paul hasjust forbidden. Verses 20 and 21 stand ten lines above this one. There is a differencebetween eating a piece of meat with a history and taking a seat at a rite — betweenbuying a chop that once passed an altar and going to the altar. The first is a questionabout property, and God owns everything. The second is a question about allegiance, and noone may hold two. Paul is not inconsistent; he is drawing a line, and the line falls exactlywhere participation begins.

There is also a quiet pastoral kindness in the instruction do not ask. Paulcould have told them to investigate carefully and then decide with a clear conscience. Heknows that for a certain sort of person the investigation never ends, and that a consciencekept permanently on duty does not become holier, only more exhausted. Sometimes the godlycourse is to close the question rather than to research it, and to eat the dinner in frontof you with thanks.

The world is not haunted. It is owned.

verseByVerse.quote: If one of the unbelievers invites you to dinner and you are disposed to go, eat whatever is set before you without raising any question on the ground of conscience. But if someone says to you, “This has been offered in sacrifice,” then do not eat it, for the sake of the one who informed you, and for the sake of conscience—
verseByVerse.commentary:
If one of the unbelievers invites you to dinner and you are disposed to go, eatwhatever is set before you without raising any question on the ground of conscience.

Note first what Paul assumes without arguing for it: that Christians will be havingdinner in the homes of people who are not Christians, and that they may accept. There is nowarning attached, no list of precautions. The apostle who has just said flee fromidolatry sees no contradiction in a believer sitting down at a pagan neighbour’stable. Fleeing idolatry is not the same as avoiding idolaters — he has already said soin this letter, and bluntly: to avoid them entirely you would need to leave the world(5:10).

You are disposed to go leaves the decision genuinely open. Some invitations arenot wise for a given believer at a given time, and Paul does not pretend otherwise. But thedefault is yes, and the manners at the table are simple: eat what you are given and asknothing. A guest who cross-examines his host about the origin of the lamb is not being holy;he is being a poor guest, and the gospel is not served by it.

Then the one situation that changes everything. But if someone says to you,“This has been offered in sacrifice,” then do not eat it, for the sake of the onewho informed you.

Nothing about the meat has changed. The information has. Once somebody has put it intowords, the meal has stopped being a meal and become a statement, and it will be read as one.Perhaps the speaker is a young believer watching to see what freedom looks like. Perhaps heis a pagan guest who has heard that these people worship one God and is curious whether itmakes any practical difference.
