Either way, a person has just told you that this matters tohim, and Paul’s instruction is to let it matter. Put the fork down. Say nothingpious.

Which is a useful principle well beyond first-century meat: the moment someone signalsthat a thing is loaded for him, your liberty stops being the only fact in the room.

Two small things about how to do it. First, do it quietly. Paul gives no speech toaccompany the refusal, and adding one would wreck it — a Christian who declines thedish and then explains at length why he is entitled to eat it but is graciously abstaininghas kept the meat and taken the credit as well. Second, do not shame the host. The wholemanoeuvre is for the sake of someone else’s conscience, and a refusal delivered as averdict on the household undoes the very thing it was meant to protect.

Underneath the etiquette is something larger. Paul is willing to be misunderstood— to look scrupulous to the free and lax to the strict — rather than harden oneperson’s conscience against Christ. He has already said he would never eat meat againif it came to that (8:13). Here he shows what it costs on an ordinary Thursday evening: nota heroic renunciation, just a hand withdrawn from a plate while nobody notices.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not mean your conscience, but his. For why should my liberty be determined by someone else’s conscience? If I partake with thankfulness, why am I denounced because of that for which I give thanks?
verseByVerse.commentary:
I do not mean your conscience, but his. For why should my liberty be determined bysomeone else’s conscience? If I partake with thankfulness, why am I denounced becauseof that for which I give thanks?

This is the hardest turn in the chapter, and it looks at first like Paul contradictinghimself inside a single sentence. He has just said do not eat, and now he asks whyanybody else’s conscience should govern him.

The resolution is in the distinction he has already drawn. What he surrenders in verse 28is the use of his freedom on that occasion. What he refuses to surrender here is thefreedom itself, and the verdict on it. His conscience is not remade by his neighbour’s.He does not walk away from that dinner thinking he was nearly defiled, or that the meat wasin fact unclean after all. He walks away free, having chosen not to spend his freedom infront of someone it would injure.

The difference matters more than it may appear, because getting it wrong produces twoopposite disasters. Collapse the distinction one way and you get the Christian who bulldozes— my liberty is real, therefore I will exercise it, and if that ruins you, learn sometheology. Collapse it the other way and you get a church governed by whoever is most easilyupset, where every scruple anyone raises becomes binding on everybody, and the strongestconscience in the room is the narrowest one. Paul will not have either. Love limits what Ido with my freedom. It does not hand my conscience over to a committee.

And there is a small warmth in if I partake with thankfulness. Paul’sinstinct at a table is to give thanks, which is what a man does who believes verse 26 —that the food, the evening and the world belong to God. He is not defending a right toindulge. He is defending a right to be grateful without apologising for it(cf. Rom 14:22; 1 Tim 4:4–5).

This gives the anxious reader a rule he can live by, and it is a relief. When you givesomething up for the sake of another Christian, you are not conceding that he was right andyou were wrong. You are not adding a rule to your own life. You are not obliged to feelguilty about the thing next Tuesday when he is not there. Paul abstains and remains free,and he tells the church he is doing both. Charity is not the same as agreement, and givingway is not the same as being convinced.

The alternative — a conscience that quietly takes on every restriction anybodyaround it holds — ends in a Christian who cannot enjoy anything and cannot say why, andwho is finally serving other people’s opinions rather than God. Paul’s way isharder and cleaner: know that you are free, and then choose, in this room, on this evening,for this person, not to use it.

verseByVerse.quote: So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.

Three chapters of hard argument about butchers, dinner parties, weak brothers and demonscome down to one sentence, and it is broad enough to cover a life.

Notice where Paul starts: eat or drink. He could have begun with prayer orpreaching. He begins with chewing and swallowing — the most involuntary, animal, whollyunremarkable thing a body does — and says that this too can be done to the glory ofGod. If eating qualifies, nothing is excluded. The line between the sacred bits of life andthe ordinary bits, which most Christians carry around without examining it, does not survivethis verse. There is no part of a Tuesday that is off the map.

But to the glory of God is exactly the sort of phrase that can be repeated foryears without meaning anything, so let it be spelled out. What has to be true of a plate offood for it to glorify God?

That it is received rather than seized — taken as a gift from a hand, not a rightthat was owed. That it is eaten with thanks, spoken and meant, since everything createdby God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving(1 Tim 4:4). That it is enjoyed and not worshipped — there is a way of eating that isreally an attempt to be comforted by something that cannot comfort. That it is not taken atsomeone else’s expense, which is the whole burden of this chapter. And that the oneeating is content for God to be looking, which is a test that can be run on any activity inabout four seconds.

Here is the practical form of it. Take the last hour of yesterday, whatever it contained— a meal, a screen, a task, a conversation, a queue. Ask what would have had to changefor that hour to have been offered to God. Very often the honest answer is: nothing at allabout the activity, and everything about the aim. That is not a loophole. That is the mercyof this verse. The Christian does not need a different life in order to have a life full ofworship; he needs the one he has, turned in a different direction.

Which is finally why God gets glory from a man eating his dinner. Not because the dinneris impressive, but because the God who made the wheat and the fire and the mouth is beingrecognised at the moment his gifts are being used, by a creature who might have eaten insilence and thought himself self-supplied. Every honest thank-you at a kitchen table is asmall correction of the world’s largest lie.

verseByVerse.quote: Give no offense to Jews or to Greeks or to the church of God, just as I try to please everyone in everything I do, not seeking my own advantage, but that of many, that they may be saved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give no offense to Jews or to Greeks or to the church of God, just as I try to pleaseeveryone in everything I do, not seeking my own advantage, but that of many, that they maybe saved.

Paul names three groups and covers the whole world with them: the Jew, the Gentile, andthe church. He has already shown what each looks like in practice — he circumcisedTimothy for the sake of the first, ate freely for the sake of the second, and would give upmeat for ever for the sake of the third (8:13).

But the last clause raises a genuine problem, and a reader who knows his Bible will spotit at once. Here Paul says I try to please everyone in everything I do. To theGalatians he wrote: if I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant ofChrist (Gal 1:10). Those cannot both be advice, so which is it?

They are the same principle applied to opposite motives, and the tell is in what eachsentence says the pleasing is for. In Galatians, the pleasing was a way of buyingsafety: certain men wanted to avoid persecution over the cross, so they trimmed the messageand kept their position. The object of that exercise was themselves. Here, the object isstated outright: not seeking my own advantage, but that of many, that they may besaved. Paul yields his preferences, his diet, his rights and his dignity to removeevery obstacle between a person and Christ — and he will not yield one syllable of thegospel to remove an obstacle between himself and trouble.

So the test is not am I accommodating people? It is who is thisaccommodation actually for? And it is easy to run. The next time you soften something,delay something, or leave something unsaid, ask which of these is more likely to be true atthe end of it: that the other person is nearer to being saved, or that you are nearer tobeing comfortable. The first is apostolic. The second is what Galatians calls the end ofbeing a servant of Christ. They can look identical from the outside and they are oppositesinside.

Behind both stands the pattern neither Corinth nor anyone since has improved on. The Sonof God had every right and used none of them for himself; the one Person in history who wasgenuinely free spent his freedom entirely on the unfree, and was not even given a bed to diein. He did not seek his own advantage. He sought many, that they might be saved — andhe got them (cf. Rom 15:3; Phil 2:6–8).

10.text: <sup>1</sup>For I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea,<sup>2</sup>and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea,<sup>3</sup>and all ate the same spiritual food,<sup>4</sup>and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ.<sup>5</sup>Nevertheless, with most of them God was not pleased, for they were overthrown in the wilderness.<sup>6</sup>Now these things took place as examples for us, that we might not desire evil as they did.<sup>7</sup>Do not be idolaters as some of them were; as it is written, “The people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play.”<sup>8</sup>We must not indulge in sexual immorality as some of them did, and twenty-three thousand fell in a single day.<sup>9</sup>We must not put Christ to the test, as some of them did and were destroyed by serpents,<sup>10</sup>nor grumble, as some of them did and were destroyed by the Destroyer.<sup>11</sup>Now these things happened to them as an example, but they were written down for our instruction, on whom the end of the ages has come.<sup>12</sup>Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall.<sup>13</sup>No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.<sup>14</sup>Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry.<sup>15</sup>I speak as to sensible people; judge for yourselves what I say.<sup>16</sup>The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ?<sup>17</sup>Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread.<sup>18</sup>Consider the people of Israel: are not those who eat the sacrifices participants in the altar?<sup>19</sup>What do I imply then? That food offered to idols is anything, or that an idol is anything?<sup>20</sup>No, I imply that what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God. I do not want you to be participants with demons.<sup>21</sup>You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons.<sup>22</sup>Shall we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?<sup>23</sup>“All things are lawful,” but not all things are helpful. “All things are lawful,” but not all things build up.<sup>24</sup>Let no one seek his own good, but the good of his neighbor.<sup>25</sup>Eat whatever is sold in the meat market without raising any question on the ground of conscience.<sup>26</sup>For “the earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof.”<sup>27</sup>If one of the unbelievers invites you to dinner and you are disposed to go, eat whatever is set before you without raising any question on the ground of conscience.<sup>28</sup>But if someone says to you, “This has been offered in sacrifice,” then do not eat it, for the sake of the one who informed you, and for the sake of conscience—<sup>29</sup>I do not mean your conscience, but his. For why should my liberty be determined by someone else’s conscience?<sup>30</sup>If I partake with thankfulness, why am I denounced because of that for which I give thanks?<sup>31</sup>So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.<sup>32</sup>Give no offense to Jews or to Greeks or to the church of God,<sup>33</sup>just as I try to please everyone in everything I do, not seeking my own advantage, but that of many, that they may be saved.

11.title: Head Coverings and the Lord’s Supper
11.overview:
Chapter 11 addresses two worship practices at Corinth, both of which reveal something about the community’s understanding of order, dignity, and the meaning of the gospel. The head covering discussion (vv. 2–16) is one of the most culturally complex passages in the NT, rooted in first-century practices of gender expression in public worship that do not translate directly into any modern context. The Lord’s Supper passage (vv. 17–34) is one of the most urgently pastoral: the Corinthians have turned the church’s central act of communion into an occasion for social humiliation, and Paul responds with the most solemn institution narrative in the NT.

The link between the two sections is the concept of order in worship — an order that reflects the character of the God being worshipped and the relationships that his gospel creates. Both the head covering practice and the Lord’s Supper abuse are symptoms of the same Corinthian disorder: the failure to take seriously the social and theological implications of what it means to worship the God who became a servant and who died for the poor.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul opens with a remarkable verse that has been separated from what follows by modern chapter divisions: “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ.” This is the hermeneutical key to the head covering discussion. The imitation Paul calls for is the imitation of the pattern of Christ — who, as the Son, submitted to the Father; who, as the Lord, humbled himself for the church; who, in his very personhood, is the image of God. The theological structure Paul draws on in vv. 3–12 is an ordered sequence of relationships: God is the head of Christ; Christ is the head of the man; man is the head of the woman. This is not a hierarchy of value or dignity (v. 11 insists on mutual dependence) but a structural ordering within relationships of genuine equality.

The specific practice Paul discusses — women covering their heads in worship, men not covering theirs — was a culturally specific expression of this theological reality in the first-century Greco-Roman context. The exegetical difficulties are genuine and should be acknowledged: the passage is among the most debated in Pauline studies. What is not debatable is the theological structure underlying the practice: the differentiation of men and women in worship is meant to reflect and honour the theological ordering Paul describes, not to express inferiority, but precisely the opposite — the glory that each sex reflects in its appropriate expression.

Three further parts of the passage carry weight and are easily skipped. Verse 2 opens with commendation — they had held the traditions handed to them — which is why correction was possible at all. Verse 10 gives the reason that has puzzled readers most, because of the angels; whatever else it means, it means a worshipping congregation is never the only company in the room. And verse 16 closes the subject by refusing to let it become a fight: if anyone is inclined to be contentious, we have no such practice, nor do the churches of God.

That last verse governs how a Christian may hold whatever conclusion he reaches. Where the covering is still a legible sign, it should be worn without apology and without scorn from anyone; where it signifies nothing, the principle must take a form the congregation can actually read. What may not be done, on Paul’s own authority, is to make a party of it.
verseByVerse.theology:
Headship, Order, and the Trinity

Paul’s grounding of the male-female relationship in the Father-Son relationship (v. 3) is one of the most important and most debated texts in trinitarian theology. If “the head of Christ is God” describes an eternal subordination within the Godhead, it supports a permanent hierarchical ordering of human relationships. Most Reformed theologians have understood this as describing the economic Trinity (the Son’s voluntary submission in the incarnation and redemption) rather than ontological subordination within the immanent Trinity. Either way, Paul is using the divine relational order as the theological model for the ordering of human relationships in worship.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The specific head covering practice was an expression of propriety and social order in a particular cultural context. A woman praying with her head uncovered may have signalled sexual availability or a rejection of the social ordering that the community needed to maintain for the sake of its witness. Now: The head covering practice is not directly applicable in most modern Western contexts. The underlying principle — that worship should reflect an ordered dignity appropriate to the God being worshipped, and that the differentiation of male and female is a gift to be honoured rather than erased — continues to speak into contemporary debates about gender in the church.

verseByVerse.quote: Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter division falls in the wrong place. This sentence is the last word of theargument that began at 8:1, and it is also the door into everything that follows.

Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ. Read on its own it sounds like the mostarrogant sentence in the letter. No pastor could say it today without causing a scandal. Butlook at what Paul has just finished describing, because that is what he is offering to havecopied: a man who gave up his right to be paid (9:12), his right to marry (9:5), his right toeat what he liked (8:13), and his right to be understood, so that people who were not hisresponsibility might be saved. He is not saying admire me. He is sayingwatch what I gave up, and do that.

And the second clause governs the first. As I am of Christ. Paul is not theoriginal; he is a copy being held up, and he is careful to say so. The pattern is the Son ofGod, who had every right there is and used none of them for himself. Paul is one step nearerin the chain, close enough to be seen.

That matters more than it may seem, because it says something about how Christianobedience is actually learned. Nobody learns to be a Christian from a definition. Peoplelearn it the way they learn a trade or an accent — by being near someone who does it,long enough to catch it. Which is why Paul can write a letter and then say, in effect: nowlook at a life. And it is why the most important thing an older believer can offer a youngerone is not advice but a visible life at close range.

It also sets the terms for the two difficult passages that follow. Paul is about to talkabout how men and women should appear in worship, and about a supper where the rich werehumiliating the poor. Both are questions about whether a congregation will lay down itsrights for the sake of others in the room. He has put the answer at the top of the pagebefore asking the questions (cf. Phil 3:17; 1 Thess 1:6).

An objection is worth meeting, because it is a good one. Is it not dangerous to tell peopleto follow a man? The history of the church is littered with the wreckage of ministries builton a personality, and this very congregation had already split into fan clubs — I am ofPaul, I am of Apollos (1:12). Paul knew that better than anyone; he had spent four chaptersdemolishing it.

The safeguard is in the second half of the sentence, and it is a safeguard anyone canapply. Follow a Christian only as far as he is following Christ, and no further — whichmeans you must know Christ well enough to see where the line falls. That is the differencebetween a disciple and a follower. A follower goes wherever his man goes. A disciple watcheshis man and keeps checking the pattern against the Master, and is ready to stop the momentthe two diverge.

Which also tells a Christian what to look for when choosing whom to learn from. Not themost gifted person available, and not the most confident. Look for the one whose life showsthe marks Paul has just described: rights not used, comfort spent on other people, awillingness to be thought less of. Gifts are impressive and they can be counterfeited. Thatpattern cannot.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I commend you because you remember me in everything and maintain the traditions even as I delivered them to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now I commend you because you remember me in everything and maintain the traditionseven as I delivered them to you.

Praise first. It is worth noticing, because this letter has not been generous with praiseand is about to become severe again in fifteen verses. Paul begins the correction by namingsomething true and good: they had held on to what he taught them. Whatever else was wrong inCorinth — and the list is long — they had not thrown out the deposit.

The word traditions makes some Christians uneasy, because it has been used tosmuggle in doctrines the Bible does not teach. But the word itself is innocent and Paul ownsit without embarrassment. Paradosis means something handed over — a parcelpassed from one pair of hands to the next. He uses the same verbs in verse 23 about theLord’s Supper: I received and I delivered. What is being handed onhere is not a set of customs invented by the church but a deposit that came from Christthrough the apostles. That is the difference that matters. A tradition is trustworthywhen you can trace the parcel back to a hand that had the right to fill it.

And there is a real compliment buried in the sentence: you remember me ineverything. This congregation, for all its arrogance, still cared what its founderthought. Nothing in the following chapters would be possible without that. A church that hasstopped listening cannot be corrected; it can only be left. Paul writes fourteen more chaptersbecause he believes these people will still hear him.

Which is a fair question to put to any congregation and any Christian. Correction onlyworks on people who are still in the room. The most dangerous position is not being wrong— the Corinthians were wrong about almost everything — but reaching the pointwhere nobody is permitted to say so.

There is also a rule here for the vexed question of what to do when a church tradition andthe Bible pull in different directions. Paul’s own test is simply whether the parcelcame from the Lord: I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you (v. 23).Where a practice can be traced to that source it is binding, however inconvenient. Where itcannot, it may be genuinely valuable — the church’s accumulated wisdom is notnothing — but it can never be made a test of obedience. Most congregational quarrelsabout how things are done would end within ten minutes if the parties agreed to sort theirpractices into those two boxes first.

And there is a debt in the verse worth pausing on. Everything the Corinthians had, theyhad been handed. So has every Christian since. Nobody in the history of the world has workedout the gospel from first principles; it reached each of us through somebody — amother, a preacher, a friend who would not let the subject drop, a translator who died forthe privilege. That is what a tradition is when it is healthy: not a dead weight but a chainof hands, and the only question that matters is whether you intend to be one of them.

verseByVerse.quote: But I want you to understand that the head of every man is Christ, the head of a wife is her husband, and the head of Christ is God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I want you to understand that the head of every man is Christ, the head of a wifeis her husband, and the head of Christ is God.

Before any of the difficult application, Paul lays down the framework, and it needshandling slowly because a great deal is loaded onto the word head.

The Greek is kephalē. In English, head has largely collapsed intoone meaning: the boss. In Greek it carried more than that. It could mean the source ofsomething, the way we still speak of the head of a river; it could mean the one who leads orrepresents; and in a body it is the part without which the rest cannot live. Paul is almostcertainly using it with both of the first two senses alive at once, and the sequence hegives shows why. The head of Christ is God — the Son is eternallyfrom the Father, and in his mission he did the Father’s will and not his own.Both source and ordering, in one relationship, with no hint of a lesser being.

That last point is where everything turns, so it must be said plainly. Whatever this versemeans, it cannot mean that a head is superior in worth to what it heads, because the thirdclause would then make Christ inferior to God — and the New Testament will not allowit. The Son is the exact imprint of his nature (Heb 1:3), in whom the wholefullness of deity dwells bodily (Col 2:9). If the head of Christ is God canstand alongside I and the Father are one (Jn 10:30), then headship and equality arenot rivals. Paul has picked the one relationship in the universe where perfect equality andwilling order are both beyond dispute, and he has made it the model.

Christians differ over how far this reaches into the eternal life of God. Most Reformedtheologians have been careful here: the Son’s submission is real, and it belongs tohis mission — the sending, the incarnation, the obedience unto death — ratherthan being a subordination of nature within the Godhead, since the Father and the Son shareone undivided divine essence. Others have argued for an eternal ordering of persons. It isa discussion worth conducting with great care and very little heat.

What the ordinary reader should take from the verse is this, and it is enough to be goingon with. Order is not the enemy of equality; it is the shape love takes when two equals aredoing something together. The Son’s submission cost him everything and diminished himin nothing. It was not the loss of his dignity. It was the display of it (cf. Jn 5:19;Phil 2:6–8).

verseByVerse.quote: Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head, but every wife who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head, since it is the same as if her head were shaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head, but everywife who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head, since it is the sameas if her head were shaven.

Two things are established in this sentence, and the first is easily missed because it isassumed rather than argued.

Women are praying and prophesying in the Corinthian assembly, out loud, and Paul does notobject. He objects to how they are dressed while doing it. That is a striking thing to findin a letter often thought to silence women, and it needs to be held onto: the apostle’scorrection here presupposes their audible participation and corrects only its manner.

Which raises immediately the hardest question in the chapter, and it should be answeredhere rather than left to ambush the reader three chapters on. In 14:34 Paul writes thatthe women should keep silent in the churches. How can the same letter assume theyspeak in chapter 11 and forbid them to speak in chapter 14?

Paul was not a fool and the letter was read aloud in one sitting; whatever he meant, hedid not think he was contradicting himself three chapters later. The resolution lies innoticing what kind of speech chapter 14 is actually discussing. That passage sits inside aparagraph about prophecy being weighed by the congregation — let the othersweigh what is said (14:29) — and it ends by telling the women to ask theirquestions at home (14:35). It is regulating a particular activity in a particular part of themeeting: the public sifting and cross-examination of prophecies, an exercise of governingjudgment over the congregation’s teaching. That is a different thing from praying andprophesying, which chapter 11 takes for granted that women do.

So the two passages are addressing two activities, not one, and the seeming contradictioncomes from reading silent as absolute when Paul has already shown, in this veryverse, that he does not mean it absolutely. This will be taken up again where it is written,at 14:34.

The second thing established here is that appearance in worship carries meaning. Paulassumes that what a person wears on his or her head in the assembly says something —and that saying the wrong thing brings dishonour. That assumption is the hinge of the wholepassage, and it is the part most likely to be dismissed today as fussiness about hats. It isnot fussiness. Every culture has clothing that speaks, which is why nobody wears a swimmingcostume to a funeral. Paul is not inventing the fact that garments talk. He is asking whatthese particular garments were saying in that room.

verseByVerse.quote: For if a wife will not cover her head, then she should cut her hair short. But since it is disgraceful for a wife to cut off her hair or shave her head, let her cover her head. For a man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God, but woman is the glory of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if a wife will not cover her head, then she should cut her hair short. But sinceit is disgraceful for a wife to cut off her hair or shave her head, let her cover herhead.

Paul argues by reduction: if she is going to abandon the sign, she may as well go thewhole way and take the shears to her hair — and everyone in Corinth knew what thatmeant, which is why the argument works. A shaved or cropped head on a woman in that worldwas the mark of disgrace: it was done to convicted adulteresses, and it was the lookassociated with prostitutes and with women advertising a rejection of ordinary respectability.It is the ancient equivalent of saying that if you are going to leave the wedding ring athome, you may as well announce what its absence implies.

Then verse 7 gives the theological reason, and it is a sentence people stumble over.For a man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God, but womanis the glory of man.

Notice carefully what is not said. Paul does not say that the man is the image ofGod and the woman is not. Genesis, which he is quoting from, is explicit: God createdman in his own image... male and female he created them (Gen 1:27). Both bear itequally, and Paul knew that text better than his critics do.

What he changes is the second noun. Man is the glory of God; woman is theglory of man. Glory here means something like the honour that is reflected back— what displays the worth of the one it comes from. And his argument is aboutwhat should be on show in a worship service. When the church gathers, God is the onebeing honoured, so nothing should be visibly competing for that honour. The man,unveiled, reflects God. The woman, in that culture, reflected the honour of her husband,and Paul asks that this reflection be gently covered while God is being worshipped —not because it is shameful, but because it is glorious, and this is not the hour for it.Every other glory in the room dims when God is being praised.

That is a strange logic to modern ears, but it is not a demeaning one. The covering is nota muzzle or a badge of inferiority. On Paul’s own account it is the veiling of agenuine glory in the presence of a greater one — which is exactly what the seraphim dowith their wings in Isaiah’s temple, covering their faces before a holiness thatoutshines them (Isa 6:2).

verseByVerse.quote: For man was not made from woman, but woman from man. Neither was man created for woman, but woman for man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For man was not made from woman, but woman from man. Neither was man created forwoman, but woman for man.

Paul now goes back to Genesis 2, and the reader should feel the weight of that move. He isnot appealing to Corinthian manners, or to what the neighbours will think, or to what hasalways been done. He is appealing to how human beings were made, before there was a cultureto have opinions about it.

Two facts from the garden. The woman was taken from the man — the onlyhuman being in history not formed from the ground but from another person (Gen 2:21–22).And she was made for him, in answer to the first thing in the creation account thatGod calls not good: It is not good that the man should be alone (Gen 2:18).

Both facts have been used badly, so let both be read as Genesis reads them. Fromdoes not mean lesser; Eve came out of Adam’s side, and Adam’s response was notto assert rank but to break into the first poetry in the Bible: bone of my bones andflesh of my flesh (Gen 2:23). And for does not mean an instrument. The wordGenesis uses for the woman’s role is helper, and it is worth knowing that thesame Hebrew word is used most often in the Old Testament of God himself helping his people(Ps 121:2). It is not a word for a subordinate assistant. It is a word for one who comes tothe aid of somebody who cannot manage alone — which is precisely what the man couldnot do.

Paul’s point in citing all this is narrow and he is about to guard it himself. He isestablishing that the difference between men and women is not a social construction that asophisticated congregation may dispense with; it is written into how we were made, and it istherefore not the church’s to abolish. He is not saying it establishes rank, and thevery next sentence will make sure nobody thinks so.

But something has to be said here about how this text has been used, because pretendingotherwise would be dishonest and would leave a wounded reader unhelped. Verses like thesehave been quoted by men to justify treating their wives as inferiors, to shut down everydisagreement, and in the worst cases to demand submission to cruelty. That is not amisapplication at the edges; it is the exact reverse of what the passage teaches, and itought to be named as the wickedness it is.

The measure of headship in the New Testament is never the authority a man may claim. It isthe death a man must die: Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gavehimself up for her (Eph 5:25). That is the standard, and it is a standard that ruinsdomineering before it starts. Christ’s headship over the church consisted of washingfeet, absorbing insult, and being executed for people who had contributed nothing. Any manwho quotes 1 Corinthians 11 to get his own way has picked up a verse about the Trinity andused it as a stick, and he will answer for it.

Order in the Bible always runs downhill in service. It never runs downhill in privilege.

verseByVerse.quote: That is why a wife ought to have a symbol of authority on her head, because of the angels.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That is why a wife ought to have a symbol of authority on her head, because of theangels.

Two puzzles in one short verse, and neither should be hurried past.

The first is the phrase rendered a symbol of authority. The Greek says simplythat she ought to have authority on her head, and the older reading of it — asign of someone else’s authority over her — is not the only one available. It isat least as natural to read it the other way round: the covering is her authority, the thingthat gives her the standing to pray and prophesy in the assembly. On that reading the veil isnot a leash but a licence. It marks her as a woman in her rightful place doing a rightfulthing, and it silences the objection before it is raised. That reading fits the flow: Paulhas been assuming since verse 5 that she prays and prophesies, and this is the garment thatmakes it unexceptionable.

The second puzzle is because of the angels, one of the most contested phrases inall of Paul’s letters. It should not be passed over with a shrug, because a reader whomeets it and gets no help will simply conclude that the Bible is obscure.

Four readings have been offered. The most widely held today takes the angels as theappointed guardians of the created order — God’s agents in the world he hasarranged. They are present when the church worships, and they have a stake in an orderingthat reflects God’s design; to overturn it deliberately in a worship service would be avisible affront to the very servants charged with upholding it. A second reading, going backto Chrysostom and taken up by Calvin, sees them as fellow worshippers: the church’sgathering joins a heavenly assembly where angels worship with perfect reverence, so decorum onearth honours the company we have walked into — the picture of Isaiah 6 and Revelation4 and 5, where angels and the redeemed praise together.

A third reading, the oldest, appealsto the strange episode of Genesis 6 and the Jewish traditions built on it, in which angelsfell through desire for women; on this view the covering was protective. Paul knew thosetraditions (cf. Jude 6; 2 Pet 2:4) and this reading dominated the early centuries, but itrequires a speculative account of angels that the text does not supply. A fourth notes thatthe law was given through angels (Gal 3:19), so their presence would call for theorder the law required.

The first two are the most defensible, and they share a conclusion which is where theordinary reader should land. Whatever else the phrase means, it means that a Christiancongregation at worship is not alone in the room. There are more present than can be countedon the chairs. That is the assumption behind the whole verse, and it is a bracing thing tocarry into a Sunday morning: the singing is overheard, the reverence is observed, and thecompany is far larger and far older than the one you can see (cf. Heb 12:22; Eph 3:10).

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, in the Lord woman is not independent of man nor man of woman; for as woman was made from man, so man is now born of woman. And all things are from God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nevertheless, in the Lord woman is not independent of man nor man of woman; for aswoman was made from man, so man is now born of woman. And all things are from God.

And there is the guard, placed by Paul himself, in case anyone should take verses 8 and 9and build a wall out of them.

Nevertheless is the hinge. Everything just said about the garden stands, and itdoes not entitle anybody to independence or superiority. The word he uses cuts both ways withdeliberate symmetry: not the woman apart from the man, not the man apart from the woman.Neither sex is a complete account of humanity, and neither can conduct its life as though theother were an optional extra.

Then he makes the point with a piece of homely wit. Yes, the first woman came out of aman. And every man since has come out of a woman. If anyone wants to argue about origins,the ledger balanced itself in the second generation and has stayed level ever since. Everyman who has ever lived, including the ones in Corinth arguing about veils, was carried,delivered and fed by a woman. The apostle knows exactly what he is doing with that sentence.

Then the last clause closes the account entirely: and all things are from God.The whole arrangement traces back past both of them to the one who made the pair, whichmeans neither party has grounds for a boast, since neither invented himself.

The phrase to hold on to is in the Lord. It is not a cancellation of what has gonebefore; it is the atmosphere in which what has gone before is now to be lived. Sin turneddifference into domination, and the curse said as much on the way out of the garden(Gen 3:16). In Christ the difference remains and the domination has no place. There is akind of Christian teaching about men and women that quotes verses 8 and 9 loudly and letsverses 11 and 12 fall silent. Paul wrote all four, ten seconds apart, and the church is notfree to keep only the half that suits it (cf. Gal 3:28; Eph 5:21).

What does dependence actually look like when it is working? In a marriage it is a man whogenuinely does not know what he thinks until he has heard his wife, and says so out loud incompany. In a congregation it is a church whose men would notice within a fortnight if thewomen stopped — and are honest enough to admit that most of what holds the placetogether is being done by them. Dependence is not a compliment paid at an anniversary. It isa thing you can see in who gets consulted before a decision.

And the last clause is where a Christian’s eyes should finally rest. All thingsare from God. Not from Adam, and not from Eve. The difference between men and women isnot a problem the church has to solve, nor a weapon either side may pick up. It is a piece ofGod’s workmanship, made deliberately, by someone who could have made us all identicaland did not want to. He looked at what he had made, male and female, and called it very goodbefore either of them had done anything at all.

verseByVerse.quote: Judge for yourselves: is it proper for a wife to pray to God with her head uncovered? Does not nature itself teach you that if a man wears long hair it is a disgrace for him, but if a woman has long hair, it is her glory? For her hair is given to her for a covering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judge for yourselves: is it proper for a wife to pray to God with her headuncovered?

Once again Paul refers a matter to the congregation’s own judgment rather thansettling it by decree, exactly as he did at 10:15. He has given the theology; now he asksthem to look at the thing itself and see whether it fits.

Then he appeals to nature, and the appeal has to be handled honestly, because amodern reader will object at once that nature does no such thing — hair grows oneveryone, and plenty of cultures have thought long hair splendid on a man.

The objection is fair and the answer is that Paul is not making a biological claim. Theword covers what is natural in the broad sense: the settled instinct of a people about whatis fitting, the sort of thing that feels obvious long before anyone can argue for it. In theGreco-Roman world a man wearing his hair long was reckoned effeminate, and a woman’slong hair was one of her recognised beauties. Paul is pointing at a shared sense of thefitting and saying that even that untutored instinct is pushing in the same direction as hisargument. It is a supporting consideration, not the foundation — the foundation waslaid in verses 3 and 8 to 12.

Then a clause that has caused endless discussion: her hair is given to her for acovering. Some have concluded that Paul means the hair is the covering, andthat no cloth was ever in view. That reads oddly against verse 6, where cutting the hair shortis the alternative to covering the head rather than a way of doing it; the two cannot be thesame thing if one is offered as the substitute for the other. The better sense is that hairis a God-given picture of the very thing the covering signifies — nature itself alreadydrapes a woman’s head, and the fabric follows the pattern that the Creator drew first.

It is worth noticing what kind of argument this is. Paul appeals to Christ, to creation, tothe angels, and now to the ordinary human sense of what is seemly. He is not embarrassed touse the last of these. Christians sometimes speak as though only a proof text may beconsulted, but the apostle here treats the shared instincts of decent people as a realwitness — not the highest one, and never one that may overrule Scripture, but notnothing either (cf. Rom 2:14–15).

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone is inclined to be contentious, we have no such practice, nor do the churches of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone is inclined to be contentious, we have no such practice, nor do the churchesof God.

The last word on the subject, and it is not another argument. It is a door closing.

Such practice is deliberately ambiguous in the Greek, and both readings end inthe same place. If it means the practice of contentiousness, Paul is saying: we do not dofighting about this, and neither does any other church. If it means the practice of goinguncovered, he is saying: no church anywhere does what you are proposing, so the innovation isyours alone. Either way the appeal is to the shared life of the churches, and either way itlands on the person who wants a fight.

Which brings the passage to the question every reader of it has been waiting for: areChristian women meant to cover their heads in church today? The question deserves an answerrather than an admiring description of how difficult it is.

Begin with what does not change. The theology of verses 3 and 8 to 12 is rooted in theTrinity and in creation, and neither of those is a first-century custom. That men and womenare equally God’s image, genuinely different, mutually dependent, and ordered inrelationship to one another is not up for revision, and a congregation that quietly erasesthe difference between men and women has departed from Paul, whatever it is wearing.

Now what does change. The visible sign is a different matter, and Paul’s own way ofarguing suggests as much. He reasons from what is disgraceful, from what nature suggests,from what the churches do — the vocabulary of things that are legible in a particularplace and time. A sign works only if people can read it. In first-century Corinth anuncovered head in worship said something specific and everyone in the room heard it. In mostWestern congregations today a hat says nothing whatever, and a woman who wore one to makePaul’s point would find that nobody received the message, which is the one thing asymbol must do.

So, practically. Where the covering is still meaningful — and there are cultures andcongregations where it plainly is — wear it, and let nobody sneer at those who do; theyare obeying Scripture in a way their neighbours can read. Where it is not, the principle mustfind a form that people can actually see: a church where men and women are equally welcome topray and are not embarrassed to be different from one another; where the distinction istreated as a gift rather than an awkwardness to be managed; where dress and manner in worshipare chosen with an eye to what honours God rather than what displays the wearer. And ineither case, verse 16 governs: whatever conclusion a Christian reaches, he is not permittedto become contentious about it. The apostle who has just spent fifteen verses on the matterends by refusing to let it become a battlefield.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–22 — Divisions at the Lord’s Supper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The shift from commendation to rebuke is sharp: “But in the following instructions I do not commend you, because when you come together it is not for the better but for the worse” (v. 17). The Lord’s Supper at Corinth had become an occasion for social stratification and humiliation. The wealthy arrived early and ate their own food — probably brought from home or from the extensive provisions available to the upper classes — leaving the poor (who arrived after their working hours) to find the food already eaten and some of the wealthier members already drunk. The meal that should have been the embodiment of the gospel — all equally sustained by the body and blood of Christ — had become a demonstration of social inequality.

Paul’s diagnosis is theological before it is ethical: they are not eating the Lord’s Supper at all (v. 20). The meal that proceeds on these terms has disqualified itself from being the Lord’s Supper; it is merely eating and drinking, devoid of its sacramental meaning. The rich who eat well have full stomachs; the poor who arrive to nothing have been humiliated and despised. “Do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing?” (v. 22) — the question is the most pointed social critique in the letter.

Two verses in the middle of the section explain how Paul handled the report. He had heard of divisions and says carefully, I believe it in part (v. 18) — neither swallowing the account whole nor dismissing it, which is the discipline every pastor needs when one member speaks about another. And he adds the hard sentence of verse 19: there must be factions among you in order that those who are genuine among you may be recognized. That is not approval of the factions but a statement about what God does with them. Trouble sorts a congregation, and the word for genuine is a metalworker’s word for metal that has been tested and passed.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord’s Supper as Enacted Gospel Equality

Paul’s critique of the Corinthian Supper is grounded in his theology of the cross. The Lord’s Supper proclaims the Lord’s death (v. 26) — the death in which the rich Son of God became poor for the sake of the poor, in which the Lord washed his disciples’ feet, in which social distinctions were overcome in the one body given for all. A Supper that reinforces social stratification is not merely socially unkind; it is a contradiction of what is being enacted. The body and blood of Christ at the table cannot be participated in rightly by those who simultaneously despise the members of his body gathered around the table.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The patronage culture of Roman Corinth structured even the shared meal around social hierarchy: the wealthy ate better food in the inner room; clients and dependents got lesser portions in the outer rooms. The Corinthians had imported this structure wholesale into the church’s gathering. Now: The Lord’s Supper remains the place where the social equalisations of the gospel are most visibly enacted — or most visibly denied. The church where wealth, race, or education creates a gradient of welcome and participation has committed the Corinthian error at its most fundamental level.

verseByVerse.quote: But in the following instructions I do not commend you, because when you come together it is not for the better but for the worse. For, in the first place, when you come together as a church, I hear that there are divisions among you. And I believe it in part, for there must be factions among you in order that those who are genuine among you may be recognized.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But in the following instructions I do not commend you, because when you come togetherit is not for the better but for the worse.

Verse 2 opened with I commend you. This one opens by taking it back, and the echois deliberate. Whatever they had held on to, they had lost the thing that mattered most.

Sit with the accusation, because it is worse than it first sounds. Paul is not saying themeetings were dull, or badly run, or unhelpful. He is saying that these people would havebeen better off staying at home. The gathering was doing damage. There is such a thing as achurch service that leaves people further from God than it found them, and an apostle says soin writing.

The cause is named at once: when you come together as a church, I hear that there aredivisions among you. And I believe it in part. That last phrase is a small masterpieceof pastoral care. Paul does not swallow the report whole and does not dismiss it. He hasheard something from Chloe’s household (1:11), he knows that reports carry exaggeration,and he refuses both to pretend it is nothing and to convict them of everything alleged. Anypastor who has had to weigh what one member says about another will recognise the disciplinein those five words.

Then a genuinely hard sentence: for there must be factions among you in order thatthose who are genuine among you may be recognized.

This is not approval. Paul has been attacking the factions since chapter 1 and is not nowblessing them. He is saying something about how God works even through what he hates. Troublesorts people. When a congregation splits along the lines of money or personality or taste, itbecomes visible who was there for Christ and who was there for the circle — and thesorting is not an accident but a providence. God permits the fracture and uses it as a sieve.It is the same principle as the wheat and the weeds growing together until harvest(Matt 13:30), and the same comfort: a church going through an ugly season is not outsideGod’s hands.

The word for genuine is a metalworker’s word, used of metal that has beentested and passed. Nobody discovers what an alloy is made of while it sits on a shelf. It isfound out in the fire, and a divided church is a furnace (cf. 1 Jn 2:19).

Which is worth knowing for anyone currently sitting inside a congregation that is comingapart, since that is a more common experience than church notice-sheets suggest. The passagegives three things to do with it. Do not conclude that God has abandoned the place; verse 19says he is at work in the very thing that feels like collapse. Do not join a party, becausethe sifting is precisely between those who are for Christ and those who are for a camp. Andask the uncomfortable question that this verse presses: when the fire came, what did it showthat I was made of? A season of trouble in a church is the only time most people ever findout what they were actually attached to.

verseByVerse.quote: When you come together, it is not the Lord’s supper that you eat. For in eating, each one goes ahead with his own meal. One goes hungry, another gets drunk. What! Do you not have houses to eat and drink in? Or do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing? What shall I say to you? Shall I commend you in this? No, I will not.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When you come together, it is not the Lord’s supper that you eat.

That is one of the most devastating sentences ever written to a church, and it is worthfeeling before it is explained. These people gathered on the first day of the week. They tookbread and a cup. They said the words. And the apostle tells them that whatever they weredoing, it was not the Lord’s Supper. The thing had lost the right to its own name.

To see why, the room has to be pictured, and archaeology at Corinth helps. A wealthybeliever’s house was the meeting place, and such a house had a dining room, thetriclinium, which held perhaps nine or a dozen at couches around a table. Everyoneelse went in the courtyard, the atrium, standing or on the floor. Roman dinners wereroutinely graded: better food and better wine went to the host’s social equals in thedining room, and the lesser stuff went outside. Nobody thought this shocking. It was simplyhow a dinner worked.

Now add the working day. The wealthy could arrive when they liked. The poor — theslaves and labourers who made up much of the congregation — came when their work letthem, which was late. So they walked in to find the meal eaten, the good wine gone, theirbrothers in the inner room flushed and full, and something left over for them if anything was.Paul’s three flat observations describe it exactly: each one goes ahead with his ownmeal. One goes hungry, another gets drunk.

Then the anger breaks out, and Paul does not tidy it. What! is an exclamation ofsheer disbelief. Four questions follow, one after another, and they are not gentle: Doyou not have houses to eat and drink in? Or do you despise the church of God and humiliatethose who have nothing? What shall I say to you? Shall I commend you in this? No, I willnot.

Notice where the sharpest word falls. Not on the drunkenness, bad as that is, but onthose who have nothing. A man who arrives late and hungry and watches the meal endwithout him has been told something about his worth, and he has been told it at the tablewhere Christ’s death for him is being celebrated. That is what Paul cannot bear. TheCorinthians thought they were having a slightly untidy dinner. They were preaching, inactions, the opposite of the gospel they said with their mouths.

And the sin is not really greed. It is the effortless importing of the world’sseating plan into the church. Nobody in that house had to decide to humiliate the poor; theyonly had to do what everyone in Corinth did, and let the ordinary arrangements stand. That ishow it usually happens. Congregations rarely resolve to grade people by money or accent orschooling. They simply fail to notice that the surrounding culture has already done it forthem, and do nothing to interfere (cf. Jas 2:1–4).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–34 — The Institution of the Lord’s Supper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The pastoral rebuke gives way to the most solemn passage in the letter: the institution narrative, delivered “from the Lord” (v. 23). This is the earliest written account of the institution of the Lord’s Supper in the NT — earlier than the Gospels — and its formulation is strikingly close to Luke 22. “I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you” — the language of sacred tradition: Paul is transmitting a deposit he himself received, not creating a new rite.

The words of institution — “This is my body which is for you. Do this in remembrance of me” and “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me” — ground the Supper simultaneously in the past event of the cross, the present act of remembrance, and the future hope of the Parousia: “you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.” The Supper is eschatological as well as historical: the community that eats and drinks at this table is living between the first and second coming, sustained by what Christ has already done, waiting for what he will complete.

The warning of vv. 27–32 is among the most solemn in the NT: eating and drinking in an unworthy manner makes one guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. Judgment has fallen on the Corinthians already — illness and death among them (v. 30) — as the Lord’s discipline. The answer is self-examination before eating — not a tortured introspection about one’s worthiness, but a discerning of the body: recognising the community as the body of Christ and treating it accordingly.

The section ends not with doctrine but with a small instruction: when you come together to eat, wait for one another (v. 33). After the upper room, the new covenant, the return of Christ and the graves in their own congregation, the remedy is that the comfortable should sit still until the working poor arrive. The cost falls on those who have something to give up, as it does everywhere in this letter. And appetite is sent home: if anyone is hungry, let him eat at home — there is nothing wrong with a good dinner and everything wrong with treating the Lord’s table as one.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Real Presence and the Reformed Understanding of the Supper

Calvin’s eucharistic theology, developed precisely in dialogue with this passage, insisted on a genuine but spiritual presence of Christ in the Supper — against both the Roman Catholic doctrine of transubstantiation (physical transformation of the elements) and Zwingli’s pure memorialism (the Supper as merely symbolic). Paul’s language of “participation” (10:16) and “proclaiming the Lord’s death” (11:26) supports a real, active, communicative presence of Christ at the table — where Christ genuinely gives himself to be received by faith, and where genuine nourishment of the soul takes place through the Spirit.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian abuse of the Supper — reducing it to a social meal stratified by class — was the practical outworking of their failure to grasp the gospel. When you understand that Christ died equally for the rich and the poor in your community, you cannot eat well while they starve at the same table. Now: The Lord’s Supper remains the church’s most powerful enacted proclamation of the gospel — which is why its abuse is so serious, and why its right practice (the community gathered equally around the cross) is so significant as a sign to the world.

verseByVerse.quote: For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it, and said, “This is my body, which is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you, that the Lord Jesus on thenight when he was betrayed took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it, and said,“This is my body, which is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”

Paul stops arguing and starts reciting. The change of register is unmistakable; this isthe language of something handed over intact, and it is the oldest written account we have ofthat night — written down before any of the Gospels, within about twenty-five years ofthe event, and already worn smooth by use in the churches.

On the night when he was betrayed. Of all the ways to date it. Not on the nightof the Passover, though it was; not on the eve of the crucifixion, though it was. Paul fixesthe Supper to the moment of treachery, and he does it because that is the point. While a manwho had eaten with him for three years was arranging the price, Jesus was breaking bread forhim and for the rest of them, none of whom would stand by him either. The Supper was notinstituted in a season of loyalty. It was given on the worst night in the history offriendship, which is precisely why an unfaithful Christian may still come to it.

He had given thanks. The Greek word is eucharisteo, which is where theold name Eucharist comes from. He gave thanks for the bread, knowing what the bread meant andwhat the next eighteen hours held.

Then the words that have divided the church for five hundred years: This is my body,which is for you. The question is what the small word is is doing, and a readerdeserves a straight account rather than a fog.

One answer, the Roman Catholic one, is that the bread ceases to be bread and becomes thebody of Christ, while continuing to look and taste like bread. A second, the Lutheran, keepsthe bread as bread but holds that Christ’s body is present in and under it. A third,associated with Zwingli, says the word means represents, and the Supper is a vividmemorial of something now absent. A fourth, the older Reformed answer, says the bread remainsbread and Christ is nevertheless truly given and received, not by his body coming down intothe elements but by the Spirit lifting the believer up to where Christ is.

Two observations help enormously, and neither requires a degree. First, when Jesus saidthese words, he was sitting at the table holding the loaf, with his body plainly in front ofthem, unbroken. Nobody at that table can have understood the sentence as a statement ofchemistry, because the body it referred to was passing the plate. Second, this is how heregularly talked. He is the door, the vine, the light, the road. Nobody has ever thought hewas made of timber.

So the bread stays bread — and something entirely real is happening, becauserepresents is far too thin a word for what the previous chapter called aparticipation in the body of Christ (10:16). The Reformed answer holds both, and it is not acompromise but the only position that keeps Paul’s own two statements in the same hand.What that means at the rail is not a puzzle: the believer who takes the bread is receivingChrist, truly, by faith, through the Spirit — and the receiving is as real as thecrumbs.

Which is for you. Two small words carrying the whole gospel. Not merely a bodybroken, but a body broken for — in the place of, on behalf of, instead of. Andhe said it to a room containing the man who would sell him, the man who would deny him, andnine men who would run.

verseByVerse.quote: In the same way also he took the cup, after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the same way also he took the cup, after supper, saying, “This cup is the newcovenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.”

After supper. A small detail that tells us which cup this was. The Passover mealmoved through a fixed sequence of cups, and the one taken after the main course was the third,the cup of blessing — the same phrase Paul used at 10:16. Fifteen centuries of Israelhad been drinking that cup annually in memory of a rescue from Egypt. On this night the hostpicked it up and quietly transferred it to himself.

The new covenant in my blood. No phrase in the Old Testament was more loaded withhope. Jeremiah had promised a day when God would make a new covenant, not like theone Israel broke, in which he would write his law on hearts rather than stone, and remembertheir sin no more (Jer 31:31–34). Every Jew at that table knew the passage andnobody knew when it would arrive. Jesus tells them, holding a wine cup, that it arrivestomorrow, and that the thing which will inaugurate it is his own death.

Covenants in that world were cut with blood. An agreement of any weight was sealed by asacrifice, so that the parties should understand what they were undertaking. This one issealed by the blood of one of the parties, poured out to secure the other party’sfaithfulness as well as his own. That is not how any covenant in human history has everworked.

As often as you drink it is also, incidentally, the nearest thing the NewTestament gives to a rule about frequency — which is to say, no rule at all, only theassumption that it will be often. Christians have settled this differently and charitably forcenturies. What the phrase does exclude is a Supper kept so rarely that it becomes anoccasion rather than a meal; the Lord assumed his people would need feeding regularly, and hewas not wrong about them.

And here is the thing to see. Israel remembered a lamb whose blood had been smeared on adoorframe so that death would pass over a household. The man saying these words would be deadby the following afternoon, at roughly the hour the Passover lambs were being killed in thetemple a few hundred yards away. He knew it, held the cup steady, and called it the newcovenant in his blood. There was no reluctance in the hand that lifted it (cf. Ex 24:8;Lk 22:20).

verseByVerse.quote: For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’sdeath until he comes.

Paul adds his own comment to the tradition he has just recited, and it draws the Supperinto three tenses at once.

Backwards: you proclaim the Lord’s death. The verb is the word forannouncing, publishing, preaching. The Supper is not a private devotional moment with theeyes closed; it is a public announcement, and it is made with hands and mouths rather thanwords. A congregation eating together says something, out loud, to everyone watching: thata man died, that his death is the whole hope of these people, and that they are not ashamedof it. It is a sermon that even the illiterate can preach and no one can misquote.

Notice which part of the story the Supper preaches. Not the teaching, not the miracles,not the example. The death. Christianity has never been able to make its central rite aboutanything else, however much it has wanted to at various times. Bread broken, wine poured— the symbols will not be repurposed.

Forwards: until he comes. Three words that turn the meal around. The Supper has abuilt-in expiry date. It is provisional, a meal for the road, and it will one day stop —not because it failed but because it will have been overtaken by the thing it pointed to.Christ himself said he would not drink of the fruit of the vine again until he drank it new inhis Father’s kingdom (Matt 26:29). So every communion service is a table with an emptyplace at it.

Which is why the Supper suits the way a Christian actually feels. It is a meal of joy thatis also a meal of hunger. It gives real food and it leaves you wanting a fuller one; it saysthe rescue has happened and it says the party has not started yet. Anyone who has taken thebread and cup in a season of grief knows the strange fitness of it — that this is theone act of worship that does not require you to pretend everything is well, because it isbuilt around a death and a waiting.

And there is the homesickness the reader may not have had a name for. Communion isdesigned to leave a person unsatisfied. Not because the food is poor but because it is aforetaste, and a foretaste is meant to make you hungry for the meal. That ache at the rail isnot a failure of devotion. It is the sacrament working (cf. Rev 19:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever, therefore, eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever, therefore, eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy mannerwill be guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord.

This verse has probably kept more Christians away from the Lord’s table than anyother sentence in the Bible, and in almost every case it has done so by being read backwards.So it must be read carefully.

The crucial word is an adverb. Paul does not write whoever is unworthy.He writes whoever eats in an unworthy manner. The word describes the eating, not theeater. That distinction is the difference between a table and a locked door.

And it has to be so, because if worthy people were the requirement, the table would beempty for ever. Nobody has ever been worthy of the body and blood of the Son of God. That isthe entire reason the body was broken. A Supper for the worthy would be a Supper for nobody,and Christ did not institute it in a room of worthy men — he handed it to a table ofdeserters.

What, then, is an unworthy manner? Paul is not speculating; he has spent seven versesdescribing it. It is what was happening in Corinth: coming to the table while treating thepeople at it with contempt. Eating well in front of the hungry. Taking the sign of a deaththat levelled everybody, and using the occasion to display that you are not level with themat all. To do that is to be guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord —to handle the holiest thing in the world carelessly, and to be answerable for it.

So the person who genuinely should hesitate at the rail is not the one who feelsunworthy. It is the one who has an unhealed contempt for a brother and intends to keep it.It is the person carrying a grudge into the queue, or nursing a sin he has decided not togive up, and reaching for the bread as though none of that were in the room with him.

If you have read this verse and stayed in your seat because you knew yourself too sinfulto come, hear this plainly: you have understood your own heart correctly and this versewrongly. The table is not a reward for the clean. It is food for the starving, and a sense ofyour own unworthiness is very close to the qualification. The one thing Christ said aboutthose who come is that they should come hungry (cf. Matt 9:12–13; Isa 55:1).

verseByVerse.quote: Let a person examine himself, then, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let a person examine himself, then, and so eat of the bread and drink of thecup.

Notice the shape of the sentence before anything else, because the shape is the pastoralpoint. Examine yourself — and so eat. The examination is not an alternative tocoming. It is the way you come. Paul assumes the person who has examined himself will be atthe table, not in the car park.

This needs saying because a whole tradition of self-examination has grown up which ends inabstaining, and it has left sincere Christians sitting through communion with their hands intheir laps for years, taking their exclusion as a mark of seriousness. It is not seriousness.It is a misreading, and it deprives the very people the meal was made for.

So what is a person actually looking for? Not a morbid inventory of every failure sincethe last Supper; that is introspection, and it ends where introspection always ends, with theself at the centre of the picture and Christ somewhere in the background. The examinationPaul has in view is short and it faces outwards. Three questions will do it.

Do I trust Christ, and not myself, for my standing before God? That is the first, and ifthe answer is yes, however shakily, the door is open. Is there anyone in this room I amrefusing to be reconciled to? That is the second, and it is the one Corinth failed —and if there is, deal with it, because the Lord himself said to leave the gift at the altarand go and settle it first (Matt 5:23–24). Am I coming to receive, or to perform? Thatis the third, and it catches the respectable.

A word too on who may come, since the question is a real one in most congregations. Thetable belongs to the Lord, not to the church that sets it out, and the historic Reformedpractice has been to welcome to it any baptised believer who trusts Christ, is walking withhis people, and is not under discipline — and to say so openly, warmly, and with thewarning of verse 27 attached. That is not a gate to keep the wrong people out. It is a fencearound a fire, which is what you build when something is precious and hot.

And the direction of travel matters. Right self-examination always ends at the same place:not with a verdict on yourself but with an empty hand held out. The bread has to be takenwith an open palm; there is no other way to receive it, and there never has been.

verseByVerse.quote: For anyone who eats and drinks without discerning the body eats and drinks judgment on himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For anyone who eats and drinks without discerning the body eats and drinks judgment onhimself.

Everything turns on what the body means here, and the context has alreadyanswered it.

The Corinthian failure was not a defective theory of the elements. Nobody in that churchwas being disciplined for a wrong view of how Christ is present in the bread. The failure wasthat they could not see the church. They ate in front of hungry members and did not perceivethat those members were the body of Christ — the very thing Paul has been saying since10:17, that the one loaf makes the many one body, and will say again at length in chapter 12.To fail to discern the body is to look around a congregation and not see Christ’sown people there.

That said, the two senses are not really separable, and Paul is not choosing between them.The bread on the table and the people around it are called by the same name in this letter,and that is not a play on words. A man who does not grasp what the bread is will not graspwhat the church is either; and a man who takes the bread seriously and the peoplecontemptuously has not, in fact, taken the bread seriously.

Which makes the practical test easier than the theology. Look up. Before the plate reachesyou, look at the row in front and the row behind, and ask whether there is anyone there youare quietly writing off — the tedious one, the difficult one, the one who has been rudeto you, the one whose politics you find intolerable, the one who has less money or lesseducation than you and whom you have never once invited home. Those people are the body ofChrist. Failing to see it is what this verse calls eating judgment.

The word for judgment here, incidentally, is not the word for damnation. It meansa verdict, a sentence handed down — and verse 32 will explain that for the believer itis a Father’s correction, not a judge’s condemnation. That distinction is comingin three verses and is worth holding onto until it arrives.

There is a further application that our own age needs more than Corinth did. The moderndanger at communion is not that we despise the poor member across the aisle; it is that wehave forgotten he is there at all. Communion has quietly become a private transaction —head bowed, eyes shut, a personal moment between the individual and his Saviour, with thecongregation an incidental crowd. That is not what Paul is describing. He assumes a mealwhere people look at each other.

The bread on the plate has already been described as one loaf making one body (10:17). Toreceive it as though the person beside you were scenery is to miss the point in a gentler waythan the Corinthians did, but to miss it nonetheless. Discerning the body is not onlyrefusing to despise; it is bothering to notice.

verseByVerse.quote: That is why many of you are weak and ill, and some have died. But if we judged ourselves truly, we would not be judged. But when we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined so that we may not be condemned along with the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That is why many of you are weak and ill, and some have died. But if we judgedourselves truly, we would not be judged. But when we are judged by the Lord, we aredisciplined so that we may not be condemned along with the world.

Paul makes a direct connection between how this church was behaving at the table and thesickness and deaths in its membership. He does not soften it and neither should anycommentary. But it must be handled with great care, because the wrong lesson drawn from thisverse has caused enormous and needless pain.

Here is what the verse does not say. It does not say that illness is generally apunishment for sin. It does not license anyone to look at a sick Christian, or a sick child,and go hunting for the hidden fault. Jesus faced that assumption head on and demolished it.Asked whose sin had caused a man’s blindness, he answered, It was not that this mansinned, or his parents (Jn 9:3). Told about Galileans killed by Pilate and eighteencrushed by a falling tower, he asked whether his hearers thought the victims were worsesinners than everyone else, and answered his own question: No, I tell you(Lk 13:1–5). The whole book of Job exists to destroy the theory that suffering is areliable index of guilt.

What Paul has here is not a general theory but a specific diagnosis, given by an apostleabout a particular congregation whose particular sin had a particular consequence. He knewwhat he knew because God had shown him. Nobody today has that information about anybodyelse’s illness, and to imitate the diagnosis without the revelation is not faith; it iscruelty with a Bible verse attached.

So if you are reading this from a hospital bed, or after a funeral, take the plain sense ofthe whole passage: this text is not an accusation aimed at you. If God has something to sayto you, he is well able to say it, and he does not do it in code.

What the verse does teach is that God takes his table seriously enough to intervene, andthat his interventions with his own children are not punishments. Verse 31 offers the way ofavoiding them, and it is the simplest thing in the world: if we judged ourselves truly, wewould not be judged. Honest self-appraisal now spares the need for correction later. Theperson who deals with his own sin is not dealt with.

And verse 32 gives the doctrine that makes the whole passage bearable, indeedcomfortable. When we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined so that we may not becondemned along with the world. Two different things are named in one sentence, and theymust never be confused. Discipline belongs to sons; condemnation belongs to the world.
