Goddoes not punish his children for sin, because the punishment fell somewhere else, on a hill,once. What he does with his children is train them, and training hurts.

Read the logic and it is astonishing: God let believers in Corinth become ill and let someof them die, in order that they should not be condemned with the world. Even theseverest thing in the passage is a rescue. The hand that struck was holding on(cf. Heb 12:5–11; Rev 3:19).

verseByVerse.quote: So then, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another— if anyone is hungry, let him eat at home—so that when you come together it will not be for judgment. About the other things I will give directions when I come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So then, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another— ifanyone is hungry, let him eat at home—so that when you come together it will not be forjudgment. About the other things I will give directions when I come.

After the institution narrative, the warning and the discipline, the remedy turns out to bethree words long. Wait for one another.

There is a lesson in the smallness of it. Paul has taken the Corinthians to the upper room,to Jeremiah’s new covenant, to the return of Christ, and to graves in their owncongregation — and what he asks them to do about it is to sit still until the slaves getoff work. That is what repentance usually looks like. Not a programme. A small, concrete,slightly inconvenient change in behaviour on the next occasion.

And notice who is being asked to wait. Not the poor, who were already waiting. Thecomfortable, the ones with the leisure to arrive early, are told to hold their hunger for anhour so that the meal can begin together. The cost falls on the people with something to giveup, which is the direction love always travels in this letter (8:13; 9:19; 10:24).

If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home. Paul is drawing the distinction theCorinthians had lost. There is nothing wrong with a good dinner; there is something badlywrong with treating the Lord’s table as one. Satisfy your appetite in your own kitchen.When the church gathers, you are not there to be fed in that sense, and what you do at thattable is not about you at all.

About the other things I will give directions when I come. A quiet ending, and areminder that a letter is not the whole of pastoral care. There were more questions, and Paulwould not settle them at a distance; some things need a face. He is coming, and they know it,and that expectation is itself part of the correction.

It is worth ending the chapter where the chapter ends: with a wealthy Corinthian sitting ona couch with food in front of him, hearing footsteps in the courtyard, and putting the breadback down until the man with the calloused hands has come in and sat down beside him. Nothinggrand happened in that room. But the death of the Son of God was preached in it, by two menstarting to eat at the same moment.

And the same sermon is preached wherever a congregation eats together on the level. TheLord of glory took bread on the night he was handed over, gave thanks for it, and broke itfor people who were about to abandon him — and he has been setting that table eversince, in cathedrals and in kitchens, for anyone who will come hungry. He waited for us. Itcosts his people very little to wait for one another.

11.text: <sup>1</sup>Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ.<sup>2</sup>Now I commend you because you remember me in everything and maintain the traditions even as I delivered them to you.<sup>3</sup>But I want you to understand that the head of every man is Christ, the head of a wife is her husband, and the head of Christ is God.<sup>4</sup>Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head,<sup>5</sup>but every wife who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head, since it is the same as if her head were shaven.<sup>6</sup>For if a wife will not cover her head, then she should cut her hair short. But since it is disgraceful for a wife to cut off her hair or shave her head, let her cover her head.<sup>7</sup>For a man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God, but woman is the glory of man.<sup>8</sup>For man was not made from woman, but woman from man.<sup>9</sup>Neither was man created for woman, but woman for man.<sup>10</sup>That is why a wife ought to have a symbol of authority on her head, because of the angels.<sup>11</sup>Nevertheless, in the Lord woman is not independent of man nor man of woman;<sup>12</sup>for as woman was made from man, so man is now born of woman. And all things are from God.<sup>13</sup>Judge for yourselves: is it proper for a wife to pray to God with her head uncovered?<sup>14</sup>Does not nature itself teach you that if a man wears long hair it is a disgrace for him,<sup>15</sup>but if a woman has long hair, it is her glory? For her hair is given to her for a covering.<sup>16</sup>If anyone is inclined to be contentious, we have no such practice, nor do the churches of God.<sup>17</sup>But in the following instructions I do not commend you, because when you come together it is not for the better but for the worse.<sup>18</sup>For, in the first place, when you come together as a church, I hear that there are divisions among you. And I believe it in part,<sup>19</sup>for there must be factions among you in order that those who are genuine among you may be recognized.<sup>20</sup>When you come together, it is not the Lord’s supper that you eat.<sup>21</sup>For in eating, each one goes ahead with his own meal. One goes hungry, another gets drunk.<sup>22</sup>What! Do you not have houses to eat and drink in? Or do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing? What shall I say to you? Shall I commend you in this? No, I will not.<sup>23</sup>For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took bread,<sup>24</sup>and when he had given thanks, he broke it, and said, “This is my body, which is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”<sup>25</sup>In the same way also he took the cup, after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.”<sup>26</sup>For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.<sup>27</sup>Whoever, therefore, eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord.<sup>28</sup>Let a person examine himself, then, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup.<sup>29</sup>For anyone who eats and drinks without discerning the body eats and drinks judgment on himself.<sup>30</sup>That is why many of you are weak and ill, and some have died.<sup>31</sup>But if we judged ourselves truly, we would not be judged.<sup>32</sup>But when we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined so that we may not be condemned along with the world.<sup>33</sup>So then, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another—<sup>34</sup>if anyone is hungry, let him eat at home—so that when you come together it will not be for judgment. About the other things I will give directions when I come.

12.title: One Body, Many Gifts, One Spirit
12.overview:
Chapter 12 is the first of three chapters addressing the abuse of spiritual gifts at Corinth — and it lays the theological foundation that the ethical application of chapter 14 and the supreme example of chapter 13 will require. The Corinthians had made spiritual gifts a competitive arena: the more spectacular the gift (especially tongues), the higher the spiritual status of the person who possessed it. Paul’s response is twofold: first, to trace all genuine gifts to their trinitarian source (Spirit, Lord, God — vv. 4–6), demonstrating that all gifts are of equal divine origin; and second, to use the human body as an extended analogy for the church, demonstrating that diversity is not a problem to be overcome but a design feature of the body that God has composed.

The profound theological claim of the chapter is v. 18: “But as it is, God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose.” The composition of the community — who has which gift, who is which member — is God’s sovereign arrangement, not the result of spiritual achievement or competitive development. No one earns their gift; no one chooses their place in the body. The one who is tempted to say “I am not needed” and the one who is tempted to say “I do not need you” are both wrong for the same reason: God composed this body, and every member is necessary to the whole.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Gifts of the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul begins with a criterion for discernment that cuts through every charismatic claim with startling simplicity: no one speaking by the Spirit of God ever says “Jesus is accursed,” and no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except by the Holy Spirit (v. 3). The content of the confession is the test. The Spirit’s signature is always christological: to exalt Jesus is to operate under the Spirit; to curse or diminish Jesus is to operate under a different spirit. This christological criterion governs all that follows: the gifts Paul lists are Spirit-given capacities for the exaltation of Christ and the building of his body.

The trinitarian structure of vv. 4–6 is one of Paul’s most explicit: varieties of gifts — but the same Spirit; varieties of service — but the same Lord; varieties of activities — but the same God who empowers them all in everyone. Three persons, three nouns (gifts/charismata, service/diakoniai, activities/energēmata), one divine source. Every genuine spiritual gift is simultaneously the work of all three persons of the Godhead — which means the competitive comparison of gifts is not merely socially divisive but theologically incoherent. They all come from the same place.

The list of gifts in vv. 8–11 is not exhaustive (compare Rom 12:6–8; Eph 4:11) but illustrative: wisdom, knowledge, faith, healing, miracles, prophecy, discernment, tongues, interpretation. These are distributed “as he wills” — the same phrase applied to the Spirit’s sovereign distribution of gifts as to the Father’s sovereign election. The Spirit does not give the same gift to all, and no individual receives all gifts. This is a design principle, not a defect.

Two verses frame the section and are easily lost between the confession of verse 3 and the list of verses 8 to 11. Verse 2 reminds the Corinthians what they came from: when you were pagans you were led astray to mute idols, however you were led. The gods they had served could not speak, and the worship in front of them was anything but quiet — which is why this church arrived already trained to grade spiritual reality by intensity of experience. Intensity is not evidence, and that is the assumption Paul is correcting.

And verse 7 supplies the sentence that governs everything after it: to each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good. There are no giftless Christians, and there are no gifts given for their holder’s enrichment. A gift is placed in one person’s hands for the benefit of the people around him.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Trinitarian Source of All Gifts

The explicit trinitarianism of vv. 4–6 is remarkable as a casual structural feature of Paul’s argument: he assumes the Trinity without arguing for it. Reformed pneumatology has always grounded the discussion of spiritual gifts in this trinitarian framework: the gifts are not the Spirit’s autonomous productions but the common work of Father, Son, and Spirit. This prevents both the elevation of the Spirit over Christ (a common charismatic error) and the diminution of the Spirit’s ongoing work (a common cessationist error): all genuine gifts are simultaneously the work of the triune God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Corinthian believers were apparently competing for the most impressive gifts, using spiritual gifts as social capital. Paul’s trinitarian grounding removes the competition from its foundation: you cannot boast in a gift that was sovereignly given to you by the Spirit who gives as he wills. Now: The same gift-competitive dynamic operates in charismatic and Reformed communities alike, in different directions: charismatics sometimes elevate dramatic gifts (tongues, healing) over quiet ones; cessationists sometimes elevate intellectual gifts (teaching, wisdom) over practical ones. Paul’s list refuses both hierarchies.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning spiritual gifts, brothers, I do not want you to be uninformed. You know that when you were pagans you were led astray to mute idols, however you were led.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now concerning spiritual gifts, brothers, I do not want you to be uninformed.

The phrase now concerning has appeared several times in this letter (7:1; 8:1),and each time it signals that Paul is turning to a question the Corinthians themselves put tohim in writing. So these three chapters are an answer to a letter, not an unprompted lecture.The church had asked about spiritual gifts. What follows is the longest sustained treatmentof the subject in the Bible, and it will take three chapters and end in a hymn.

Then verse 2, which is easily skipped and should not be, because it establishes the groundon which everything else stands. You know that when you were pagans you were led astrayto mute idols, however you were led.

Paul reminds them what they used to be, and he chooses one detail out of everything hecould have chosen: the gods they served could not speak. The word is mute, dumb,voiceless. The Old Testament says this about idols with something close to contempt —they have mouths, but do not speak (Ps 115:5) — and Elijah said it on Carmelwith open scorn while four hundred and fifty men shouted at a silence that lasted all day(1 Kgs 18:26–29).

Stand in one of those temples for a moment. There is incense, and a crowd, and drums, anda statue with painted eyes that has never said a word to anybody. The priest interprets. Theoracle is ambiguous. Whatever comes out of the ecstasy, nobody can check it, because the godin the room has no voice with which to confirm or deny anything at all.

And the phrase however you were led is not an aside. It admits that something didlead them. Pagan worship in Corinth was not dull; it involved genuine ecstatic states, frenzy,trance, utterance. The Corinthians had seen impressive spiritual phenomena long before theyhad ever heard of the Holy Spirit — and that is exactly the problem Paul is about toaddress. A congregation full of former pagans had arrived in the church already trained tobelieve that the more overwhelming an experience is, the more divine it must be. They weregrading the Spirit’s gifts by the standard of the temple they had left.

Which is a warning worth carrying into any discussion of the Spirit, then or now.Intensity is not evidence. Something can be powerful, sincere, moving, and entirelyunconnected to God — the idols were mute, but the worship in front of them was notquiet. The question is never how strongly a thing was felt. The next verse gives the questionthat matters.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I want you to understand that no one speaking in the Spirit of God ever says “Jesus is accursed!” and no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except in the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore I want you to understand that no one speaking in the Spirit of God ever says“Jesus is accursed!” and no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except in theHoly Spirit.

Here is the test, and its brilliance is that it moves the question from the experience tothe content. Not how did it feel? but what did it say about Jesus?

Whether anyone in Corinth actually shouted Jesus is accursed is debated. Perhapssomeone in an ecstatic state had said it and the church was shaken. Perhaps Paul is namingthe worst thing imaginable in order to establish the principle at its extreme. Either way therule holds at both ends: the Spirit never speaks against Christ, and no one comes to confessChrist without him.

Take the second half first, because it is the sweeter half. No one can say “Jesusis Lord” except in the Holy Spirit. Anyone can pronounce the syllables; parrots andhypocrites manage it. Paul means the confession that comes from a person who means it —who has genuinely handed the government of his life to a crucified Jew from Nazareth. Thatsentence, meant, cannot be manufactured. It is not the product of good arguments, a strongupbringing, or an emotional evening. It is the fingerprint of God on a human heart.

Which is the answer to a question that troubles thoughtful Christians more than theyusually say: how do I know I am not simply talked into this? Here is one honest place tolook. If Christ is genuinely your Lord — not merely your preference or your heritage— then according to this verse somebody did that to you, and the somebody was the thirdperson of the Trinity. The most ordinary Christian confession in the world is a supernaturalevent.

Now the practical use of the test, which is considerable. Corinth wanted a way to tell theSpirit’s work from spiritual theatre, and Paul gives them one that requires no specialinsight: listen to what is being said about Jesus. The Spirit’s whole business is toglorify Christ — he will glorify me, for he will take what is mine and declare itto you (Jn 16:14). So a movement, a meeting, a teacher or a book that makes much of theSpirit and comparatively little of Christ has failed the only test the New Testament gives,however remarkable the phenomena. And a quiet congregation where Christ is honoured andtrusted has passed it, however unremarkable the phenomena.

The Spirit is the least self-advertising person in the universe. He is like a floodlighttrained on a building at night: doing all the work, entirely unlooked at, and content thatwhat people see is the building (cf. Rom 10:9; 1 Jn 4:2–3).

verseByVerse.quote: Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of service, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of activities, but it is the same God who empowers them all in everyone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties ofservice, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of activities, but it is the same God whoempowers them all in everyone.

Three sentences with the same shape, and the shape is the argument. Variety on one side,sameness on the other, three times over. Paul is doing something more than making a pointabout unity; he is showing where the unity comes from.

Look at the three persons named. The same Spirit, the same Lord (whichin Paul always means Jesus), the same God. Father, Son and Holy Spirit, laid out inone breath, in a paragraph about church squabbles — and Paul does not stop to explainor defend it. That is worth noticing in itself. The doctrine of the Trinity is sometimespresented as a late invention of arguing bishops. Here it is, twenty-odd years after thecrucifixion, so settled in the apostolic mind that it can be used as a passing illustrationin a letter about who is showing off in church.

And the three nouns are worth having. Gifts is charismata, from the wordfor grace — a gift is grace made specific, grace with a shape. Service isdiakoniai, where we get the word deacon: a gift is not an ornament but a job. Andactivities is energēmata, from which we get energy: it is God actuallydoing something through a person, not a talent the person owns and operates.

Put those three together and the Corinthian competition collapses on the spot. If a gift isgrace, nobody earned it. If it is service, it was never given for display. And if it is Godworking, then boasting about it is as odd as a chisel congratulating itself on thefurniture.

Here is a test worth running on any church, including a healthy one. When the gifted peoplein a congregation gather, is the conversation about what God is doing, or about who is doingit? The two sound similar and they are not the same. Paul’s three sentences make thesecond sort of conversation not merely uncharitable but incoherent, because the whole diversityhe is describing comes out of one source, and that source has no rivals inside itself.

And there is a comfort in this that is worth having for its own sake. Christians sometimesworry that they do not know how to relate to three persons at once — whether to pray tothe Spirit, whether attention paid to one is attention withheld from another. Paul’sthree sentences quietly settle it. There is no dividing them up, because they are neverworking separately. The gift in your hands was given by the Spirit, is a service rendered tothe Lord, and is God at work in you. One act, three persons, no seams.

Look at what that means about the God being described. Within his own life there has neverbeen a moment of competition. The Father is not diminished by the Son’s glory; theSpirit does not resent being the one nobody looks at; nothing in that fellowship has everneeded to be negotiated. And out of that life — unhurried, unthreatened, entirely atpeace with itself — came a world, and a cross, and a church full of quarrelling peoplein a Greek port, handed grace with a shape and set to work.

verseByVerse.quote: To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.

Fourteen words, and two of them settle questions that trouble a great many Christians.

To each. Not to some. Not to the impressive. Not to the ordained or thearticulate or the ones who were converted dramatically. Every believer in Corinth — andthis was a church containing slaves, dockworkers, and people Paul had already described asnot wise, not powerful, not of noble birth (1:26) — had received a manifestation of theSpirit. There are no giftless Christians. If you belong to Christ, something has been put intoyour hands.

Which is worth pressing, because a lot of people quietly believe otherwise aboutthemselves. The usual reasoning runs: I am not a teacher, I do not sing, I have never ledanything, I would not know what to say to a stranger about the gospel — therefore I amone of the ones who simply attends. This verse says that is not a category. It does not sayevery Christian has a prominent gift. It says every Christian has one.

For the common good. There is the purpose, and it is the sentence that ruins giftcompetition permanently. The Spirit does not hand out gifts as personal enrichment, spiritualsouvenirs, or evidence of standing. A gift is given to one person for the benefit of otherpeople. It is not the reward of the recipient; it is the property of the congregation, held inhis hands for a while. A gift used for self-display has not merely been used badly; it hasbeen used for the opposite of its purpose.

Which leaves the practical question that every honest reader wants answered, and it isusually left vague when it should not be: how do I find out what mine is?

Not, in the first place, by introspection. Gifts are discovered in use, not in analysis,and the New Testament never once instructs anyone to take an inventory of himself. Fourthings will do more than any questionnaire. First, start serving something — anythingthe church actually needs — and notice what happens. Second, watch for the thing thatleaves other people strengthened rather than merely impressed; that is the mark of a gift asagainst a talent. Third, ask two or three Christians who know you well and will tell you thetruth, because gifts are far easier to see from outside than from inside. Fourth, notice whatyou keep being asked to do; congregations are usually better at spotting gifts than thepeople who have them.

And notice what is not on that list: whether you enjoy it, and whether you arenaturally good at it. Both are useful signs and neither is decisive. This is amanifestation of the Spirit, not a personality test, and the Spirit has been known towork through people who found the work difficult all their lives.

verseByVerse.quote: For to one is given through the Spirit the utterance of wisdom, and to another the utterance of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by the one Spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For to one is given through the Spirit the utterance of wisdom, and to another theutterance of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith by the same Spirit, toanother gifts of healing by the one Spirit.

The list begins, and Paul offers no definitions, which suggests the Corinthians knew whathe meant. We have to work a little harder, and it is worth doing rather than hurrying pastthe names.

The utterance of wisdom and the utterance of knowledge are both, in theGreek, a word of wisdom and a word of knowledge — something said, notmerely something possessed. Wisdom in this letter is not cleverness; Paul has spent twochapters saying that the wisdom of God is a crucified man (1:23–24). So this gift is thecapacity to say the thing that applies the gospel to the situation in front of you. Everyonehas met it: the believer who is not especially learned but who, in a crisis, says the onesentence that helps. Knowledge is its companion — grasping the truth of God and beingable to put it into words that hold.

Then faith, which is puzzling at first, since every Christian has faith. Paul mustmean something beyond saving faith, which he never treats as a special endowment. The bestsense is a particular God-given confidence for a particular thing: the believer who iscertain God will provide for a work when everyone else is doing sums, and is proved right.It is the sort of faith Jesus described as moving mountains, and Paul will use exactly thatimage in the next chapter.

And gifts of healing — both nouns plural in the Greek, which is itselfinstructive. Not the gift of healing, a standing power a man carries around, butgifts of healings: particular acts of mercy, given occasion by occasion.

Which raises the question every reader brings to this verse, and it deserves an honestanswer rather than a slogan. Does God still heal? Yes. He is not less able than he was, andChristians should pray for the sick expectantly and without embarrassment, becausethey are told to (Jas 5:14–15).

And does he always? Plainly not, and the New Testament is remarkably candid about it. Paulleft Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Tim 4:20). Epaphroditus nearly died, and Paul calls hisrecovery a mercy rather than an entitlement (Phil 2:27). Timothy had a chronic stomachcomplaint and got advice about wine, not a healing (1 Tim 5:23). And Paul himself asked threetimes for his own thorn to be removed and was told no, with a reason: my grace issufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness (2 Cor 12:8–9).

That is enormously important for anyone who has prayed and not been healed, or who hasbeen told that the failure was theirs. If the apostle who raised a man from the dead atTroas could not heal his own friend or himself, then unhealed sickness in a Christian is notevidence of a lack of faith. It is evidence that the gifts are given as he wills, andthat the will in question is wiser than ours.

verseByVerse.quote: to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the ability to distinguish between spirits, to another various kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues. All these are empowered by one and the same Spirit, who apportions to each one individually as he wills.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the ability todistinguish between spirits, to another various kinds of tongues, to another theinterpretation of tongues. All these are empowered by one and the same Spirit, who apportionsto each one individually as he wills.

Five more, and three of them will occupy the whole of chapter 14, so a short account herewill do.

Prophecy in the New Testament is not primarily prediction. It is speech that comesto a congregation from God for that congregation, and its effect is described plainly in thenext chapters: it builds up, encourages and consoles (14:3), and it can lay bare the secrets ofa heart so that an outsider falls down and worships (14:24–25). Crucially, Paul assumesit must be tested. Let the others weigh what is said (14:29) is not a thing anyonewould say about Scripture. So whatever prophecy is, it stands under the written Word and neverbeside it, and no genuine prophecy has ever added a line to the Bible or ever will.

The ability to distinguish between spirits is the companion gift, and its presencein the list is telling: Paul assumes that not everything claiming to be from God is from God,and that some believers are given a nose for the difference. Verse 3 has already supplied thepublic test; this is the discernment that goes with it.

Various kinds of tongues and their interpretation are the gifts Corinthprized most and understood least, and chapter 14 is Paul’s careful, unhurried treatmentof them. It is enough to note here that he includes them without a hint of scorn — theyare on the list, given by the Spirit, and he will say himself that he speaks in tongues morethan any of them (14:18).

Then the closing sentence, which governs the whole chapter: who apportions to each oneindividually as he wills.

There is real comfort in that clause and real rebuke. The rebuke is to anyone who thinks agift reflects credit on its holder. The comfort is for anyone who has begged for a gift andnot received it, and has been told by someone confident that the fault lies in his faith. Thedistribution is the Spirit’s free act. He is not a machine that dispenses on demand,and he has never given anybody grounds for despising a Christian who lacks something.

Christians differ, and have differed for centuries, over whether the more spectacular itemson this list continue today or belonged to the church’s foundation. Both convictions areheld by people who love the Bible and each other, and the passage on which the question turnsis 13:8–12, where it will be taken up properly. What this verse settles, whichever way areader lands, is that no one may look down on another Christian over it. The Spirit apportionsas he wills, and that clause has never yet been amended by a committee on eitherside.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The body metaphor is one of the most extended analogies in Paul, and it carries more theological weight than most analogies. The human body is composed of many different members, all necessary, all interdependent, all contributing to the functioning of the whole. The application is precise: just so the body of Christ. Every member is placed by God’s sovereign act (v. 18); every member is necessary (vv. 22–24); no member can claim independence from the rest (v. 21); all members share in the suffering and honour of every other (v. 26).

The two failure modes Paul addresses are complementary: the inferiority complex (“because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,” v. 15) and the contempt of the strong for the weak (“I have no need of you,” v. 21). Both stem from the same mistake: valuing members by the world’s criteria of impressiveness rather than God’s criteria of design. The feebler members are indispensable (v. 22); the less presentable members are given greater honour (v. 23–24). This inversion of the world’s hierarchy within the body of Christ is the social expression of the cross.

Two further strokes complete the picture. Verse 17 presses the absurdity: a body that is all eye is not a better body but a monster, deaf and unable to smell smoke — which is what a congregation becomes when it quietly settles on one approved kind of Christian. And verse 25 states God’s purpose in composing the body as he did: that there may be no division in the body, but that the members may have the same care for one another. The unity of a church is not a project the members thought up. It is what God was aiming at when he handed out the gifts in the first place.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Body of Christ: Ecclesiology and Soteriology United

Paul’s body metaphor is not merely sociological (a useful way to describe community life) but soteriological: the church is the body of Christ because the Spirit has baptised all believers into the one body of the crucified and risen Lord (v. 13). The union is real — not metaphorical — which is why the suffering of one member is genuinely felt by the whole (v. 26). The theology of the body of Christ is the foundation of Paul’s entire ethic of community: you cannot be indifferent to the suffering of a fellow member of Christ’s body any more than your left hand can be indifferent to the pain in your right foot.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian gift-competition had produced both contempt (the tongues-speakers dismissing those with lesser gifts) and despair (those with lesser gifts feeling excluded). Paul’s body metaphor addresses both directly: the despairers are told they belong; the contemptuous are told they need those they despise. Now: Every church community has its impressive and its unimpressive members by the world’s standards. Paul’s insight is that the one who seems indispensable and the one who seems marginal are both placed by the same God — and the functioning of the body requires both.

verseByVerse.quote: For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so it is with Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body—Jews or Greeks, slaves or free—and all were made to drink of one Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body,though many, are one body, so it is with Christ.

The image arrives, and Paul will spend fifteen verses on it. But notice how the firstsentence ends, because he does not finish it the way anyone expects. The natural conclusion isso it is with the church. What he writes is so it is with Christ.

That is not a slip. The church is not merely like a body; it is his body,and Paul means the identification more literally than most of us are comfortable with. It iswhat the risen Lord said to a man on the Damascus road who had never laid a finger on himpersonally: Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4). Saul had beenarresting Christians in Jerusalem. Christ counted it as an assault on himself. The man whoheard that sentence is the man writing this one.

For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body — Jews or Greeks, slaves orfree — and all were made to drink of one Spirit.

Two of Paul’s favourite words, all and one, are doing heavy workhere, and they answer a question many Christians have been troubled by. Is there a secondexperience after conversion, a baptism in the Spirit, which some believers have and otherslack?

Paul’s sentence is hard to get round: we were all baptized intoone body — and he is writing to a church whose spiritual life was a shambles, withfactions, a man in gross immorality, lawsuits and drunkenness at the Lord’s table. Ifany congregation could have been described as second-class in the Spirit, it was this one, andhe says all of them have had it. Baptism in the Spirit, in this verse, is not an advancedstage. It is what happened to every Christian when he became one. It is the entrance, not theupgrade.

That should be said clearly, and something else should be said just as clearly, becausebrothers and sisters who use the phrase differently are usually reaching for something real.Scripture plainly teaches repeated, fresh, powerful fillings of the Spirit after conversion.The same believers in Acts who were filled in chapter 2 are filled again in chapter 4(Acts 4:31), and Christians are commanded to go on being filled with the Spirit(Eph 5:18) — a present tense, a continuous thing, not a single event. So the hungerbehind the question is right and should not be shamed. A Christian may and should ask formore of God. What he need not ask for is admission to a body he has already been baptisedinto.

And see what the Spirit does with the categories. Jews or Greeks, slaves or free.Those were the deepest divisions in that world — religious and economic, the two thatstill do most of the damage. The Spirit does not abolish the differences; a Jew was still aJew and a slave still went back to his master. He does something better. He puts them in onebody, so that the differences remain and stop being walls (cf. Gal 3:27–28;Eph 2:14–16).

verseByVerse.quote: For the body does not consist of one member but of many. If the foot should say, “Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body. And if the ear should say, “Because I am not an eye, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the body does not consist of one member but of many. If the foot should say,“Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it anyless a part of the body.

Paul now gives the body a voice, and the first thing it says is a complaint about itself.It is worth noticing whom he addresses first. Not the proud — they come at verse 21.The discouraged.

Listen to the logic of the foot. It has looked at the hand, admired what the hand can do,concluded that it cannot do any of it, and drawn the inference: therefore I am not really partof this. The reasoning feels like humility. It is not. It is a verdict passed on God’sarrangement by a body part that has decided it knows better, and Paul answers it with a shrug:saying so would not make it any less a part of the body.

That is the whole reply, and it is beautifully unimpressed. The foot’s membership isnot a matter of the foot’s opinion. Feelings of not belonging do not detach anybody fromChrist’s body, any more than a man’s low view of his own left foot detaches it fromhis leg. Belonging was settled by the Spirit’s baptism in verse 13, and it is notreopened every time a member feels unimpressive.

Which is worth stating plainly for the sort of Christian who reads a passage on gifts with asinking heart. If your reasoning has ever run I cannot teach, I cannot sing, I have nostory worth telling, so I am really just making up the numbers — that is the foottalking, and the apostle’s response is not to reassure you about your abilities. It is totell you that the question of belonging was never yours to settle.

And notice the comparison that started it. The foot did not compare itself to a foot. Itcompared itself to a hand — which is precisely the trick that makes the comparisonuseless and painful at once. Nobody is ever discouraged by comparing himself with someone doingthe same job; discouragement comes from measuring yourself against a gift you were never givenand then treating the shortfall as a personal failing. It is a fixed law of the Christian lifethat comparison always looks upward and never sideways.

There is a practical consequence, and it is one of the quiet tragedies of church life. Thefoot in this parable does not merely feel bad. It withdraws. People who conclude they do notbelong stop offering, stop coming forward, and eventually stop coming; and because they leaveslowly and apologetically, nobody chases them. If that has been your own drift, the verse isaddressed to you directly, and its answer is not a compliment but a fact: your leaving wouldnot make you any less a part of the body, and it would leave the body without a foot.

And there is something for everyone else in it too. The discouraged rarely announcethemselves. They do not say I do not belong here; they say they are busy that week.A congregation that waits to be told will never find out. Which is why the ordinary work ofasking a quiet member what he is finding hard, and meaning the question, is not small talk. Itis body maintenance.

verseByVerse.quote: If the whole body were an eye, where would be the sense of hearing? If the whole body were an ear, where would be the sense of smell?
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the whole body were an eye, where would be the sense of hearing? If the whole bodywere an ear, where would be the sense of smell?

Paul argues by absurdity, and it is worth letting the absurdity land rather than treatingit as a figure of speech. Picture it. A body that is one enormous eye. Not a better body— a monster, and a helpless one, unable to hear a shout or smell smoke.

Which is exactly what Corinth was trying to become. If tongues is the true mark of theSpirit, then the ideal congregation is one where everybody speaks in tongues and nothing elsehappens. Paul says: look at what you are asking for. A church where every member has the samegift is not a super-church. It is a church that has lost the ability to do everything that giftdoes not do.

And the argument works just as well against the opposite error, which is more common insober congregations. A church where everyone is a teacher is a church that talks and nevervisits. A church of activists is one that never thinks. A church that has quietly decidedwhich sort of Christian it approves of — and every church has one — is a bodygrowing a second eye where an ear should be.

Here is a test that any congregation can run and few do. Look at who has left over the lastfive years, and who has quietly stopped coming. Then ask what kinds of people they were. Ifthey were all one kind, the church has been growing a monoculture, and it will have lost thesense that those members carried before it noticed the loss. A body does not usually announcethat it has gone deaf. It simply stops responding to things.

The point is not that variety is pleasant. It is that variety is functional. Goddid not scatter different gifts around a congregation for the sake of interest. He did itbecause the work requires all of them, and no member has been given a gift that makes theothers optional.

There is a second thing hiding in the two senses Paul names. Hearing and smell are notalternative ways of doing what the eye does; they are ways of knowing what the eye cannotknow. An eye cannot detect a gas leak. This is why a church with a narrow range of gifts isnot merely less varied but genuinely less aware: there are things about its own situationthat it has no organ to perceive. The pastoral instinct that notices a family is in trouble,the practical instinct that notices the accounts are drifting, the discerning instinct thatnotices a teacher has begun to say something slightly wrong — these are differentsenses, and a body without them is not simply plainer. It is walking about with its eyes openand no idea what is happening.

Which is why the members a church finds least congenial are so often the ones it mostneeds. The person whose questions are awkward, whose concerns are always about the thingnobody else is worried about, whose temperament grates — that person may be thecongregation’s sense of smell, and a body that silences him will not notice the smoke.

verseByVerse.quote: But as it is, God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose. If all were a single member, where would the body be? As it is, there are many parts, yet one body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But as it is, God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose. Ifall were a single member, where would the body be? As it is, there are many parts, yet onebody.

Here is the answer to the discouraged foot, and it is not encouragement. It is doctrine.

God arranged. The verb is deliberate placement — the word for settingsomething where you have decided it should go. And then, in case anyone should think thishappened at the level of general policy, Paul adds three words that make it personal:each one of them. Not the body arranged in general, with individuals falling wherethey may. Each member, placed.

Sit with what that means for an ordinary Christian in an ordinary church. The gift youhave was chosen for you. The gift you do not have was withheld on purpose. The congregationyou are in, with its particular needs and its particular gaps, is the place you were setdown. None of it is a leftover arrangement after the interesting decisions were madeelsewhere.

As he chose is the same note struck at verse 11, and it is the doctrine ofGod’s sovereign choosing applied to the most everyday thing imaginable — who doeswhat on a Sunday. It cuts in two directions at once, which is how you can tell it is beingused properly. To the person who is proud of his gift: you were handed it, and a man who isproud of a present has misunderstood the transaction. To the person who wishes he weresomebody else: your wish is a complaint about the placement, and the one who did the placingknew exactly what he was doing.

There is a particular ache this speaks to, and it is worth naming because most people carryit privately. It is the sense of having been assigned a smaller life than the one you wouldhave chosen — a quieter role, a less visible service, a set of abilities that will neverbe remarked on. That is not a mistake in the distribution. The body has parts nobody has everphotographed, and it dies without them.

Then the closing line, and it is the whole doctrine of the church in six words: manyparts, yet one body. Not many parts that ought to become one; many parts that alreadyare. Unity is not the church’s achievement. It is the church’s startingcondition, and everything Paul asks of the Corinthians is simply that they stop contradictingwhat is already true of them (cf. Eph 4:3–4).

One caution, since this doctrine can be turned into a cushion. God arranged is nota licence to refuse anything you have not been specially equipped for. Plenty of what a churchneeds done is not a gift at all; it is simply obedience, and it is required of everyone. EveryChristian is commanded to give, to pray, to show hospitality, to speak the truth in love, tobear with difficult people, and to tell others about Christ, whether or not any of it comeseasily. Nobody is excused from the ordinary duties on the grounds that generosity is not hisgifting.

The distinction is simple enough to apply. Gifts describe how you will serve mostfruitfully. They never describe the limits of what you will do. A hand that declines to helpbecause carrying is properly the shoulder’s work has misread the whole chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: The eye cannot say to the hand, “I have no need of you,” nor again the head to the feet, “I have no need of you.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eye cannot say to the hand, “I have no need of you,” nor again the headto the feet, “I have no need of you.”

Now the other failure, and Paul has waited seven verses to get to it. The first speech wasthe discouraged member talking about himself. This one is the impressive member talking aboutsomebody else.

Notice who is speaking. The eye and the head — the noble parts, the ones in theportrait, the ones that get named when people describe you. And notice whom they dismiss: thehand that does the work and the feet that do the walking. It is a precise little satire on theCorinthian situation, where the members with the visible gifts had concluded that the rest ofthe congregation was decorative.

The word to weigh is cannot. Paul does not say the eye should not say it,or that it is unkind to say it. He says the eye cannot, meaning the statement is notmerely rude but false. An eye that announces it has no need of hands has said something untrueabout itself. It will be needing those hands within the hour, and it will be needing themwithout ever noticing that it does.

Which is how contempt in a church almost always works. It is not usually spoken. Very fewpeople have ever said I have no need of you out loud to another believer, and anyonewho did would be rebuked for it. It is expressed by omission: who gets consulted, who getsinvited, who is treated as background. The sentence gets said by a seating plan, a rota, aconversation that stops when a certain person joins it.

So here is a test with teeth. Think of the person in your congregation whose absence nextSunday would make the least difference to you. Now ask what would actually stop if that personstopped — and be honest, because you may well not know, which is itself the answer. Theparts of a body you never think about are precisely the ones you find out about when theyfail.

And there is a reason the impressive members are the ones warned here. The temptation todespise is not evenly distributed. It belongs almost entirely to the gifted, the busy and thecapable, who can generally manage without help and so come to believe that they do.

What does repentance look like here? Not a warmer feeling about people you find tedious;feelings are not directly available to the will, and trying to manufacture them producescondescension, which is worse. Something more practical is required. Ask a member you haveoverlooked for advice about something that matters to you, and then take it. Put a name youhave never put there onto the list of people whose opinion you seek. Sit somewhere else.Discover, by asking rather than assuming, what a person you had filed as marginal actuallydoes with his week.

Contempt is broken by finding out that the sentence was false, and the only way to findthat out is to need the person and see what happens. The eye cannot argue itself into valuingthe hand. It has to try picking something up.

verseByVerse.quote: On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable, and on those parts of the body that we think less honorable we bestow the greater honor, and our unpresentable parts are treated with greater modesty, which our more presentable parts do not require. But God has so composed the body, giving greater honor to the part that lacked it,
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable, and onthose parts of the body that we think less honorable we bestow the greater honor, and ourunpresentable parts are treated with greater modesty, which our more presentable parts do notrequire. But God has so composed the body, giving greater honor to the part that lackedit.

Paul now turns the world’s ranking upside down, and he does it with an observationanybody can verify on his own person.

The parts that seem weaker are in fact indispensable — the wordmeans you cannot do without them. Think of what is actually true of a body. The strong partsare the ones on show: the arms, the shoulders, the face. The parts you cannot survive withoutare soft, hidden and defenceless — the heart, the lungs, the eyes themselves, all ofthem tucked behind bone precisely because they could not take a blow. And the parts nobodyphotographs are the ones we clothe with the greatest care, which is Paul’s secondobservation and a delicate one: we spend more effort covering what is unpresentable thandisplaying what is presentable. A man will leave his face bare in all weathers and would notdream of leaving the rest of himself so.

Then the theological punchline: God has so composed the body, giving greater honor tothe part that lacked it. This is not human sentiment about the underdog. It is the design.God deliberately built compensation into the arrangement, so that the members with no naturalstanding receive an honour that is given rather than earned.

Which means a congregation that honours its unimpressive members is not being nice. It isbeing accurate. So who are they? Be concrete, because vagueness here costs somebodysomething real. They are the housebound woman who has not been in the building for threeyears and prays through the church list every morning. The man with a learning disabilitywhose questions in the Bible study slow everybody down. The elderly member whose memory hasgone, who cannot follow the sermon, and who is still, on this verse, a load-bearing part ofthe body. The person who cleans up afterwards. The one who is simply hard work.

The world grades people by what they contribute. Paul says the body of Christ is composedon the opposite principle, and he says it because of the cross. The pattern was set by a Lordwho was despised and rejected, who had no form or majesty that we should look athim (Isa 53:2–3), and who turned out to be the one part of the whole arrangementthat nothing could do without. A church that measures its members by prominence has forgottenwhat its own head looked like.

verseByVerse.quote: that there may be no division in the body, but that the members may have the same care for one another. If one member suffers, all suffer together; if one member is honored, all rejoice together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That there may be no division in the body, but that the members may have the same carefor one another. If one member suffers, all suffer together; if one member is honored, allrejoice together.

Here is the purpose of the whole arrangement, and it is stated as God’s aim ratherthan as a target for the congregation: he composed the body so that there would beno division in it. The unity of a church is not a project that the members dreamt up. It iswhat God was after when he handed out the gifts in the first place.

Then verse 26, which is not an appeal. Read it carefully: Paul does not say the membersought to suffer together. He says they do. It is a statement about howbodies work.

And it is exactly true of the physical body, in a way that repays a moment’sthought. Stub one toe in the dark and the whole organism reacts — the breath catches,the eyes water, the hands reach, the voice makes a sound it did not plan. Nobody has topersuade the shoulder to care about the foot. The body does not hold a meeting about whetherthe injury is serious enough to warrant a response. It responds because the foot is notsomebody else.

Which turns the usual application inside out. The question this verse puts to acongregation is not are you being sympathetic enough? It is diagnostic. A churchwhere a member can lose a job, a marriage or a child and the rest of the body carries onundisturbed is not an unkind body. It is a body with nerve damage, where the signal is beingsent and nothing is arriving. That is a more serious condition than a failure of effort, andit is not cured by exhortation.

Note also the second half, because it is the harder half in practice. If one member ishonored, all rejoice together. Most Christians find it easier to weep with those whoweep than to rejoice with those who rejoice. Sympathy costs nothing but time; gladness atanother’s success costs you the comparison. When someone else in the congregation getsthe thing you have prayed for and not received — the child, the recovery, the post, theinvitation — the body’s health is measured by what happens in you at that moment,and it is measured more accurately there than at any funeral (cf. Rom 12:15).

How does a body actually come to feel what its members feel? Not by resolving to. Nervesare built out of information, and the practical form of this verse is unglamorous: knowingpeople’s names, knowing what is happening in their lives, and asking again the followingweek. Suffering that nobody knows about cannot be shared, and a great deal of the suffering inmost congregations is invisible because nobody has ever asked a second question.

Note too that the sharing runs in both directions and neither direction is optional. Amember who tells nobody anything has, with the best intentions, cut his own nerve. Privacy isnot a Christian virtue in a body; it is how a limb goes numb. Letting people know that you arestruggling is not weakness or self-indulgence, and this verse quietly requires it, because abody cannot suffer together with a member who has determined to suffer alone.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–31 — Varieties of Gifts: The Greater Gifts
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chapter closes by affirming the diversity of gifts in the body of Christ, listing a series of roles that are distributed by God’s sovereign appointment: apostles, prophets, teachers, miracles, healing, helping, administration, tongues. The rhetorical questions — “Are all apostles? Are all prophets?...” — all expect the answer “no” and reinforce the diversity of the body. Spiritual unity does not require spiritual uniformity.

The closing verse — “earnestly desire the higher gifts. And I will show you a still more excellent way” — is the hinge between chapters 12 and 13. The encouragement to desire higher gifts (presumably prophecy, which builds up the community, over tongues, which edifies only the speaker) is consistent with the chapter’s logic: the higher gifts are those that most benefit the whole body. But the “still more excellent way” is not another gift; it is the quality that makes all gifts truly excellent: love.

The section opens with the sentence everything else rests on: now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it (v. 27). Not you should be, not you will be if you improve — to a factional, arrogant congregation Paul says you are. The identity comes first and the instructions follow, which is the order the New Testament always uses. And both halves of the sentence hold: no one is the body alone, and no one is swallowed by it. A hand in a body is more itself, not less.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Ordering of Gifts and the Priority of Love

The list of gifts in vv. 28–30, with its implied ordering (first, second, third), suggests that Paul does see a hierarchy of value in gifts — not because some are intrinsically superior but because some are more directly edifying for the whole community. Apostles and prophets lay the doctrinal foundation; teachers expound it; the other gifts serve the body in various ways. But the “still more excellent way” of chapter 13 is not a further gift above tongues and prophecy; it is the character quality that makes the exercise of any gift genuinely excellent.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian gift-competition had inverted the hierarchy: tongues (the most self-focused gift in Paul’s analysis) was being treated as the most prestigious. Paul’s list puts tongues last. The correction is not to dismiss tongues but to reorder values: gifts that build the community outrank gifts that edify only the speaker. Now: The principle applies in every community: the gifted teacher who uses his gift to impress rather than to build up the body has missed what gifts are for. The “excellent way” is available to every gift-user who submits his gift to love.

verseByVerse.quote: Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it. And God has appointed in the church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healing, helping, administrating, and various kinds of tongues.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it.

Paul lands the metaphor. And the verb is the one to watch: you are. Not you shouldbe, not you must strive to become, not you will be if you sort yourselves out. To thiscongregation — factional, arrogant, drunk at communion, tolerating scandal — theapostle says: you are the body of Christ. The identity comes first and theinstructions come afterwards, which is the order the New Testament always uses and the reverseof the order that comes naturally to religious people.

Then individually members of it. Both halves of that matter. You are not the bodyon your own; and you are not swallowed by it either. Christianity has never asked anyone todissolve into a collective. A hand in a body is more itself, not less.

And God has appointed in the church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers,then miracles, then gifts of healing, helping, administrating, and various kinds oftongues.

This list is numbered, which the earlier one was not, and the numbering is doing something.The first three all have to do with the word of God — apostles who received anddelivered it, prophets who brought it to the congregation, teachers who explain it. Those comefirst because everything else in a church is built on what God has said. Take the word out andthe rest is activity.

Two things in the list are easily overlooked and should not be. Helping is a wordassociated with practical aid to those in need — and Paul has just put it in the samelist as miracles and healing. Administrating is a nautical word: it means steering,what a helmsman does. So the person who keeps the accounts straight, arranges the rota andmakes sure the widow gets visited is exercising a gift of the Holy Spirit, named alongsidethe spectacular ones by the apostle himself. A great many churches would be transformed bybelieving that sentence.

And apostles — are there any now? The office as Paul describes it hadconditions attached that cannot now be met: an apostle had seen the risen Lord (9:1) and wascommissioned directly by him, and the apostles together are called the foundation of thechurch, with Christ as the cornerstone (Eph 2:20). A foundation is laid once; a building witha permanent foundation-laying department has a serious problem. So the office in that senseclosed. The word also has a broader use in the New Testament — a sent one, a pioneer— and that work has never stopped: church-planters and missionaries doing today whatPaul did at Corinth. Christians who use the title for such people usually mean the secondthing, and the disagreement is often smaller than the vocabulary makes it sound.

verseByVerse.quote: Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all work miracles? Do all possess gifts of healing? Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all work miracles? Do allpossess gifts of healing? Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret?

Seven questions, and in Greek each is framed to expect the answer no. Paul is notwondering aloud. He is closing a door.

The sixth question is the one Corinth cared about. Do all speak with tongues? No.That single syllable dismantles the whole system the church had built — the idea thatone gift is the badge of the Spirit’s presence and that the believers without it are inthe lower division. If the Spirit had intended tongues as the mark of genuine Christianity, hewould have given it to everyone. He has not, and the fact that he has not is itself theargument.

It is worth saying that this cuts both ways, and it should, because congregations havefound more than one way to make the same mistake. Any church which decides that a particulargift is the test of spiritual seriousness has fallen into the Corinthian error, whatever thegift is. Some do it with tongues. Some do it with a certain kind of doctrinal precision, orevangelistic boldness, or emotional expressiveness in worship, or a particular pattern ofquiet time. In every case the same sentence answers it. Do all? No.

And there is a mercy in that no which the discouraged reader should take. Theseven questions are usually read as a rebuke to the proud, and they are. But turn them roundand they are a release for everyone who has spent years feeling second-rate in church. Youwere never meant to be able to do all of it. The Spirit did not distribute the whole list toanybody, including the apostle writing the sentence. There has only ever been one person whocould do everything, and the whole point of the body is that he chose to do it throughthousands of people who cannot.

That is worth standing still in front of. Christ needed nothing. He could have preachedevery sermon, healed every sufferer, comforted every widow and administered every fundhimself, and done all of it better than the whole church put together has ever done any ofit. Instead he ascended, sent his Spirit, and handed the work out in fragments to fishermenand slaves and housewives and dockworkers, so that no one of them could manage without theothers and none of them could manage without him.

He did not need a body. He wanted one (cf. Eph 4:15–16).

verseByVerse.quote: But earnestly desire the higher gifts. And I will show you a still more excellent way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But earnestly desire the higher gifts. And I will show you a still more excellentway.

Two clauses, and each of them turns the argument.

The first looks, at first glance, like a contradiction. Paul has spent thirty verses sayingthe Spirit apportions as he wills, and now he tells them to want the higher gifts. Ifthe distribution is sovereign, what is the point of desiring anything?

But the two sit together perfectly well, and in fact they always do in Scripture. God issovereign over who is saved, and Christians are told to pray for the lost. He is sovereignover daily bread, and we are taught to ask for it. Sovereign distribution does not make desirepointless; it makes desire safe, because the asking is finally in the hands of someone whowill not give a stone to a child asking for bread (Matt 7:9). And note that the command isplural. Paul is not telling individuals to lobby for personal upgrades. He is telling acongregation what to want for itself.

Which explains what higher means, since it obviously cannot mean more impressiveafter everything just said about eyes and feet. It means more useful to other people. Paulwill spell it out at 14:5: the one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks intongues, because prophecy builds up the church. That is the whole scale. A gift ranks higherin proportion to how much good it does the person sitting next to you. By that measure thefaithful visitor of the sick outranks a great deal that gets applauded.

Then the last clause, and it is one of the great hinges in the Bible. And I will showyou a still more excellent way.

Everything is set up for Paul to name the top gift. He does not. He steps off the ladderaltogether, because the more excellent way is not a gift at all and cannot be distributedas he wills to some and not others. It is required of everybody, available toeverybody, and without it the entire list is worth nothing — which is precisely whatthe next chapter opens by saying.

So the sentence is doing two things at once. It is a promise, and it is a rebuke aimed ata church that had been arguing about rank for three chapters. They wanted to know which giftwas best. Paul is about to tell them that the question was wrong, and that a man may haveevery gift on the list, exercise them all with power, and be nothing whatever.

Notice, finally, the verb. I will show you. Not I will describe it, or define it,or commend it. Paul is about to put something in front of them and let them look at it, whichis why chapter 13 is written the way it is — not as an argument but almost as a portrait,sentence after sentence of what love does and does not do. And the portrait, when it arrives,will turn out to be recognisable. There has been exactly one life that was patient, kind, notenvious, not boastful, not irritable, bearing all things and enduring all things to the end.The more excellent way has a face.

12.text: <sup>1</sup>Now concerning spiritual gifts, brothers, I do not want you to be uninformed.<sup>2</sup>You know that when you were pagans you were led astray to mute idols, however you were led.<sup>3</sup>Therefore I want you to understand that no one speaking in the Spirit of God ever says “Jesus is accursed!” and no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except in the Holy Spirit.<sup>4</sup>Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit;<sup>5</sup>and there are varieties of service, but the same Lord;<sup>6</sup>and there are varieties of activities, but it is the same God who empowers them all in everyone.<sup>7</sup>To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.<sup>8</sup>For to one is given through the Spirit the utterance of wisdom, and to another the utterance of knowledge according to the same Spirit,<sup>9</sup>to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by the one Spirit,<sup>10</sup>to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the ability to distinguish between spirits, to another various kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues.<sup>11</sup>All these are empowered by one and the same Spirit, who apportions to each one individually as he wills.<sup>12</sup>For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so it is with Christ.<sup>13</sup>For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body—Jews or Greeks, slaves or free—and all were made to drink of one Spirit.<sup>14</sup>For the body does not consist of one member but of many.<sup>15</sup>If the foot should say, “Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body.<sup>16</sup>And if the ear should say, “Because I am not an eye, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body.<sup>17</sup>If the whole body were an eye, where would be the sense of hearing? If the whole body were an ear, where would be the sense of smell?<sup>18</sup>But as it is, God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose.<sup>19</sup>If all were a single member, where would the body be?<sup>20</sup>As it is, there are many parts, yet one body.<sup>21</sup>The eye cannot say to the hand, “I have no need of you,” nor again the head to the feet, “I have no need of you.”<sup>22</sup>On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable,<sup>23</sup>and on those parts of the body that we think less honorable we bestow the greater honor, and our unpresentable parts are treated with greater modesty,<sup>24</sup>which our more presentable parts do not require. But God has so composed the body, giving greater honor to the part that lacked it,<sup>25</sup>that there may be no division in the body, but that the members may have the same care for one another.<sup>26</sup>If one member suffers, all suffer together; if one member is honored, all rejoice together.<sup>27</sup>Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it.<sup>28</sup>And God has appointed in the church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healing, helping, administrating, and various kinds of tongues.<sup>29</sup>Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all work miracles?<sup>30</sup>Do all possess gifts of healing? Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret?<sup>31</sup>But earnestly desire the higher gifts. And I will show you a still more excellent way.

13.title: The Most Excellent Way: Love
13.overview:
Chapter 13 is one of the most celebrated passages in the Bible — and one of the most misread. It is not a lyric poem about romantic love inserted into a letter about spiritual gifts. It is a devastating critique of the Corinthian community’s spiritual life, placed between the diagnosis of gift-competition (ch. 12) and the prescription for ordered worship (ch. 14). The Corinthians had impressive gifts and no love; Paul tells them that without love, their gifts are precisely nothing. Worse than nothing: they are noise, vanity, and worthlessness.

Calvin made the greatest single observation about this chapter: read vv. 4–7 substituting “Christ” for “love,” and you have a portrait of Christ himself. Love is patient — Christ was patient with his disciples’ dullness, with the Pharisees’ hostility, with Pilate’s cowardice. Love is kind — Christ touched the leper no one would touch. Love does not envy or boast — Christ, who had every right to all glory, emptied himself. The chapter is therefore christological before it is ethical: love is not a human virtue to be cultivated but a character description of the One in whom we are hidden, who is being formed in us by his Spirit.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Three conditional sentences, each more devastating than the last. Tongues of men and of angels, without love — a noisy gong, a clanging cymbal. The image is precise: the most spectacular sound, the loudest, the most impressive, producing nothing but noise. Prophetic powers, fathomless knowledge, faith that moves mountains, without love — nothing. Not less valuable, not somewhat diminished — absolutely nothing. Give away everything, surrender the body to be burned, without love — I gain nothing.

The Corinthians had elevated tongues to the apex of the spiritual gift hierarchy. Paul says: tongues without love is noise. They prided themselves on their knowledge. Paul says: knowledge without love is nothing. They admired faith capable of miraculous acts. Paul says: miracle-working faith without love is nothing. The repetition is not accidental; it is cumulative and crushing. Every spiritual trophy the Corinthians had been polishing is worth exactly zero without the one thing they had failed to cultivate.

This is not an attack on the gifts themselves. Paul has not changed his mind about tongues, prophecy, or knowledge. He is attacking the assumption that the gifts are, in themselves, evidence of spiritual health. The most spiritually spectacular community can be the most spiritually bankrupt if love is absent. The cross, not spiritual performance, is the criterion of authentic Christianity.

Note the shift between the two verdicts, because it is deliberate. In verse 2 the gifts without love leave a man saying I am nothing; in verse 3 the sacrifices without love leave him saying I gain nothing. The first is about what a person is, the second about what he takes away with him. A whole life can be poured out, admired and written up, and yield its owner precisely nothing, because love is the only currency that will still be legal tender on that day.
verseByVerse.theology:
Love as the Form of All Virtues

Augustine called love (caritas) the form of all virtues — the quality without which no virtue is genuinely virtuous. Paul’s three strophes make the same point: spiritual gifts without love are not merely incomplete but negated. Reformed theology has grounded this in the law of love (Matt 22:37–40): the whole law is fulfilled in love, and therefore the whole Christian life, including the exercise of spiritual gifts, finds its telos and criterion in love. The gift that is not exercised in love has been severed from its own purpose.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian tongues-speaker who exercised his gift in a public meeting, leaving the congregation uninstructed and himself privately edified, was exhibiting Paul’s noisy gong in practice. The spiritual trophy was real; the love was absent; the gift had become noise. Now: The preacher who loves the sound of his own voice more than the people he is preaching to, the theologian who loves winning arguments more than the person he is arguing with, the worship leader who loves the experience he generates more than the congregation he is leading — all are producing noise, not music.

verseByVerse.quote: If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This chapter is read at weddings, and there is nothing wrong with that. But it was writtento a church that was tearing itself apart over which gifts were most impressive, and it landslike a blow. Chapter 12 ended with a promise of a more excellent way. Here it is, and itbegins by pricing everything the Corinthians were proud of.

If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am a noisy gong ora clanging cymbal.

Paul starts at the top. Not merely every human language, but the speech of angels —he grants his opponents more than they were claiming, and then demolishes it. The gong andthe cymbal are worth picturing, because the choice of instruments is not random. These werethe instruments of the pagan temples the Corinthians had come out of — bronze, loud,resonant, and carrying no words. Someone in that congregation had heard those cymbals crashin a temple courtyard as a boy. Paul is telling him that his gift, exercised without love,makes the same sound.

Note the picture precisely. A gong is not silent. It is the loudest thing in the room, andthat is the trouble with it: it fills a space, everyone turns round, and afterwards nobody cansay what it said.

And if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and ifI have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing.

The stakes rise. Prophecy, which chapter 14 will call the greatest of the speaking gifts.Understanding all mysteries and all knowledge — not a great deal oftheology but the whole of it, without gaps. Faith enough to move mountains, which is theLord’s own image for the largest faith imaginable (Matt 17:20).

And then the verdict, and it is not the one anyone expects. Paul does not say that such aman has less than he thinks, or that his ministry is diminished. He says I am nothing— not my gift is nothing, but I am. The failure is not in the performance; it reachesback to the performer. A man can be a first-class instrument and not be a Christian at all,and the gifts will not tell him which he is.

That is a sobering thing to put to anyone who serves in a church, and it should be putpersonally rather than left in the air. It is entirely possible to preach well, pray inpublic with feeling, know your Bible thoroughly, give generously of your time, be thanked forall of it — and be nothing. The gifts are given as he wills (12:11), whichmeans they are no evidence about the man holding them. Judas had them all and used them, andnobody at that table suspected him until the night he left (cf. Matt 7:22–23).

verseByVerse.quote: If I give away all I have, and if I deliver up my body to be burned, but have not love, I gain nothing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If I give away all I have, and if I deliver up my body to be burned, but have not love,I gain nothing.

Paul has finished with the gifts and moves to the deeds — and he goes straight to thetwo that no one has ever been able to top.

The first is total divestment. Not generous giving; the Greek suggests parcelling outeverything you own, morsel by morsel, until there is nothing left. The second is martyrdom.A man walks into the fire rather than deny his Lord. Between them, these are the summit ofwhat Christian devotion has ever been asked to produce, and they are the two acts that nocongregation on earth would dare to question.

Paul questions them.

And the fact that he can shows how far he is willing to press the point: it is possible todo the most extreme thing a human being can do and have the wrong reason for it. A man maygive away his fortune because he cannot bear to be thought ordinary. A man may go to thestake because his own consistency has become the thing he worships, or because he cannotface what climbing down would cost him in front of people who are watching. Sacrifice provesthat something mattered more than comfort. It does not prove what.

There is a small textual matter here worth mentioning, since a reader comparing translationswill meet it. Two Greek words differing by a letter or two lie behind the phrase; one meansthat I may be burned, the other that I may boast, and the manuscripts aredivided. Either way the sentence works, and the second is almost bleakly appropriate to thepoint — a sacrifice offered so that one has something to say about it.
