Then the phrase that has been quietly changed. In verse 2 it was I am nothing;here it is I gain nothing. The first was about what a man is; this is about what hetakes away with him. A whole life could be poured out, admired, written up, and yield itsowner precisely nothing at the end, because the only currency that will still be legal tenderon that day is love.

Which raises a question this chapter deserves to have asked of it early: if love is theone thing that counts, and I look inside myself and find rather little of it, what am Isupposed to do? The answer is not to try harder to feel it, and the chapter never suggeststhat. It is coming, and it lies in the direction of verse 12 — being fully known andloved anyway. We love because he first loved us (1 Jn 4:19). Nobody has evergenerated this from a standing start.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Here is the portrait of love — and if Calvin is right (and he is), here is the portrait of Christ. Fifteen characteristics, expressed as a series of verbal predicates: love is patient, love is kind; love does not envy or boast, is not arrogant or rude; love does not insist on its own way, is not irritable or resentful; love does not rejoice at wrongdoing but rejoices with the truth; love bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.

The list is not abstract; it is surgical. Every negative attribute that Paul names was visibly present at Corinth. Envy — present in the faction fights. Boasting — the characteristic sin of the chapter. Arrogance (physioutai) — the word used for Corinthian pride throughout the letter. Insisting on its own way — the “strong” in ch. 8. Resentful — the factions carrying their grievances. Rejoicing at wrongdoing — the community “proud” of tolerating the incestuous relationship (ch. 5). Paul is not offering a general description of a virtue; he is diagnosing Corinth by the negative of love.

The four great “all things” of v. 7 deserve particular attention: “bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.” This is not naive credulity or doormat passivity; it is the resilience of a love that is rooted in something deeper than circumstances — the love that suffers without giving up, that trusts without demanding guarantees, that hopes when evidence is thin, that endures when endurance costs everything. This is the love of the cross: patient, determined, costly, final.

Two items in the middle of the list repay slowing down over. Not resentful (v. 5) translates an accountant’s phrase: love does not reckon up the evil, does not enter the wrong in a ledger where it can be produced later. It is the same verb used of God not counting our trespasses against us (2 Cor 5:19). And verse 6 — it does not rejoice at wrongdoing, but rejoices with the truth — catches the small private pleasure that rises when bad news turns out to be true about someone we resent. Its positive half settles a standing question: love and honesty are not rivals but allies, glad about the same things.

A guard is needed on the four all things of verse 7, because they have been used to do harm. They describe what love does with the wrongs it suffers, not what it does with the wrongs it discovers. The apostle who wrote them told this same church to put a man out of its fellowship (5:11–13), named Alexander the coppersmith in a warning (2 Tim 4:14), and rebuked Peter publicly (Gal 2:11). Love covers an insult without publishing it; it never covers an assault and calls that patience.
verseByVerse.theology:
Love as a Christological Description

Calvin’s insight deserves full weight: replace “love” in vv. 4–7 with “Jesus Christ” and the sentences remain true. Christ is patient — he waited thirty years before beginning his public ministry; he bore with his disciples for three years; he endured the cross. Christ is kind — he touched lepers, welcomed children, ate with sinners. Christ does not insist on his own way — “not my will, but yours be done.” Christ does not rejoice at wrongdoing but rejoices with the truth. Christ bears all things, believes all things (his faith was perfect toward the Father), hopes all things (the joy set before him, Heb 12:2), endures all things (the cross). Love is not primarily a commandment to be obeyed but a Person to be united with — and as Christ is formed in us (Gal 4:19), his character becomes our character.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s list is a mirror held up to Corinth. Every community that reads 1 Corinthians 13 should see itself in it — not as an aspiration but as a diagnostic. Where is the envy? The boasting? The resentment carried from meeting to meeting? The delight when a rival stumbles? The catalogue of love’s character is simultaneously a catalogue of the community’s failures. Now: The most powerful apologetic for Christianity in the twenty-first century is not a philosophical argument but a community that actually loves this way — that bears, believes, hopes, and endures. The watching world knows what love looks like; it is waiting to see if the church produces it.

verseByVerse.quote: Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant.

Now the portrait. And notice at once that every item is a verb, not an adjective. Paul doesnot say love is a patient thing; he says love acts patiently, behaveskindly, refuses to envy. This is not a description of a feeling. It is a description ofconduct, which means it can be checked.

Patient. The Greek is a compound of long and anger: love has along fuse. It is not the patience of waiting for a bus but the patience of putting up withpeople — the same word the New Testament uses of God bearing with sinners forcenturies. The measure of it is not how you behave the first time someone irritates you butthe fortieth.

Kind. The other side of the same coin, and the pair belongs together. Patience iswhat love does not do; kindness is what it does. It is possible to endure someoneindefinitely while giving them nothing at all, and there are marriages and churches heldtogether on exactly those terms. Patience alone is endurance. Patience with kindness islove.

Does not envy or boast. Put those two side by side and something surfaces. Envyis what this disease does when the other person has it; boasting is what it does when youhave it. They look like opposites and they are the same illness in two positions, and theillness is the habit of measuring yourself against other people. The word behindboast is a rare one that means something like windbag — the man who cannot leta story pass without improving his own part in it.

Not arrogant. The verb is physiousthai, to be puffed up, inflated withair — and this is Paul’s signature word for Corinth. He has used it about theirfactions (4:6), about the men who thought he would not come (4:18), about their pride over thescandal in chapter 5 (5:2), and about their knowledge of idols (8:1). Now it appears in thelist of what love is not. Corinth would have recognised the word instantly.

Here is the test for this verse, and it takes ten seconds. Think of the person you findhardest in your congregation or your family. Now read the four items again, substituting thatperson’s name after each verb. Am I long-tempered with him? Do I actively do him good?Am I glad when he does well? That is what the verse means, and it means nothing else. Love inthis chapter is never a general benevolence toward humanity. It always has a name attached(cf. 1 Jn 3:18).

verseByVerse.quote: or rude. It does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or rude. It does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful.

Four more, and every one of them is a photograph of the Corinthian church.

Not rude. The word means to behave in a way that is unseemly, that shames. It isstriking to find manners in a list of Christian virtues, and it should give pause to a certainkind of believer who prides himself on being blunt. Rudeness is not a personality type in theNew Testament; it is a failure of love. There is no gift, no calling and no strength ofconviction that entitles a Christian to make another person feel small in front of others.

Does not insist on its own way. Literally, love does not seek its own— and it is exactly the phrase Paul used at 10:24 and again at 10:33. This is the wholeargument of chapters 8 to 10 compressed into four words, and it is the hardest item on thelist, because insisting on one’s own way rarely feels like selfishness from the inside.It feels like being right. The strong at Corinth were right about idols and were destroyingpeople with it.

Not irritable. The word gives us paroxysm; it means sharpened, provokedto a flash. Everyone knows what this looks like: the person a whole household reads beforespeaking, the man whose mood determines the temperature of a room. It is usually treated as atemperament rather than a sin, and Paul files it here.

Not resentful — and this is the one to slow down over, because the Greek issharper than the English. The phrase is an accountant’s: love does not reckon upthe evil. It does not enter the wrong in a ledger. And that is precisely what resentment is— not the memory of an injury, which is involuntary, but the keeping of it in aplace where it can be produced later.

Anyone can find out whether he is doing this. When a quarrel starts, does a list arrive?Are you able, without any preparation, to give the date and the wording of things said to youyears ago? Nobody has that at his fingertips by accident. It is there because it was filed.

And behind the accounting image lies the gospel, which is why Paul reached for it. The sameverb is the one used of God not counting our trespasses against us (2 Cor 5:19;Rom 4:8). The Christian is a person whose own ledger has been destroyed — not settled,not reduced, destroyed — and who is therefore in no position to keep one on anybodyelse. Forgiveness is the closing of an account you were entitled to keep open.

verseByVerse.quote: it does not rejoice at wrongdoing, but rejoices with the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It does not rejoice at wrongdoing, but rejoices with the truth.

A single verse, and it exposes something most people have never admitted to themselves.

Paul is not talking about approving of sin. He is talking about the small, privatepleasure that rises when something bad turns out to be true about somebody else. Theverb is to be glad. And it is very hard to deny, because it is so quick: the flicker ofsatisfaction at hearing that a colleague’s promotion has fallen through, that acritic’s marriage is in difficulty, that a preacher you found insufferable has beenfound out. Nobody chooses that flicker. But the fact that it arrives uninvited is exactly whatmakes it such an accurate reading of the heart.

At Corinth it had a public form. The church had been arrogant about a case ofgross immorality in its membership instead of mourning (5:2), and the factions were surelycheering when a rival group came off badly. But the private form is the commoner one, and itis the one this verse catches.

Here is the test, and it is the sharpest one in the chapter. Bad news arrives about someoneyou have a grievance against. What happens in the first two seconds — before you havehad time to arrange your face, before the appropriate sentence is composed? That flicker is atruer report on your love for that person than anything you would say about him out loud.

Then the positive, and it is not the balance we would have written. The opposite ofrejoicing at wrongdoing ought to be grieving at wrongdoing. Paul writes rejoices with thetruth instead, and the truth is almost personified — love and the truth standingside by side, glad about the same things.

Which settles a question that comes up constantly in Christian life: whether love andhonesty are in tension, so that being loving means going quiet about what is true. This versesays they are allies. Love does not celebrate a wrong even when the wrong is convenient; itdoes not suppress a truth even when the truth is awkward. A love that requires lies is notlove, and a truth-telling that takes pleasure in the damage is not truth-telling either(cf. Eph 4:15).

There is a practical form of this sin that most Christians take part in without evercalling it what it is, and it has a name: gossip. Nobody says I am glad this happened tohim. What people say is I only mention it so that you can pray. The versesupplies a way of telling the two apart. Ask whether you would be disappointed to discover thereport was false. If the correction would come as a relief, the interest was love. If it wouldcome as a small deflation, the interest was the flicker.

And how is the flicker killed? Not by scolding yourself for having it, which only drives itout of sight. It dies when the other person stops being a competitor, and he stops being acompetitor when you genuinely believe that God arranged the members in the body, each oneof them, as he chose (12:18). A man who is certain his own place was given him hasnothing to gain by another man losing his.

verseByVerse.quote: Love bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures allthings.

Four verbs, each with all things attached, and the effect is of a wall that willnot come down.

Bears. The word is a roofing word — it means to cover, to keep the weatheroff. Love puts a roof over the person it loves, so that his failures are not exposed toeverybody. That is not the same as pretending they are not there; it is refusing to broadcastthem. Love covers a multitude of sins (1 Pet 4:8) means that love does not repeatthe story.

Believes. Love reads the other person generously — assumes the betterexplanation until it cannot, gives the benefit of the doubt where doubt genuinely exists.

Hopes. When the evidence has run out, love goes on expecting God to do somethingwith a person. It is the parent still praying for a son twenty years after the lastconversation.

Endures. The word means to remain under a weight rather than get out from underit. Love does not leave when loving becomes expensive.

Now a guard has to be put on these four, because they have been used to do great harm andit would be dishonest to leave them undefended. Bears all things has been quoted ata woman to persuade her to keep silent about what is being done to her at home.Believes all things has been quoted to a congregation to persuade it that acredible allegation must be a misunderstanding. Endures all things has been used tosend people back into danger.

That is not what Paul means, and the proof is in his own letter. This is the man who, eightchapters earlier, told this church to put a man out of the fellowship for his sexual conductand not even to eat with him (5:11–13). He names Alexander the coppersmith by name andwarns Timothy about him (2 Tim 4:14–15). He rebuked Peter to his face, publicly(Gal 2:11). The apostle who wrote verse 7 did all of that, and he did not think he wascontradicting himself.

So the four verbs describe what love does with the wrongs it suffers, not what itdoes with the wrongs it discovers. Love will absorb an insult without publishing it.Love will not absorb an assault and call it patience. Believing all things means refusing toassume the worst about a person’s motives; it has never meant refusing to believe avictim, and using this verse to silence one turns it exactly on its head. Where someone isbeing hurt, love’s roof goes over the person being hurt, and the wrongdoer is broughtinto the light — which is itself the most loving thing that can happen to him.

Read that way, the verse is not a doormat. It is a description of the only love that hasever actually held. It bore what was done to it without answering back, went on believing theFather in the dark, hoped when there was nothing visible to hope on, and stayed under theweight until it was finished.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“Love never ends.” Never: not in this age, not in the age to come, not in the consummated kingdom. The word for “ends” carries the force of falling or collapse — love is the one thing that will not fall when everything else does.

Prophecies, tongues, and knowledge will pass away or be rendered inoperative. Not because they are worthless — they are genuine gifts of God for this age — but because they are provisional provisions for the period of incompleteness. Now we prophesy in part; we know in part; we see as in a mirror dimly. Then — when the perfect comes, when we see face to face, when we know fully even as we are fully known — the partial will be superseded. The gifts will be made redundant not by failure but by fulfilment: the seeing replaces the mirror image; the direct knowledge replaces the partial knowledge; the face-to-face vision replaces the prophetic announcement.

The climax — “So now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; but the greatest of these is love” — is not a claim that faith and hope are less important than love in this age. It is a claim about what survives into the age to come. In the age to come, faith will be sight and hope will be possession. But love — the love with which God loves his people and with which redeemed people love God and one another — is the very quality of the new creation. Love is the greatest not because it outranks faith and hope in a spiritual hierarchy but because it alone characterises both the present age and the age to come, both the pilgrim life and the eternal rest. Love is the quality of eternity itself.

On the disputed question of the perfect (v. 10), Paul defines his own terms two verses later: then we shall see face to face, and know fully even as I have been fully known (v. 12). Nobody began to see God face to face when the last book of the New Testament was finished, so the then of this passage is the day we see him, not a date in the first century. That means the passage does not by itself settle whether the miraculous gifts continue — a point worth conceding plainly, since the case for their ceasing is argued far better from Ephesians 2:20 and Hebrews 2:3–4 than from here.

And verse 11 supplies the picture that holds the whole section together. A child’s speech is not false; it is small. Our present knowledge of God is real knowledge on a child’s scale, which rules out both the confidence that thinks it has God mapped and the false humility that says nothing can be known. Growing up is not something a child achieves by concentrating. It is done to him.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Eschatology of the Gifts and the Permanence of Love

Paul’s teaching that prophecy, tongues and knowledge will pass away is often taken as the foundation of the cessationist argument — the gifts being provisional for an age of incomplete revelation and superseded when the perfect comes. Whether the perfect means the completion of the New Testament canon, the maturity of the church, or the return of Christ has been debated for centuries; but Paul defines his own terms in verse 12, where then is when we see face to face and know fully even as I have been fully known. Since no one began to see God face to face when the canon closed, this passage by itself does not settle the question, and the stronger arguments for cessation are made from Ephesians 2:20 and Hebrews 2:3–4 rather than from here.

What the passage does settle is the structure: the gifts are for now, and love is for now and for ever. A church that pours its energy into the spectacular while neglecting love has it exactly backwards, clinging to the provisional and letting go of the permanent — and that is true of every party to the argument, whichever side it takes. A man who wins this debate uncharitably has lost the chapter it is in.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian community that prized tongues above all else was, on Paul’s analysis, investing heavily in something that would not survive the transition to the coming age, while neglecting the one quality that would. Now: The church that is rich in programmes, gifts, and spiritual activity but thin in genuine love has the Corinthian problem in contemporary dress. Every spiritual tradition — charismatic, Reformed, liturgical — can produce communities that are impressively gifted and loveless. Paul’s word is the same to all of them: love never ends; everything else is provisional.

verseByVerse.quote: Love never ends. As for prophecies, they will pass away; as for tongues, they will cease; as for knowledge, it will pass away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love never ends. As for prophecies, they will pass away; as for tongues, they willcease; as for knowledge, it will pass away.

The portrait stops and the argument resumes, and the hinge is the word never.

The verb behind ends means to fall — the way a leaf falls, or a flower, or abuilding. Everything else in the chapter has a collapse in its future. Love does not.

Then three things named, and they are precisely the three the Corinthians had been ranking:prophecy, tongues, knowledge. Paul says all three have an expiry date. This is a devastatingthing to say to a church that had built its whole status system on them. The gifts they werefighting over were, on the apostle’s own account, temporary equipment.

And it is worth being clear about the reason, because it is not that the gifts areinferior. They came from the Spirit, they were given for the common good, and Paul will tellthis church to desire them earnestly and not to forbid them (14:1, 39). They pass awaybecause they are the equipment of a journey, and journeys end. A map is a wonderful thing.Nobody consults one after arriving.

Which is the point that ought to survive every argument that has ever been conducted overthis passage. Whatever a Christian concludes about when these gifts pass away, theapostle’s reason for raising the subject was not to settle a timetable. It was to tell achurch obsessed with the temporary that it had its heart set on things with a shelf life,while neglecting the one thing that will still be standing when the sun burns out.

There is a picture worth carrying. The most gifted preacher who has ever lived will oneday preach his last sermon, and there will never be any need for another. Every translator,every commentary, every sermon series, every one of these words will be as obsolete as acandle at noon. And the smallest act of love done by the least-noticed believer in thecongregation will still be there, because it belongs to what is coming rather than to what ispassing (cf. 1 Pet 1:24–25).

One detail of the wording should be mentioned, since it is often pressed into service inthe argument that follows. Paul uses one verb of prophecy and knowledge — they will berendered inoperative, put out of use — and a different verb of tongues: theywill cease, in a form that can suggest ceasing of themselves. Some have built on thatthe claim that tongues were to stop of their own accord at an earlier point than the othertwo. It is a slender foundation for a large conclusion; Greek writers use that form loosely,and Paul’s three clauses are plainly parallel in force. A doctrine should not be hung ona verb ending.

The deeper question is why love should be the exception, and the answer is not that loveis more useful. It is that the other three are things we do in a world where God isnot yet seen, while love is what God is (1 Jn 4:8). Prophecy exists because we cannotsee him; knowledge exists because we do not yet know him; tongues exist because we are stillon the road. Love existed before there was a road, in the giving between Father, Son andSpirit, and it will still be there when the road has been rolled up.

verseByVerse.quote: For we know in part and we prophesy in part, but when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we know in part and we prophesy in part, but when the perfect comes, the partialwill pass away.

Here is the verse Christians have argued over for centuries, and it deserves a straightaccount rather than a diplomatic fog. The question is simple to state: what is theperfect, and when does it come? On the answer hangs the question of whether gifts such asprophecy, tongues and healing continue in the church today.

Three answers have been given. Some have said the perfect is the completed New Testament— once the last book was written, the church had God’s finished word and no longerneeded revelatory gifts. Others have taken it as the maturity of the church, grown up out ofits infancy. Others take it as the return of Christ and the state of things that follows.

The third is almost certainly right, and the reason is that Paul himself defines his termsthree verses later. Then we shall see face to face; then I shallknow fully, even as I have been fully known (v. 12). Whatever else may be said, noChristian began to see God face to face when the book of Revelation was finished, and nobodyalive knows God as fully as God knows him. The then of this passage is not a date inthe first century. It is the day we see him.

That has to be said even though it cuts against a conclusion many careful and belovedteachers have drawn, because honesty about a text matters more than tidiness. This passagedoes not, by itself, prove that the miraculous gifts ended with the apostles.

But it would be equally dishonest to leave the impression that the case for their ceasingrests on this verse, because it does not, and the men who have made that case were notcareless readers. Their argument runs on other ground. The apostles and prophets are calledthe foundation of the church, with Christ as the cornerstone (Eph 2:20) — and afoundation is laid once.

The signs and wonders of the first generation are described as Godbearing witness to a message declared by those who heard the Lord (Heb 2:3–4), whichsuggests a purpose tied to that generation. Scripture is sufficient, and a church expectingfresh revelation is exposed to every confident voice. And there is the honest observationthat what is called prophecy or tongues in many places today bears little resemblance to whatis described in Acts. B. B. Warfield argued the case a century ago, and in our own day JohnMacArthur has argued it with conviction and love for the Word. These are serious argumentsmade by serious men, and they deserve a serious answer rather than a sneer.

The answer from the other side is also serious. Paul told this church plainly, do notforbid speaking in tongues (14:39), and told another church do not quench the Spirit,do not despise prophecies, but test everything; hold fast what is good(1 Thess 5:19–21). Those are commands, and no verse anywhere announces their repeal.And the observation that today’s claimed gifts often look nothing like the NewTestament’s may be an argument for testing them rather than for abolishing thecategory.

So where should an ordinary believer land? Three things can be said with confidence, andthey are enough to live by. First, whichever conclusion a Christian reaches, this passageforbids him to look down on a brother who reached the other one; the chapter it sits in isabout love, and a man who wins this argument uncharitably has lost the chapter. Second, nogift is the mark of the Spirit’s presence — that was settled at 12:3, and the markis the confession that Jesus is Lord. Third, and this is Paul’s actual point, all of itis partial. Both sides of this debate are arguing about equipment for a journey thatis nearly over, and the chapter was written to say so.

verseByVerse.quote: When I was a child, I spoke like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. When I became a man, I gave up childish ways.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When I was a child, I spoke like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like achild. When I became a man, I gave up childish ways.

An illustration, and it is regularly misused as a rebuke — as though Paul weretelling the Corinthians to stop being childish, which he does elsewhere but not here. Read itin its place: he is explaining what he means by partial.

Notice that there is nothing wrong with the child’s speech. A three-year-old namingthings is not lying. His thinking is real thinking, his reasoning is real reasoning, andwithin its own scale it works perfectly well. It is simply small. He is not mistaken aboutthe world; he has less of it.

That is what Paul says about our present knowledge of God, and it is a wonderfullybalanced thing to say. It rules out two errors at once. It rules out the confidence thatimagines our theology has God taped — that the systems and the creeds have got himmapped and there is nothing left to be astonished by. And it equally rules out the fashionablehumility that says nothing can really be known, that all our talk of God is guesswork. Thechild does know his mother. He simply does not yet know what she gave up for him, what shefears at three in the morning, or what she was like at twenty.

So the Christian’s knowledge of God is true knowledge and it is knowledge on achild’s scale. What comes next is not a correction of it but a growing up into it.

And there is a quiet comfort in the picture that should not be missed. Nobody blames achild for being a child. The smallness is not a fault to be repented of; it is a stage to beoutgrown, and the outgrowing is not something a child achieves by concentrating. It happensto him. Growing up is done to us, and so is this (cf. 1 Jn 3:2).

There is a consequence for how a Christian holds his convictions, and it follows directlyfrom the verse before this one. If our knowledge is genuine and partial, then two attitudesare ruled out and one is required. Ruled out is the man who will not commit to anythingbecause certainty is arrogant; the child does know his mother, and hedging every sentence isnot humility but evasion. Also ruled out is the man who treats his own grasp of a disputedquestion as though it were the view from the throne. What is required is conviction heldfirmly and carried lightly — believing what God has said with your whole weight, andholding your own conclusions about the harder questions with the awareness that you are, atpresent, three feet tall.

Which is exactly the temper the previous verses were asking for. A church divided overprophecy and tongues is a nursery of children shouting about a subject on which every one ofthem is speaking like a child. That is not an argument for indifference. It is an argumentfor the kind of patience that this chapter has been describing all along.

verseByVerse.quote: For now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part; then Ishall know fully, even as I have been fully known.

Corinth was famous for its bronze. The city exported polished mirrors, and every reader ofthis letter had looked into one. They did not work like ours. A bronze mirror gives you back adarkened, slightly warped version of a face — recognisably you, and never quite you.

The phrase translated dimly is literally in a riddle, which is where theword enigma comes from. That is our present sight of God. Not blindness. A face in dark metal,and a riddle that is genuinely about him.

But then face to face. Refuse to let that phrase stay vague, because Scripturedoes not leave it vague and it is the hope of the whole Bible in four words. Moses asked forthis one thing — please show me your glory — and was told, you cannotsee my face, for man shall not see me and live; he was put in a cleft of rock, coveredwith a hand, and allowed to see the back of God going past (Ex 33:18–23). That is thehigh-water mark of the old covenant. The greatest prophet in Israel’s history asked tosee God’s face and was refused it.

And the last page of the Bible says of ordinary redeemed people, without ceremony:they will see his face (Rev 22:4). What Moses was not given, the least believer inthe congregation is promised. We shall see him as he is (1 Jn 3:2).

Then the last clause, and it is the most tender sentence in the chapter. Then I shallknow fully, even as I have been fully known.

Sit inside that. Every human being alive is caught in one of two positions, and there is nothird. Either you are loved by people who do not fully know you — who love a version ofyou assembled from your better hours — or you are known by someone who has seen theworst and whose affection you can feel adjusting itself. The fear that runs underneath mosthuman relationships is the same fear: if they knew everything, they would not stay.It is why people edit themselves in company, and why being loved often fails to settleanything.

Paul writes, of God, I have been fully known. Past tense, already accomplished.There is no discovery still to come, no file not yet opened, nothing that will emerge in thelast hour and change the verdict. The one who knows the whole of it — the thing you havenever told anyone, the thing you would not put in a prayer — is the one who set his loveon you before you had done anything at all.

And that is the ground of everything this chapter has asked for. A person who is fully knownand fully loved has nothing left to protect, and a person with nothing to protect can afford tobe patient, kind, unenvious, and free of the ledger. Love like this is not squeezed out of theloveless by effort. It leaks out of people who have stopped being afraid of being foundout.

The Son of God knew exactly what he was buying. He looked at the whole record — notthe edited version, the whole of it — and went to the cross for it anyway, so that onsome morning still ahead he could stand in front of the people he died for with nothinghidden on either side, and be looked at. That is what he wanted. Not servants at a distance,but a face to face.

verseByVerse.quote: So now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; but the greatest of these is love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; but the greatest of these islove.

Paul has just said that prophecy, tongues and knowledge will fall. Now he names threethings that will not.

The three appear together all over his letters — your work of faith and labourof love and steadfastness of hope (1 Thess 1:3) — and they map the Christian lifeonto time. Faith takes hold of what God has done. Hope leans forward to what he will do. Lovedoes the present tense. Between them they cover everything a believer has.

Then the last clause, and it needs explaining rather than admiring, because at first sightit is odd. Why is love greater? Faith saves; love does not. Faith is how a sinner isjustified, and Paul of all people is not about to demote it.

The answer is in the word abide. Consider what happens to each of the three whenChrist returns. Faith is trusting a God you cannot see — and on that day you will seehim, so faith will have become sight. Hope is waiting for what has not yet arrived — andon that day it will have arrived, so hope will have become possession. Neither is lost;each is swallowed by its own fulfilment.

Love alone arrives unchanged. There is nothing love turns into, because there is nothingbetter than love to turn into. It is the only thing in the Christian life that will be doingin eternity exactly what it does now — which is why practising it is the one activity ofthis life that is not preparation for something else.

And behind that lies the deepest reason of all. Faith and hope are things creatures do;God has neither. He does not trust, because he knows, and he does not hope, because he holds.But God is love (1 Jn 4:8) — not merely loving, but love itself, in theunbroken giving between Father, Son and Spirit that was going on before there was anythingelse at all. Love is greatest because love is the one item on the list that is a descriptionof God.

Which means the whole chapter has been leading somewhere other than self-improvement. Itbegan by pricing the gifts and it ends by naming the eternal life of God, and it turns outthat the patient, unenvious, unbookkeeping love it describes is not a standard the Corinthianswere failing to reach. It is a Person, who was patient with them, who did not insist on hisown way, who bore all things and endured all things, and who was at that moment holding thatquarrelsome church together with his own hands.

They wanted to know which gift was the greatest. He gave them himself and called it themore excellent way.

13.text: <sup>1</sup>If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal.<sup>2</sup>And if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing.<sup>3</sup>If I give away all I have, and if I deliver up my body to be burned, but have not love, I gain nothing.<sup>4</sup>Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant<sup>5</sup>or rude. It does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful;<sup>6</sup>it does not rejoice at wrongdoing, but rejoices with the truth.<sup>7</sup>Love bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.<sup>8</sup>Love never ends. As for prophecies, they will pass away; as for tongues, they will cease; as for knowledge, it will pass away.<sup>9</sup>For we know in part and we prophesy in part,<sup>10</sup>but when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away.<sup>11</sup>When I was a child, I spoke like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. When I became a man, I gave up childish ways.<sup>12</sup>For now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known.<sup>13</sup>So now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; but the greatest of these is love.

14.title: Prophecy, Tongues, and the Order of Worship
14.overview:
Chapter 14 is the practical resolution of the gift discussion: having established the theological framework (ch. 12) and the supreme criterion (ch. 13), Paul now applies both to the specific question of tongues vs. prophecy in corporate worship. The governing principle, stated and restated throughout the chapter, is edification: “Let all things be done for building up” (v. 26). Every decision about worship — which gifts to use, in what order, in what manner — must be evaluated by this single criterion: does it build up the whole community?

By this criterion, prophecy (intelligible proclamation of the word of God that addresses the congregation) consistently outranks tongues (speaking in an uninterpreted language) in the corporate setting. This is not because tongues is a lesser gift in itself — Paul says he speaks in tongues more than all of them (v. 18) and does not forbid the practice (v. 39). It is because in a public gathering, intelligibility is a prerequisite for edification. The tongue-speaker who blesses God in an unknown language is genuinely worshipping; but the assembled community cannot say “Amen” to what they cannot understand. And a community that cannot say “Amen” together is not being built up together.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The command to pursue love at the beginning of chapter 14 connects directly back to chapter 13’s “still more excellent way.” Love is to be pursued (diōkete — run after, chase); spiritual gifts are to be earnestly desired. The two are not in tension; they are in sequence. Love is the supreme orientation; within that orientation, the gifts are to be eagerly sought, particularly prophecy. Why prophecy above all? Because prophecy, in Paul’s usage, is the Spirit-given capacity to speak words that strengthen, encourage, and console the gathered community. This is the paradigm of a community-building gift: intelligible, directly edifying, addressed to everyone present.

The contrast with tongues is introduced immediately: the tongue-speaker speaks to God (genuine worship, real communication with the divine), but no one understands unless there is interpretation; the prophet speaks to people (genuine proclamation, real communication with the community). Both are genuine; but in the corporate setting, the second does what the first cannot do alone. “The one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues, unless someone interprets” (v. 5) — the qualifier is important: interpreted tongues can function like prophecy, and is equally valuable.
verseByVerse.theology:
Intelligibility as a Prerequisite for Edification

Paul’s governing principle for corporate worship — intelligibility — has deep theological roots. The God who speaks is a God who communicates; the Word became flesh precisely to be heard and understood. Worship that renders the word of God inaccessible to the gathered community is, at a structural level, working against the grain of the incarnation. The Reformers’ insistence on vernacular worship (against the Latin Mass) was an application of precisely this principle: if the people cannot understand what is being said and done, they cannot be edified.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian preference for tongues in corporate worship was driven by the same status-seeking that produced the faction fights: tongues was the impressive gift, the spectacular performance. Paul’s preference for prophecy is a preference for the communal over the spectacular, the edifying over the impressive. Now: The principle of intelligibility has applications beyond tongues: jargon-laden sermons, inaccessible liturgy, and culturally opaque worship practices all fail the same criterion. Does the person who attends understand what is happening? Are they being built up?

verseByVerse.quote: Pursue love, and earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, especially that you may prophesy. For one who speaks in a tongue speaks not to men but to God; for no one understands him, but he utters mysteries in the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pursue love, and earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, especially that you mayprophesy.

Two commands, and it matters that they are both here. After a chapter saying that thegifts without love are worth nothing, the obvious inference would be to stop caring about thegifts. Paul heads that off in his first sentence. Love is not an alternative to gifts; it isthe way gifts are to be used.

Both verbs are strong. Pursue is a hunting word — chase it down, run afterit. Earnestly desire is the verb behind our word zeal. So the Christian is to bezealous about both, and there is a definite order: love first, gifts within it.

Then the whole chapter’s argument in one word: especially that you mayprophesy. That is a startling preference to put to this church, and it will takethirty-eight verses to justify. But the reason is simple enough to state now, and it will notchange: prophecy can be understood by the people in the room.

For one who speaks in a tongue speaks not to men but to God; for no one understandshim, but he utters mysteries in the Spirit.

Before going further, the reader deserves an honest account of what tongues actually is,because the chapter assumes a knowledge we no longer have.

The Greek word is simply tongue — the same word used for a language. AtPentecost the gift produced recognisable human languages: visitors from fifteen regions eachheard the wonders of God in his own dialect (Acts 2:6–11). What happens in Corinth isplainly different in its effect, because here no one understands him, and a separategift of interpretation is required. Paul himself speaks of various kinds of tongues(12:10) and once, in passing, of the tongues of men and of angels (13:1), whichsuggests the category was broader than one thing.

So what can be said with confidence? Four things, and they are enough. It is genuinespeech, given by the Spirit. It is addressed to God, not to the congregation — which iswhy Paul will describe it as praying, singing and giving thanks (vv. 14–16) rather thanas teaching. It is unintelligible to hearers unless interpreted. And it uttersmysteries — not riddles, but the things of God that he has revealed and thatstill exceed us.

What cannot be said is that it is the badge of a real Christian, or the proof of anadvanced one. That was settled two chapters ago: not all speak with tongues (12:30), and themark of the Spirit is the confession that Jesus is Lord (12:3). Corinth had made adistinction out of a distribution, and the whole chapter is a patient dismantling of it.

verseByVerse.quote: On the other hand, the one who prophesies speaks to people for their upbuilding and encouragement and consolation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the other hand, the one who prophesies speaks to people for their upbuilding andencouragement and consolation.

Here is the contrast that governs the chapter. Tongues speaks to God; prophecy speaks topeople. Both are real, both are given by the Spirit, and only one of them does anything forthe person in the next seat.

And notice how Paul defines prophecy. He does not define it by its source, or by how itfeels, or by whether it predicts anything. He defines it by its effect, and he names threeeffects. That is a remarkable way to identify a gift, and it gives the church a usable test:look at what happened to the people who heard it.

Upbuilding is the builder’s word again — the congregation is astructure going up, and this speech adds a course of stone. Encouragement translatesa word close to the name Jesus gives the Holy Spirit, the one called alongside: it meanscoming up beside someone and putting strength into him, whether by urging or by comfort. Andconsolation is the plain word for what you say to the grieving.

Stand those three next to the popular idea of prophecy and the difference is striking.Prophecy as most people imagine it is dramatic, predictive, and slightly alarming. Prophecyas Paul describes it leaves a congregation stronger, braver and comforted. A word that leavespeople frightened, confused, or impressed with the speaker has not passed this test, whateverit claimed about its source.

This is also why prophecy is not preaching, though the two overlap. Preaching expounds atext that is already given. Prophecy in this chapter is something said into a particular roomon a particular day, which must then be weighed by the others (v. 29) — athing no one would ever say about Scripture. So whatever else must be settled about thisgift, it stands under the written Word and never beside it, and it has never added a line tothe Bible.

What is not in dispute is that these three effects are wanted, and that any Christian mayaim at them. Even a believer entirely certain that the gift itself has ceased may take verse3 as a description of what his conversation after the service ought to do. Somebody in theroom this Sunday needs to be built up, somebody needs courage, and somebody needs consoling— and the words that do it are the nearest thing to this verse that most of us willever handle (cf. 1 Thess 5:11; Heb 3:13).

verseByVerse.quote: The one who speaks in a tongue builds up himself, but the one who prophesies builds up the church. Now I want you all to speak in tongues, but even more to prophesy. The one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues, unless someone interprets, so that the church may be built up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who speaks in a tongue builds up himself, but the one who prophesies builds upthe church.

Read the first half slowly, because it is easily heard as a sneer and it is not one. Paulis not saying the tongue-speaker is being selfish. He is stating a fact about what the giftdoes: it strengthens the person exercising it. That is a genuine good, and Paul will shortlysay he does it himself more than any of them (v. 18).

The problem is not the gift. It is the setting. Corinth had taken something that builds upthe individual and made it the centrepiece of the gathering, and the gathering exists for adifferent purpose.

Now I want you all to speak in tongues, but even more to prophesy. Nobodyexpecting a crackdown expects that sentence. Paul’s wish for the whole church is thatthey should all have the gift they are abusing. He is not trying to remove anything. He istrying to reorder it — which is the harder and better kind of correction, and much rarerin churches than either enthusiasm or suppression.

The one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues, unless someoneinterprets, so that the church may be built up.

And there is the qualifier that shows exactly where the ranking comes from. Interpretedtongues is no longer inferior to prophecy, because interpreted tongues does what prophecy does— the room understands and is built up. So the greatness Paul is measuring is notintrinsic to the gift at all. It is entirely a question of how many people benefit. The samegift moves up or down the scale depending on whether anyone else in the room can follow it.

That principle reaches a great deal further than tongues, and it is worth applying tothings nobody would call a spiritual gift. The sermon full of allusions the congregationcannot catch. The prayer meeting conducted in a register that a newcomer could not join. Themusic pitched where only the musicians can sing it. In every case the activity may beexcellent, and the same question decides the matter: is anyone else being built by this, oronly the one doing it?

There is also a quiet permission here for private devotion, and it should not be lost inthe corporate argument. Paul never tells the tongue-speaker to stop; he tells him where. Atverse 28 he will say plainly: if no interpreter is present, keep silent in church and speak toyourself and to God. That is not a demotion. It is a place.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul deploys three analogies to make the case for intelligibility: musical instruments (a flute or harp playing indistinct notes produces no music, v. 7), military signals (a bugle giving an uncertain sound produces no army response, v. 8), and language itself (if I do not know the meaning of a language, I am a foreigner to the speaker, v. 11). All three make the same point: the content of a communication is only as effective as the recipient’s capacity to receive it. Uninterpreted tongues in a corporate meeting fails on all three counts: it produces no music (no shared worship), no battle readiness (no community mobilised for mission), and no genuine communication (speaker and hearer are mutually foreign).

Paul’s personal testimony in vv. 18–19 is striking: “I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you. Nevertheless, in church I would rather speak five words with my mind in order to instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue.” Five to ten thousand: the ratio expresses the absolute priority of intelligibility in corporate worship. Paul is not disparaging his own practice of tongues; he values it greatly. But he refuses to import into corporate worship what belongs in personal devotion.

Between the analogies and the five-to-ten-thousand ratio lie two passages that carry the section’s pastoral weight. In vv. 13–15 Paul refuses the choice most Christians think they have to make: I will pray with my spirit, but I will pray with my mind also; I will sing praise with my spirit, but I will sing with my mind also. Worship as pure experience, where thinking interrupts the feeling, and worship as pure instruction, correct and cold, are both amputations, and each is usually adopted as a reaction against the other.

And in vv. 16–17 the whole argument comes down to one word: Amen. When a congregation says it, it signs the prayer and makes it its own. The outsider who cannot say Amen has been present at the church’s prayer and shut out of it. Paul concedes that the thanksgiving itself was real — you may be giving thanks well enough — and rules it out of the assembly anyway, because sincerity is nowhere the criterion in these three chapters. The person next to you is.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Corporate Criterion and the Nature of Worship

Paul’s insistence on intelligibility in corporate worship reflects a deep theological conviction about the nature of Christian assembly: it is not a private spiritual experience shared simultaneously by many individuals but a genuinely corporate event in which the whole body is built up together. Worship is not merely my encounter with God in the presence of other people; it is our encounter with God as a body. This corporate dimension requires intelligibility: I cannot say “Amen” to what I cannot understand, and a community of “Amens” is the sign that the body is genuinely worshipping together.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian tongues-enthusiasts were essentially importing an individual spiritual practice into the corporate meeting without consideration for the community’s ability to participate. Paul’s five-to-ten-thousand ratio is not a rule to be calculated but a principle to be embodied: always ask, in corporate worship, whether what is done can be received and responded to by the whole community. Now: The principle applies to any element of worship that prioritises the experience of some over the edification of all.

verseByVerse.quote: Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, how will I benefit you unless I bring you some revelation or knowledge or prophecy or teaching?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, how will I benefit you unless Ibring you some revelation or knowledge or prophecy or teaching?

Paul puts himself in the frame, which is his habitual courtesy in this letter. He does notsay when you speak in tongues you are useless. He says: suppose I turn up and do it— what good would that do you?

The word benefit is the key term, and it is worth watching it recur. It hasalready governed the argument about idol meat (10:23, 33) and it governs this one. Paul isnot asking whether an activity is spiritual, permitted, or sincere. He is asking whetheranyone is better off.

Then four things he could bring instead, and they are not four synonyms. Revelationis something disclosed by God; knowledge is grasp of the truth; prophecy isthat truth spoken into this room now; teaching is the patient explanation that makesit hold. Between them they describe how the word of God actually reaches a congregation, andevery one of them has this in common: the hearer understands.

Behind the whole argument lies something about the character of God, and it is worth sayingbecause it settles more than this chapter. Our God speaks. He is not the mute idol of 12:2. Hemade the world by speaking, he gave a book, and when he came in person he came asthe Word. Everything about him leans toward being understood. A form of worship thatmakes God’s truth inaccessible to the people present is not merely inconvenient; it isrunning against the grain of who he is.

That conviction did real work in history. It is why the Reformers fought for services inthe language of the people, and why Tyndale would rather a ploughboy knew the Scriptures thana scholar did. A Latin liturgy in an English village fails this verse exactly as anuninterpreted tongue in Corinth failed it: the words may be true, reverent, and beautiful, andthe man in the back row goes home with nothing.

The same test can be turned on things that are nobody’s fault. A preacher who quotesGreek without translating it, a prayer packed with phrases a person would only know fromhaving grown up in church, a hymn whose language was ordinary in 1780 and is now a puzzle— none of these is done with any bad intent, and each of them leaves somebody in thebuilding outside the conversation. The remedy is small and unglamorous: explain the word,give the reference, say what you mean.

And notice that Paul is asking about benefit, not about interest. A congregationcan find a sermon interesting and go home with nothing to do, nothing to believe more firmly,and nobody comforted. Interest is not the test. Somebody stronger by the end is the test.

verseByVerse.quote: If even lifeless instruments, such as the flute or the harp, do not give distinct notes, how will anyone know what is played? And if the bugle gives an indistinct sound, who will get ready for battle?
verseByVerse.commentary:
If even lifeless instruments, such as the flute or the harp, do not give distinctnotes, how will anyone know what is played? And if the bugle gives an indistinct sound, whowill get ready for battle?

Two pictures, and Paul chose them well.

The first is a flute or a harp producing sound without distinction — notes that donot resolve into a tune. Everyone has heard it. An orchestra tuning up is a wonderful noiseand nobody hums it on the way home. There is nothing wrong with any individual sound; what ismissing is the shape that makes sound into music. Paul says that is what uninterpreted tonguesdoes to a service.

The second is sharper, because it has consequences. A bugle in a camp was not decoration;it was command. Different calls meant advance, retreat, stand to. And an army only marchesif the call is distinct. A bugler who blows something ambiguous does not produce aslightly confused response; he produces a camp of men looking at each other while the enemycomes over the ridge.

The change of image is the point. The flute makes indistinctness a matter of aesthetics;the bugle makes it a matter of survival. Paul is telling a church that treats the question ofclarity as a matter of taste that it is in fact a matter of readiness. A congregation thatcannot make out what is being said cannot obey it.

Which lands on anyone who speaks to God’s people, and it lands as a duty rather thana style preference. Clarity is not a gift some preachers happen to have. It is the whole job.A sermon that is admired and not understood has failed in the way the bugle failed, andnobody in the congregation will be able to say what they are supposed to do on Monday.

It is worth adding that the instrument is not blamed for having no mind of its own —Paul calls these lifeless things. The people in the church are not lifeless. They canchoose to be distinct, and this chapter tells them to (cf. Num 10:9; Neh 8:8).

The trumpet image was not a figure of speech to Israel. God gave Moses two silver trumpetswith a fixed code of signals: one blast summoned the leaders, two summoned the wholecongregation, an alarm meant the camps on the east should set out (Num 10:1–7). Liveswere arranged around the certainty that the same sound meant the same thing every time.

Which is why muddled teaching is a more serious failure than it feels. A congregation thatcannot tell what its Bible requires does not become mildly less informed; it becomes an armythat will not move. And the people most damaged are always the ones with the leastbackground — the new believer, the visitor, the man who came in troubled and needed oneclear sentence and was given a beautiful fog.

verseByVerse.quote: So with yourselves, if with your tongue you utter speech that is not intelligible, how will anyone know what is said? For you will be speaking into the air. There are doubtless many different languages in the world, and none is without meaning, but if I do not know the meaning of the language, I will be a foreigner to the speaker and the speaker a foreigner to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So with yourselves, if with your tongue you utter speech that is not intelligible, howwill anyone know what is said? For you will be speaking into the air.

There is the phrase that sums up the whole chapter, and it is more desolate than it firstsounds. Speaking into the air. Not speaking nonsense, and not speaking wickedly.Speaking real words that reach nobody — sound going out into an empty room and simplydispersing.

Paul then presses the point with the most ordinary observation imaginable. There aredoubtless many different languages in the world, and none is without meaning, but if I do notknow the meaning of the language, I will be a foreigner to the speaker and the speaker aforeigner to me.

Notice the concession he makes first, because it is generous and deliberate: every languagein the world means something. He is not saying that tongues is gibberish. Every one of thoselanguages is a real language, full of poetry and law and love and grief, to somebody. Theproblem is never with the language. It is with the gap.

The word for foreigner is barbaros — and its origin is a small jokeat the Greeks’ expense. It is onomatopoeic: to a Greek ear, foreign speech sounded likebar-bar-bar, so a foreigner was a bar-bar-ian, a person who made noises. Anyone whohas stood in a market or a hospital corridor in a country whose language he does not haveknows the feeling exactly: surrounded by meaning, cut out of all of it, reduced to guessing atfaces.

And now put that feeling in a church. That is Paul’s argument. The gift thatCorinth prized most highly was producing, in the person sitting three feet away, theloneliness of a stranger in a foreign country — and producing it in the one place onearth where nobody is supposed to be a foreigner. This is the church Paul has already toldthat Jews and Greeks, slaves and free were baptised into one body (12:13). Now they hadinvented a new way to be strangers to each other, and they were proud of it.

The application is not confined to tongues, and it is worth putting bluntly to acongregation that would never dream of the Corinthian error. Any church can manufacturebarbarians. It happens through unexplained jargon, through in-jokes and shared history,through a way of praying that outsiders cannot join, through assuming everyone knows where thebook is kept and what the notice means. None of it is malicious. All of it says the samething to the person standing at the back: you are not from here.

verseByVerse.quote: So with yourselves, since you are eager for manifestations of the Spirit, strive to excel in building up the church.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So with yourselves, since you are eager for manifestations of the Spirit, strive toexcel in building up the church.

One verse, and it is a model of how to correct people without crushing them.

Look at what Paul affirms before he redirects. Since you are eager — hetakes their eagerness as given, and he does not condemn it. He could easily have said: yourappetite for spiritual experience is the whole problem, calm down. Many pastors would. Insteadhe treats their hunger as the raw material and simply turns it round: you want theSpirit’s manifestations, so excel at the thing his manifestations are for.

That is worth learning as a way of handling zeal. Misdirected enthusiasm in a church is agreat deal easier to work with than no enthusiasm at all, and it is usually killed by the wrongkind of correction. Paul does not want less eagerness. He wants it pointed at thecongregation.

Strive to excel is a competitive phrase — the verb means to abound, tooverflow, to have more than enough. Paul takes the Corinthian instinct to outdo one anotherand does not abolish it either. He gives it a new field. If you must compete, compete at this:who can do the most good to the people in this room.

Which is an almost comic reversal when you think about the church it was written to. Hereis a congregation ranking itself by gifts, and the apostle proposes a different league table— and the people at the top of it will be the ones nobody has been counting. The memberwho has quietly rebuilt the confidence of a family going through a bad year is winning thiscompetition. He does not know there is one.

Here is the test, and it can be applied to any activity in a church. Not was itspiritual? Not did I feel God in it? Simply: who is stronger because of it? Ifthe honest answer is nobody, the thing may still be innocent, but it has not yet been whatthis verse is asking for.

There is a warning in the verse for the opposite temperament too, and it should be said,because in most sober congregations there are more of these people than there areCorinthians. Some Christians are eager for nothing at all. They have never wanted amanifestation of the Spirit, never asked God for anything they could not arrange themselves,and mistake their flatness for maturity. Paul does not commend that. He does not say stopbeing eager; he says be eager about the right thing, which assumes the eagernessis there to be redirected.

So the verse asks two questions rather than one. Am I eager? And is my eagerness pointed atthe people around me? A church that cannot answer the first has a problem this chapter neveraddresses, because the Corinthians never had it.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, one who speaks in a tongue should pray that he may interpret. For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays but my mind is unfruitful. What am I to do? I will pray with my spirit, but I will pray with my mind also; I will sing praise with my spirit, but I will sing with my mind also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, one who speaks in a tongue should pray that he may interpret. For if I prayin a tongue, my spirit prays but my mind is unfruitful. What am I to do? I will pray with myspirit, but I will pray with my mind also; I will sing praise with my spirit, but I will singwith my mind also.

The instruction is practical: if you have the one gift, ask God for the other, so that whatyou are doing can be shared.

Then a phrase that has been made to carry a great deal: my mind is unfruitful.It does not mean the speaker has left his mind behind, or that he is in a trance and notresponsible. Paul’s own next sentence rules that out, because he says I will— four times. This is a man deciding what to do, which is not a description of anyoneoverwhelmed. Unfruitful means it is not bearing fruit for others: the mind is notproducing anything the congregation can pick up.

And then the resolution, which is neither of the two answers people usually reach for.I will pray with my spirit, but I will pray with my mind also. Both. Not a choice.Paul refuses the two great mistakes about worship in a single sentence.

The first mistake is to want the spirit without the mind — worship as pureexperience, where thinking is felt to interrupt the feeling, where the aim of a service is astate and doctrine is an obstacle to it. The second is to want the mind without the spirit— worship as instruction only, correct and cold, where a congregation could sing aboutthe blood of Christ with the expressions of people reading a timetable, and where any warmthis suspected of being manipulation.

Both are amputations, and both are common, and each is usually adopted as a reactionagainst the other. Paul will not have either. And notice that he applies the rule to singingas well as praying, which is where most Christians meet it. Singing with the mind meansactually thinking the words — and anyone who has arrived at the end of a hymn with nomemory of the middle verse knows how possible it is to sing with neither.

There is a simple discipline in it. Before the service, read the words of what you areabout to sing. During the prayers, mean the Amen. Afterwards, ask what was said. That ispraying with the mind, and it does not cost a Christian one degree of warmth — theopposite, in fact, since nobody has ever been moved by something he did not take in(cf. Ps 47:7; Col 3:16).

verseByVerse.quote: Otherwise, if you give thanks with your spirit, how can anyone in the position of an outsider say “Amen” to your thanksgiving when he does not know what you are saying? For you may be giving thanks well enough, but the other person is not being built up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Otherwise, if you give thanks with your spirit, how can anyone in the position of anoutsider say “Amen” to your thanksgiving when he does not know what you aresaying? For you may be giving thanks well enough, but the other person is not being builtup.

Paul brings the argument down to one word, and it is a word every congregation sayswithout thinking about it.

Amen is Hebrew, and the church took it over from the synagogue withouttranslating it, which is itself a small marvel — the same syllables have been said byGod’s people for three thousand years. It means something firm, reliable, sure. When oneperson prays aloud and the congregation says Amen, they are not being polite. They aresigning the prayer. It becomes theirs. Nehemiah records the whole assembly answeringAmen, Amen, lifting their hands, and bowing their heads to the ground (Neh 8:6).

So the outsider who cannot say Amen has not merely missed a nice moment. He has beenexcluded from the congregation’s prayer — present at it, unable to join it. AndPaul’s word for him, outsider, means someone occupying the position of theuninitiated: the enquirer, the newcomer, the person who came because a friend asked him. Theone guest in the building who most needed to be included has been quietly left out by thething everyone else found most exciting.

Then the fairness of verse 17, which keeps the whole rebuke honest: you may be givingthanks well enough. Paul concedes the point completely. The thanksgiving is real, it isdirected to God, and God has heard it. Nothing about it is fake. But the other person isnot being built up — and in a gathering of the church, that is decisive.

This is the sentence to carry out of the chapter, because it applies to a hundred thingsthat are not tongues. It is possible to do something in a church service that is entirelygenuine, entirely God-directed, entirely sincere — and still wrong, because of who elsewas in the room. Sincerity is not the criterion Paul uses anywhere in these three chapters.The criterion is always the person next to you.

Here is a test with immediate application. Think of the last time you took part audibly ina gathering — a prayer, a reading, a comment in a study, a testimony. Could a nervousnewcomer with no church background have said Amen to it, and known what he was agreeing to? Ifnot, the fault was not his.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you. Nevertheless, in church I would rather speak five words with my mind in order to instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you. Nevertheless, in church Iwould rather speak five words with my mind in order to instruct others, than ten thousandwords in a tongue.

This is the verse that stops the argument from being a caricature, and it should beallowed its full force before anything is built on it.

Paul speaks in tongues. Not occasionally, and not reluctantly — more than all ofyou, said to the congregation in the New Testament most famous for the gift. And hisattitude to it is not tolerance but gratitude: I thank God. Whatever a readerconcludes about the gift today, he is not entitled to a lower view of it than the man who wrotethis chapter of restrictions. Every rule in this chapter comes from someone who prized thething he was regulating.

It also tells us where he did it, by simple elimination. Nobody in Corinth knew aboutPaul’s tongues-speaking until this letter arrived, and he has just spent seventeenverses saying it does not belong in the assembly without interpretation. So this was private,in his own praying, and by his own account there was a great deal of it. The apostle whotravelled constantly, was beaten, imprisoned and shipwrecked, and carried the anxiety of allthe churches, had a private prayer life more extensive than that of a whole congregation.

Nevertheless, in church. Two words that divide the whole question. Paul is notweighing tongues against prophecy in the abstract; he is asking what belongs in a publicgathering. The same activity can be excellent in one setting and out of place in another, andthe distinction is not hypocrisy but wisdom.

Then the ratio, and it is a deliberate absurdity: five against ten thousand. Two thousandto one. He is not proposing a calculation. He is saying that in the assembly, comprehensiblespeech and incomprehensible speech are not on the same scale at all — that fiveintelligible words which teach somebody outweigh an entire evening of the other.

Five words is worth sitting with. It is one sentence. Christ died for sinners.God will not let you go. Paul is saying that a single plain sentence, understood bya struggling believer, is of more value in a church than a display that lasts all night. AnyChristian can manage five words. That is the point of choosing such a small number.

And note the aim attached to them: in order to instruct others. Paul is notpraising brevity for its own sake, and this verse is no charter for the person who thinkssermons should be shorter. He is praising speech that lands somewhere. The measure is notlength but transfer — whether something that was in one head is now in another.

There is real freedom in this for anyone who has ever felt they had nothing to offer in achurch. You do not need ten thousand words. You do not need a platform, a gift you can name,or a way with an audience. Five plain words that instruct one person are, on theapostle’s own scale, worth more than the most impressive thing that happened in Corinththat year.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now introduces a typological argument from Isaiah 28:11–12: “By people of strange tongues and by the lips of foreigners will I speak to this people, and even then they will not listen to me, says the Lord.” God’s judgment on unbelieving Israel took the form of foreign languages — the speech of the Assyrian conquerors that Israel could not understand, signalling divine abandonment. Paul applies this: tongues in the church is a sign for unbelievers, not believers — but a sign of judgment, not of welcome. Prophecy, by contrast, is a sign for believers (it builds them up) and can also convict and welcome the unbeliever who walks in.

The scenario of vv. 23–25 makes the pastoral point concrete: if the whole church is speaking in tongues and an unbeliever walks in, they will say “you are out of your minds.” But if all prophesy, the unbeliever is convicted, judged, the secrets of his heart are disclosed, and he falls on his face and worships God. This is the result Paul wants: genuine encounter with the living God mediated through intelligible proclamation. Tongues in a corporate meeting, without interpretation, produces the opposite: it signals disorder, not the presence of God.

The section opens with the rebuke that sets its tone: do not be children in your thinking. Be infants in evil, but in your thinking be mature (v. 20). A church that considered itself spiritually advanced is told it is assessing things the way a small child does, by whatever is loudest and shiniest — and that the one respect in which it should be childish, inexperience in evil, is the one it has neglected.
verseByVerse.theology:
Worship and Witness

Paul’s concern for the unbeliever who might walk in to the church meeting is a significant ecclesiological statement: corporate worship is not only for the already-converted. The community that worships in such a way that the outsider can be addressed, convicted, and drawn to worship is doing something the tongues-heavy meeting cannot do. This does not make evangelism the primary purpose of corporate worship — the primary purpose is the glorification of God — but it recognises that intelligible worship of the living God is inherently missionary in its effect.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian meetings were apparently chaotic — multiple tongues-speakers simultaneously, no interpretation, no order. Paul’s Isaiah citation turns their spiritual pride upside down: the tongues without interpretation is a sign associated with divine judgment, not divine favour. Now: The church that makes its corporate worship impenetrable to the outsider — whether through uninterpreted ecstatic experience, impenetrable theological jargon, or cultural inscrutability — is failing the unbeliever who walks through the door. The word of God should be the thing that disturbs, not the incomprehensibility of the proceedings.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, do not be children in your thinking. Be infants in evil, but in your thinking be mature. In the Law it is written, “By people of strange tongues and by the lips of foreigners will I speak to this people, and even then they will not listen to me, says the Lord.” Thus tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers, while prophecy is a sign not for unbelievers but for believers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers, do not be children in your thinking. Be infants in evil, but in your thinkingbe mature.

A beautifully turned rebuke. Corinth thought of itself as spiritually advanced, and Paultells them they are behaving like toddlers — drawn to whatever is loudest and shiniest,which is exactly how a small child assesses value. And he adds the one respect in which hedoes want them childish: in evil, be infants. Be the sort of person who has to have wickednessexplained to him.

Then the hardest argument in the chapter. In the Law it is written, “By people ofstrange tongues and by the lips of foreigners will I speak to this people, and even then theywill not listen to me, says the Lord.” Thus tongues are a sign not for believers but forunbelievers, while prophecy is a sign not for unbelievers but for believers.

The quotation is from Isaiah 28, and the setting must be known or the argument makes nosense. Isaiah is preaching to the drunken leadership of Israel, and they mock him — hisplain speech sounds to them like baby-talk, a string of nonsense syllables. Very well, saysGod: if my clear word through a prophet is only babble to you, you shall have a message yougenuinely cannot understand. He means the Assyrian army, whose foreign speech would soon beheard in their streets. Unintelligible language was the judgment. It was the sound of Godhaving stopped speaking to them in words they could follow.

That unlocks verse 22, which otherwise seems to contradict what comes next. When Paul saystongues are a sign for unbelievers, he does not mean tongues is a good way to reachthem. He means it functions as the sign it functioned as in Isaiah: a mark of people who areoutside, hearing sounds that carry nothing to them. It is a sign of judgment, not of welcome.And prophecy is a sign for believers in the opposite way — the mark of a God who ispresent with his people and speaking to them in words they understand.

Which is why the next verse can say that unbelievers walking into a room full of tongueswill conclude the church is mad. That is not a contradiction of verse 22; it is thedemonstration of it. The sign does exactly what Isaiah said such a sign does: it leaves theoutsider outside.

And there is a sobering thing here for any church, quite apart from tongues. The mostfrightening judgment God ever brings on a people is not fire. It is unintelligibility —a famine of hearing the words of the LORD (Amos 8:11), a pulpit full of noise, a religion thathas stopped saying anything. That can happen to a congregation without anybody deciding it,and the people inside are usually the last to notice.

verseByVerse.quote: If, therefore, the whole church comes together and all speak in tongues, and outsiders or unbelievers enter, will they not say that you are out of your minds? But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or outsider enters, he is convicted by all, he is called to account by all,
verseByVerse.commentary:
