If, therefore, the whole church comes together and all speak in tongues, and outsidersor unbelievers enter, will they not say that you are out of your minds?

Paul asks them to picture their own meeting through the door. Someone has come —perhaps a neighbour, perhaps a husband who finally agreed to come once. He steps in, and everyperson in the room is speaking words he cannot understand, all at the same time. What does heconclude?

The Greek says he will think they are raving. Not that the doctrine is false; hehas not heard any doctrine. He will simply decide that these people are unhinged, and he willgo home, and he will not come back. And here is the sting: he was never given the chance toreject Christ. He rejected a room.

That deserves to be said plainly, because the objection is always available that the worldfinds the gospel foolish anyway. It does — Paul said so at 1:23. But there is adifference between the offence of the cross and the offence of a shambles, and this chapterexists to say that a church may not confuse the two. If people are put off, let it be byChrist crucified, and not by the fact that nobody explained anything.

But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or outsider enters, he is convicted by all, heis called to account by all.

The second scenario, and everything is different. Notice that it is not one gifted speakerdoing the work. All prophesy — the whole congregation is speaking words thatbuild up, encourage and console. And the visitor is convicted by all, which is acourtroom word, and called to account by all, which is another.

Nobody has cross-examined him. Nobody has singled him out; the whole point is that thecongregation is talking about God to each other, and the truth spoken plainly begins doing itsown work on a man who came in only to keep somebody company. He came to observe and findshimself on trial — which is what always happens when the word of God is intelligible ina room (cf. Heb 4:12–13).

It is worth noticing how ordinary the mechanism is. Nothing in these two verses requires aspecial word of knowledge about the visitor. It requires a congregation in which people areplainly saying true things about God to one another, and a man who happens to be in the roomwhile they do it. The conviction is the word’s own work, not the speaker’sinsight.

Which is a comfort to anyone who has ever felt that evangelism requires a technique he doesnot have. The most effective thing a congregation can do for the friend it has finallypersuaded to come is not to arrange something special for him. It is to be, on thatparticular Sunday, a body of people who genuinely mean what they are saying — and to sayit in words he can follow.

verseByVerse.quote: the secrets of his heart are disclosed, and so, falling on his face, he will worship God and declare that God is really among you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The secrets of his heart are disclosed, and so, falling on his face, he will worship Godand declare that God is really among you.

This is what Paul wants a church service to do, and it is worth stopping over, because itis far more ambitious than most of us expect on a Sunday morning.

The secrets of his heart are disclosed. Not published — disclosed, madeplain, brought into the light. And disclosed to whom? Chiefly to himself. Anyone who has satunder plain preaching and had the sensation of being described knows exactly what this means.Nothing supernatural has to be assumed about the speaker. The word of God has a way of walkinginto a man’s private rooms and turning on the lights, and the effect is that he stopslistening to what is being said about people in general and starts hearing about himself.

Then falling on his face. Not nodding. Not thoughtfully agreeing. This is theposture of a man who has met something and lost his footing — the posture of Ezekiel bythe river, of John on Patmos, of every person in Scripture who found himself unexpectedly inthe presence of God.

And then the sentence that Paul wants said about a congregation: God is really amongyou. It is not the sentence anyone expects him to want. It is not these people arewarm, or that was a fine argument, or they made me feel welcome. Everyone of those is good and none of them is this. He wants the visitor to walk out havingconcluded that God was in the building.

Here is what a church can take from it, practically. The thing most likely to convert theperson who visits is not the excellence of the arrangements, the quality of the music, or theskill of the welcome, though all of them help and none should be neglected. It is acongregation talking plainly about a God who is actually there. Corinth thought the way toimpress an outsider was to show him something extraordinary. Paul says the way is to saysomething true, and let God be extraordinary.

And what he came for was not a religious experience. He came for that man — the oneat the back, on his face, saying the only sentence that matters. There has never been aservice anywhere that God attended reluctantly (cf. Isa 45:14; Zech 8:23).

The words the visitor speaks are not new, either. God is really among you is whatthe Old Testament promised would one day be said by outsiders about Israel — foreignersfalling down and confessing that God was there and nowhere else (Isa 45:14), ten men fromevery nation taking hold of the robe of a Jew and saying they had heard God was with him(Zech 8:23). Paul takes those promises and lays them on a house church in a Greek port. Thenations coming in has begun, and it is happening in an ordinary room, one man at a time.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–40 — Orderly Worship and Final Rules
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chapter’s practical climax: “What then, brothers? When you come together, each one has a hymn, a lesson, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. Let all things be done for building up.” The snapshot of the Corinthian meeting is lively and participatory — not a one-man performance but a multi-voiced gathering where each person brings a contribution. Paul affirms this participatory dynamic; he does not suppress it. But he channels it through the criterion of edification and the principle of order.

The specific rules: tongue-speakers two or at most three, in turn, with interpretation; prophets two or three, with the others weighing what is said; women to be silent in the weighing of prophets. The rule for women in vv. 34–35 is one of the most contested in the NT. The most natural reading in context is that Paul is restricting women from the public evaluation (diakrinein) of prophets — a specific speech act in the context of ordered judgment, not a general prohibition on women speaking. Verse 37 grounding the whole in the Lord’s command ensures Paul is not merely offering preference but apostolic authority.

The chapter closes with the summary of everything: “Let all things be done decently and in order.” Order in worship is not a cultural preference; it is a theological statement about the character of the God being worshipped: “God is not a God of confusion but of peace” (v. 33). The orderliness of Christian worship reflects the orderliness of the God from whose own ordered life (Father, Son, Spirit in eternal communion) the community draws its life.

Two verses near the end govern how the whole chapter should be held. Verse 36 names what was really wrong at Corinth — not tongues but independence: Or was it from you that the word of God came? Or are you the only ones it has reached? The gospel arrived there from somewhere else, carried by people who had received it themselves.

And verse 39 places a command exactly where a lesser writer would have placed a ban: earnestly desire to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues. Having spent the chapter restricting the practice, Paul closes by forbidding the church to suppress it. He knows what happens when a congregation is corrected about an excess: it swings, and the next generation treats the thing as an embarrassment. Order is what he wants around the fire, not instead of it.
verseByVerse.theology:
God as the Ground of Ordered Worship

The theological ground for orderly worship — “God is not a God of confusion but of peace” — is a direct application of the doctrine of God to liturgical practice. The triune God is the most perfectly ordered being there is: the three persons in eternal, loving, ordered communion. Worship that is chaotic and disorderly is, at a deep level, a misrepresentation of the God being worshipped. Conversely, worship that is ordered, intelligible, and participatory is an enacted icon of the divine order. The Reformers understood this: the liturgical reforms of Geneva and Zurich were not mere preference but a theological conviction that worship should reflect the character of the God it addresses.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian meeting was apparently chaotic: multiple simultaneous tongues, no weighing of prophecies, a general air of competitive spiritual display. Paul’s practical rules — two or three, in turn, with evaluation — are not bureaucratic restrictions but pastoral wisdom about how a community can actually benefit from the gifts God has given it. Now: “Decently and in order” is the guiding principle for every aspect of church life, from Sunday worship to congregational meetings to pastoral care. Order is not the suppression of the Spirit; it is the condition in which the Spirit’s gifts can be received and used by the whole community.

verseByVerse.quote: What then, brothers? When you come together, each one has a hymn, a lesson, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. Let all things be done for building up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What then, brothers? When you come together, each one has a hymn, a lesson, arevelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. Let all things be done for building up.

Paul stops arguing and describes, and the description is one of the most interestingsentences in the New Testament about what a church meeting looked like.

Each one has. People arrived with something. One had a psalm to sing, another apiece of teaching, another something God had shown him, another a tongue, another theinterpretation of it. It is a room of contributors, not an audience. Whatever else was wrongat Corinth — and the list has been long — nobody was there as a spectator.

And Paul does not put a stop to it. That is the thing to notice, given everything he hasjust said about their disorder. He could have written: from now on, one man speaks and therest listen. Instead he regulates what he finds, and the regulation is a single clause:let all things be done for building up.

Which raises the honest question of what a church service should look like now, becausemost churches today are far more like a lecture with music than like this room. Two thingscan be said without pretending to more than the text gives.

The first is that the binding instruction here is not the format but the criterion.Paul lays down no order of service, no timings, no minimum number of contributions. Heinsists on one thing: that everything done should build people up. A church may meet thatstandard in many shapes, and the New Testament plainly leaves room for teaching to becentral, since it lists teachers before most other gifts (12:28).

The second is that the picture is nonetheless a rebuke to passivity, and most of us needthe rebuke more than we need the format. Whatever the Sunday structure, the question whatam I bringing? is a fair one to put to any Christian on the way in. It need not be aplatform contribution. It may be a conversation prepared for a person you know is struggling,a burden carried into the prayers, an invitation to lunch. The instinct of verse 26 is thatbelievers come to a gathering with something in their hands, and that instinct survives everydifference of tradition.

Because the phrase governing all of it is the one that has governed the whole chapter, andit is measured on other people. Not let all things be done sincerely, orreverently, or with excellence. For building up.

verseByVerse.quote: If any speak in a tongue, let there be only two or at most three, and each in turn, and let someone interpret. But if there is no one to interpret, let each of them keep silent in church and speak to himself and to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If any speak in a tongue, let there be only two or at most three, and each in turn, andlet someone interpret. But if there is no one to interpret, let each of them keep silent inchurch and speak to himself and to God.

The rules, and they are strikingly specific for a man who has just affirmed the gift sowarmly.

Three limits. A maximum number: two, or at the outside three, in one meeting — whichimplies that Corinth had been running many more. An order: each in turn, whichimplies they had been speaking over one another. And a condition: interpretation, withoutwhich the whole thing stops.

Notice what these rules assume. If a person can be told to wait his turn, then he is ableto wait his turn — which Paul will say outright at verse 32. The Spirit does not seizepeople and make them speak against their will, and no one in that congregation could pleadthat he had no choice. That single assumption quietly settles a great deal, then and since.Any claim to a spiritual experience that cannot be paused when the elder raises his hand hasalready been answered by this verse.

And notice the tone of the last clause, because it is easy to hear as a dismissal and isnot one. Let him keep silent in church and speak to himself and to God. Thetongue-speaker without an interpreter is not told his gift is bogus, or that he should stopusing it, or that he should be ashamed of it. He is told where it belongs. Between him andGod, in his own praying, it stands exactly as it was. What it may not do is take up thecongregation’s time producing nothing for anybody.

That is a model for how a church should handle a great many things that are good inthemselves and unsuited to the assembly. A believer’s hobby-horse doctrine, hisparticular burden, his favourite emphasis, the experience that changed his life — noneof these need be denied to be given their proper place. The question is never is thisreal? The question is is this the room?

And there is an implied instruction to the church as well as to the speaker. Ifinterpretation is what makes tongues useful, a congregation should want interpreters and prayfor them (v. 13). Paul’s rules are not designed to reduce the gift to a minimum. Theyare designed to make it useful.

There is a further thing hidden in the numbers, and it applies far beyond tongues. Two orthree, and no more — even of a good thing, even of a thing the Spirit gave. Paul assumesthat a congregation’s time is finite and that not everything genuine can be fitted intoit. Somebody with something real to offer will have to go home without offering it, and thatis not a tragedy; it is what happens in a room with other people in it.

That restraint is a form of love, and it is one of the harder ones. It means holding backsomething you were looking forward to, because the meeting has already had enough of thatkind of thing. The person who can do that has understood the chapter better than anyone whomerely agrees with it.

verseByVerse.quote: Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others weigh what is said. If a revelation is made to another sitting there, let the first be silent. For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all be encouraged,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others weigh what is said. If a revelationis made to another sitting there, let the first be silent. For you can all prophesy one byone, so that all may learn and all be encouraged.

Prophecy gets the same numerical limit as tongues, and then something tongues did not get:let the others weigh what is said.

The verb means to sift, to judge, to discriminate. Prophecy in the Corinthian assembly wasto be examined by the congregation. That one instruction settles more about the nature of thisgift than any definition could, and it must be held onto firmly, because it is where a greatdeal of harm has been done in the church.

Nobody weighs Scripture. Nobody sifted Isaiah to see how much of him to keep. If aprophecy in this room is to be tested by the people listening, then this gift is not on thesame footing as the written Word of God, and a man who claims to speak for God in a way thatplaces him beyond examination has misunderstood what he is claiming. Thus says theLord, said in a manner that forbids questioning, is precisely what this verse rulesout.

So how is it weighed? Four questions do most of the work. Does it agree with Scripture?— and anything that does not is finished at once, whatever accompanied it. Does it exaltChrist, or the speaker? Does it build up, encourage and console, which is what Paul saidprophecy does (v. 3)? And what is the speaker like — is this a person whose lifecommends what he says? The Bible never asks anyone to accept a spiritual claim withoutexamination, and the Berean Jews are commended precisely for checking an apostle against theScriptures (Acts 17:11; 1 Thess 5:21; 1 Jn 4:1).

Then the courtesy of verse 30: if something is given to a person sitting down, the one onhis feet stops. That is a small rule with a large implication. It means no one has the floorby right. Even a genuine speaker from God may be interrupted, and the mark of a man who istruly hearing from God is that he does not mind sitting down.

So that all may learn and all be encouraged. There is the purpose again, and bothhalves matter. Learning without encouragement produces a congregation that is informed andflat. Encouragement without learning produces one that is cheerful and hollow. Paul asks forboth from the same activity, which is a high standard and the right one.

verseByVerse.quote: and the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets. For God is not a God of confusion but of peace. As in all the churches of the saints,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets. For God is not a God of confusionbut of peace. As in all the churches of the saints.

Two of the most useful sentences in the New Testament for anyone who has to lead a church.

The spirits of prophets are subject to prophets. That is the answer to the onedefence the Corinthians could still have offered, and it is the defence that has been offeredever since: I could not help it. The Spirit came on me. Are you telling me to quench theSpirit?

Paul’s answer is that the prophet is in charge of his own mouth. The spiritual impulseis under the control of the person who has it. This has to be true, or Paul’s ruleswould be unenforceable: you cannot tell a man to wait his turn if he genuinely cannot.

And it exposes something important about how the Holy Spirit works, over against everycounterfeit. The pagan oracle was possessed; the priestess at Delphi was taken over, and herloss of control was the proof of the god’s presence. The Holy Spirit does not do that. Henever overrides a person; he restores him to himself. Self-control is the last item in thefruit of the Spirit (Gal 5:23), and a spiritual experience that removes it is not evidence ofmore of the Spirit but of something else altogether. The man out of whom Jesus cast the legionwas found sitting at his feet, clothed and in his right mind (Lk 8:35). That is theHoly Spirit’s signature.

Then the theological ground: God is not a God of confusion but of peace. Paul doesnot settle the question of order by taste, or by temperament, or by what is customary. Hesettles it by the character of God. Worship is meant to be a true statement about the onebeing worshipped, and a congregation in uproar is making a false one.

But the guard must be set here too, because this sentence has been used to smother thingsit was never aimed at. Peace is not the same as quiet, and order is not the same aspredictability. A church can be so orderly that nothing whatever happens in it — whereno one would ever weep, or stay behind, or say anything that was not on the sheet. Thatcongregation has not obeyed this verse; it has merely avoided the problem the verse addresses.Paul is regulating a fire, not a filing cabinet, and he will end the chapter by forbiddingthem to put the fire out (v. 39).

The last clause — as in all the churches of the saints — remindsCorinth that it is not the only congregation in the world, and that its practice is not its owninvention to make. It is an unglamorous point and a healthy one. A church that does somethingno other church anywhere does should at least ask itself why.

verseByVerse.quote: the women should keep silent in the churches. For they are not permitted to speak, but should be in submission, as the Law also says. If there is anything they desire to learn, let them ask their husbands at home. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in church.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The women should keep silent in the churches. For they are not permitted to speak, butshould be in submission, as the Law also says. If there is anything they desire to learn, letthem ask their husbands at home. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in church.

Few passages in the Bible are harder, and the reader who has been waiting since chapter 11for this to be faced deserves it faced rather than hurried.

The difficulty is not the culture. It is Paul. Three chapters ago, in this same letter, heregulated the way women should be dressed when they pray and prophesy in theassembly (11:5) — and he did not object to their doing it. A man does not lay downguidance for how women should pray aloud in church and then, three chapters later, forbid themto open their mouths. Whatever this passage means, it cannot mean the flat opposite of what hewrote on the previous page, and any reading that produces that result has gone wrongsomewhere.

Four readings are on the table. Some have taken it as a universal ban on women speaking inchurch; that founders on 11:5, and also on the fact that Christians who hold it do notactually apply it — the women in such congregations sing, confess, and answer.

Some have suggested the two verses were not written by Paul at all, noting that a fewmanuscripts place them after verse 40. That displacement is real and worth knowing, but everymanuscript we possess contains the verses somewhere, so they cannot simply be removed. Theyare part of the text.

Some read verses 34 and 35 as a Corinthian slogan that Paul quotes in order to demolish itin verse 36 — Or was it from you that the word of God came? It is an ingeniousreading and it has the merit of taking verse 36 seriously, but the letter gives no signal thata quotation has begun, and verse 37 calls what he is writing the Lord’s command.

The reading that fits the passage best takes it from its own context. Look where theseverses sit: in the middle of the paragraph about prophecy being weighed by thecongregation (v. 29). That weighing was a public, judicial act — the assembly sitting injudgment on what had been said, testing a claim to speak for God. And notice what verse 35regulates: asking questions. The instruction is not addressed to praying or prophesying at all;it is addressed to the cross-examination and the questioning that went with it. Wives are toldnot to take part in publicly weighing the prophecies, and to bring their questions home ratherthan conducting them across the room during the meeting.

Read that way, the two passages agree completely. A woman may pray and prophesy in theassembly (11:5). She is not to exercise the congregation’s governing judgment over thechurch’s teaching, which belongs with the same ordering Paul roots in creation elsewhere(1 Tim 2:12). And the practical setting fits the ancient room, where the sexes often satapart, where most women had far less schooling than the men, and where an honest questioncalled across a courtyard could stop the meeting.

Two things should be said before leaving it, and they matter more than the exegesis to mostpeople who will read this. The first is that nothing here is a verdict on the worth,intelligence or spirituality of women. The same apostle wrote that in Christ there is neithermale nor female (Gal 3:28), named a woman among those outstanding among the apostolic workers(Rom 16:7), and owed his own churches to the labour of Priscilla, Phoebe, Euodia andSyntyche. The second is that this passage has been used to shame women into silence far beyondanything Paul wrote, and that misuse has done real damage. A congregation where women areafraid to speak at all has not obeyed this text; it has ignored chapter 11.

verseByVerse.quote: Or was it from you that the word of God came? Or are you the only ones it has reached?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or was it from you that the word of God came? Or are you the only ones it hasreached?

Two questions, dripping with irony, and they are the sting in the tail of the wholechapter. This verse is often skipped in the argument about the two before it, and it shouldnot be, because it tells us what Paul thought the Corinthians’ real problem was.

It was not tongues. It was independence.

Behind every fault in this letter lies a congregation that had come to believe it was thecentre of things — that its practices were its own to invent, its judgments its own tomake, and its founder’s instructions a matter for consideration. Paul asks the twoquestions that puncture it. Did the gospel start here? Are you the only place it has got to?Both answers are humiliating and both are obvious. The word of God came to Corinth fromsomewhere else, brought by a man who had received it himself, and it had already reached agreat many other cities where the churches did not do what Corinth was doing.

The link with verse 33 is exact. As in all the churches of the saints — andnow, are you the only ones? Paul is placing this congregation back among its peers.Whatever they had concluded about worship, they had concluded it alone, and that alone was awarning sign.

Which is a useful thing to hold up to any church, and it is not an argument for mereconformity. Truth is not decided by counting congregations, and there have been moments whenone church was right and the rest were wrong. But novelty is worth examining, and a churchthat finds itself doing something no other body of Christians anywhere has thought necessaryshould at least ask whether the Spirit really has told it alone. The same Spirit is at work inthe church in the next town, and in the churches of the last twenty centuries.

There is a humility in this for individuals too. The believer convinced that he has seensomething in Scripture that the whole church has missed is occasionally right and is usuallya man who has been reading alone for too long. Paul’s questions are worth asking of anyprivate certainty: did this begin with me, and am I the only one it has reached?

And there is a warmer thing in the verse than the sarcasm suggests. The word of Godcame to Corinth. It arrived. Somebody carried it across the Aegean to a city with abad reputation and no interest in it, and a synagogue ruler and a purple-seller and somedockworkers heard it and believed. Nobody in that congregation had generated a word of it.They were the beneficiaries of a long chain of people who had received something and passed iton.

That is true of every Christian who has ever lived. Whatever any of us knows about Godreached us because it was handed over. There is no self-made believer, and a congregation thatremembers how the word got there is a great deal harder to make arrogant.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone thinks that he is a prophet, or spiritual, he should acknowledge that the things I am writing to you are a command of the Lord. If anyone does not recognize this, he is not recognized.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone thinks that he is a prophet, or spiritual, he should acknowledge that thethings I am writing to you are a command of the Lord. If anyone does not recognize this, he isnot recognized.

Paul now supplies the test he knew would be needed, because he could predict exactly whowould object to this chapter. It would be the people most confident of their own spirituality.

So he sets a trap and states it openly. Do you consider yourself a prophet? Do you consideryourself spiritual? Then here is how that claim is checked: you will recognise that what I amwriting is the Lord’s command. Any spirituality that arrives at a different conclusionfrom apostolic instruction has failed at the only point where it could ever have been tested.

Notice how large a claim that is about this letter. Paul does not present these chapters ashis best judgment, his temperament, or a policy for a difficult congregation. He calls thema command of the Lord. That is the apostolic authority the whole New Testament restson: not that these men were wise, but that they were sent, and that what they wrote to thechurches carries the weight of the one who sent them (cf. 2 Pet 3:15–16).

Then verse 38, which is short and cold. If anyone does not recognize this, he is notrecognized. The manuscripts vary slightly here between he is not recognized andlet him not be recognized, and the difference is small, because either way the man isoutside the circle he was claiming to lead. He wanted to be acknowledged as a prophet. He isnot acknowledged at all — and the passive voice leaves open by whom, which is the mostuncomfortable thing about the sentence.

The principle has a long reach and it is worth having, because it settles the commonestform of spiritual manipulation. Whenever anyone claims an authority, an insight or anexperience that places him above correction from Scripture, this verse answers him. The claimis self-refuting. A genuine work of the Spirit will always submit to the Word the Spirit gave;the test is not whether a man sounds spiritual, but what he does when the Bible contradictshim.

The test works on ordinary Christians as well as on leaders, and it is easy enough to runon yourself. Everyone has a place where Scripture cuts across something he wants — agrudge, a habit, a plan, an opinion held for thirty years. The question is what happens inthat moment. A man who reaches for a reason why the passage does not quite apply to his owncase has just learned something about the real source of his convictions, whatever else hebelieves about the Bible.

And there is mercy in Paul’s verb. He says the spiritual man will recognisethis — will come to see it, the way one recognises a face. He does not say he will agreeat once, or without a struggle, or without wanting to argue first. Recognition can take awhile, and often does.

verseByVerse.quote: So, my brothers, earnestly desire to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues. But all things should be done decently and in order.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So, my brothers, earnestly desire to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues.But all things should be done decently and in order.

The chapter ends with two commands and a governing principle, and the balance of them isthe whole point.

Earnestly desire to prophesy. The same verb he opened with. After forty verses ofregulation, Paul does not want a subdued church. He wants them hungry for the gift that buildspeople up.

And do not forbid speaking in tongues. That is a command, and it is placed exactlywhere a lesser writer would have put a ban. Paul has spent the chapter restricting thepractice of tongues in the assembly — two or three, in turn, interpretation required,otherwise silence — and he closes by forbidding the church to forbid it. He knowsperfectly well what happens when a congregation is corrected about an excess: it swings, andthe next generation treats the thing as an embarrassment.

Whatever a Christian concludes about whether these gifts continue, that sentence shouldtemper the way he holds it. The instinct to shut down anything that cannot be controlled isnot a Christian virtue, and it is not what this apostle did with a church that had abusedalmost every gift it had. He regulated, and then he protected.

But all things should be done decently and in order. The last word, and it is aphrase from the drawing room and the parade ground: with dignity, and in formation. It is asentence often quoted by people who want a quiet church, and it will not quite serve thatpurpose, because verse 39 stands in front of it. Order is what Paul wants around the fire, notinstead of it.

And that is the balance the whole chapter has been holding: a church that is neitherchaotic nor cold, where the Spirit’s gifts are wanted and not feared, where what happenscan be understood by a stranger at the back, and where every single thing is measured bywhether anybody was built up. Corinth had the fire and no grate. Many congregations since havehad a beautiful grate and no fire.

Underneath it all is the God of verse 33 — not a God of confusion but of peace, whoseown life is perfect order and perfect love at once, who has never had to choose betweenliveliness and dignity, and who gave gifts to men so that a room full of ordinary people mightbe built up into something that will last after every tongue has fallen silent(cf. Eph 4:11–13).

14.text: <sup>1</sup>Pursue love, and earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, especially that you may prophesy.<sup>2</sup>For one who speaks in a tongue speaks not to men but to God; for no one understands him, but he utters mysteries in the Spirit.<sup>3</sup>On the other hand, the one who prophesies speaks to people for their upbuilding and encouragement and consolation.<sup>4</sup>The one who speaks in a tongue builds up himself, but the one who prophesies builds up the church.<sup>5</sup>Now I want you all to speak in tongues, but even more to prophesy. The one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues, unless someone interprets, so that the church may be built up.<sup>6</sup>Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, how will I benefit you unless I bring you some revelation or knowledge or prophecy or teaching?<sup>7</sup>If even lifeless instruments, such as the flute or the harp, do not give distinct notes, how will anyone know what is played?<sup>8</sup>And if the bugle gives an indistinct sound, who will get ready for battle?<sup>9</sup>So with yourselves, if with your tongue you utter speech that is not intelligible, how will anyone know what is said? For you will be speaking into the air.<sup>10</sup>There are doubtless many different languages in the world, and none is without meaning,<sup>11</sup>but if I do not know the meaning of the language, I will be a foreigner to the speaker and the speaker a foreigner to me.<sup>12</sup>So with yourselves, since you are eager for manifestations of the Spirit, strive to excel in building up the church.<sup>13</sup>Therefore, one who speaks in a tongue should pray that he may interpret.<sup>14</sup>For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays but my mind is unfruitful.<sup>15</sup>What am I to do? I will pray with my spirit, but I will pray with my mind also; I will sing praise with my spirit, but I will sing with my mind also.<sup>16</sup>Otherwise, if you give thanks with your spirit, how can anyone in the position of an outsider say “Amen” to your thanksgiving when he does not know what you are saying?<sup>17</sup>For you may be giving thanks well enough, but the other person is not being built up.<sup>18</sup>I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you.<sup>19</sup>Nevertheless, in church I would rather speak five words with my mind in order to instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue.<sup>20</sup>Brothers, do not be children in your thinking. Be infants in evil, but in your thinking be mature.<sup>21</sup>In the Law it is written, “By people of strange tongues and by the lips of foreigners will I speak to this people, and even then they will not listen to me, says the Lord.”<sup>22</sup>Thus tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers, while prophecy is a sign not for unbelievers but for believers.<sup>23</sup>If, therefore, the whole church comes together and all speak in tongues, and outsiders or unbelievers enter, will they not say that you are out of your minds?<sup>24</sup>But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or outsider enters, he is convicted by all, he is called to account by all,<sup>25</sup>the secrets of his heart are disclosed, and so, falling on his face, he will worship God and declare that God is really among you.<sup>26</sup>What then, brothers? When you come together, each one has a hymn, a lesson, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. Let all things be done for building up.<sup>27</sup>If any speak in a tongue, let there be only two or at most three, and each in turn, and let someone interpret.<sup>28</sup>But if there is no one to interpret, let each of them keep silent in church and speak to himself and to God.<sup>29</sup>Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others weigh what is said.<sup>30</sup>If a revelation is made to another sitting there, let the first be silent.<sup>31</sup>For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all be encouraged,<sup>32</sup>and the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets.<sup>33</sup>For God is not a God of confusion but of peace. As in all the churches of the saints,<sup>34</sup>the women should keep silent in the churches. For they are not permitted to speak, but should be in submission, as the Law also says.<sup>35</sup>If there is anything they desire to learn, let them ask their husbands at home. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in church.<sup>36</sup>Or was it from you that the word of God came? Or are you the only ones it has reached?<sup>37</sup>If anyone thinks that he is a prophet, or spiritual, he should acknowledge that the things I am writing to you are a command of the Lord.<sup>38</sup>If anyone does not recognize this, he is not recognized.<sup>39</sup>So, my brothers, earnestly desire to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues.<sup>40</sup>But all things should be done decently and in order.

15.title: The Resurrection of the Dead
15.overview:
Chapter 15 is the theological climax of the entire letter — and one of the most important chapters in the New Testament. Everything else in 1 Corinthians has been application; this is foundation. The resurrection of Christ from the dead is not an appendix to the gospel; it is the gospel. And the resurrection of the body is not a peripheral eschatological detail; it is the goal toward which all of creation is moving.

Some at Corinth were denying the resurrection of the dead — not necessarily the resurrection of Christ (which they apparently accepted as historical) but the future bodily resurrection of believers. Paul treats this as the most catastrophic doctrinal error possible: “if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain” (v. 14). The resurrection is the structural load-bearing wall of the entire Christian building. Remove it and nothing stands.

Paul’s response moves in three great movements: the historical certainty of Christ’s resurrection, established by testimony (vv. 1–11); the logical and theological necessity of the resurrection for the whole Christian faith (vv. 12–34); and the nature of the resurrection body, answering the philosophical objections about how the dead are raised (vv. 35–58). The chapter ends with one of the most electrifying doxologies in Scripture: “O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Resurrection of Christ: The Apostolic Testimony
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul begins with the most important word in this chapter: “I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received.” En prōtois — of first importance, of primary significance: not first in a sequence of equally important things but first because everything else depends on it. The resurrection of Christ is not one doctrine among many; it is the doctrine from which all others derive their force. And Paul has both received it (from the tradition, from the Lord himself) and delivered it (to the Corinthians, faithfully, without alteration).

The content of the tradition is the gospel in miniature: Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures; he was buried (confirming the reality of the death); he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures; he appeared to Peter, then to the Twelve, then to more than five hundred brothers, then to James, then to all the apostles, then to Paul himself. The list of appearances is a legal brief — evidence gathered from multiple witnesses, most of whom are still alive and can be questioned. Paul is not asking for faith without evidence; he is pointing to the evidence and asking for faith proportionate to it.

Paul’s self-description in vv. 9–10 is the most concentrated theological autobiography in his letters: the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle because he persecuted the church of God; yet what he is, he is by the grace of God, and the grace was not in vain — he worked harder than all of them, yet not he but the grace of God that was with him. The paradox of grace and effort, of unworthiness and productivity, of receiving and working, is compressed into two verses that describe every genuine Christian life.

The opening two verses set the terms. Four verbs describe the gospel’s whole relation to a believer: it was preached, it was received, it is what they stand in, and it is what they are being saved by. Then the clause that unsettles some readers — if you hold fast… unless you believed in vain. Paul is not threatening a believer with loss; he raises the possibility that a profession was empty from the start. Holding fast is never the cause of being kept, but it is the evidence of it.

And verse 11 closes the section by putting the whole apostolic company on one footing: whether then it was I or they, so we preach and so you believed. After all the autobiography, the messenger is not the point — which is exactly what a congregation dividing over Paul, Apollos and Cephas needed to hear.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Resurrection as the Foundation of Salvation

Paul’s phrase “Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures” is the earliest creedal formulation we possess, pre-dating the letter (Paul received it). The resurrection “in accordance with the Scriptures” grounds both events in OT prophecy — Psalm 16:10, Isaiah 53, Hosea 6:2 being the primary candidates. The conjunction of death and resurrection is crucial: the resurrection is not an isolated miracle but the divine vindication of the atoning death. Without the resurrection, the death has no declared meaning; without the death, the resurrection has no redemptive content. Together they constitute the gospel.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Greek philosophical tradition was deeply ambivalent about bodily resurrection. The famous scene in Acts 17:32 — when Paul mentions the resurrection, some mock and some are interested — captures the standard Hellenistic reaction. The Platonic tradition prized the release of the soul from the body; the idea of the body being raised was not an upgrade but a retrogression to the bodily existence the soul was trying to escape. Paul’s case for the resurrection runs directly against this deeply embedded cultural instinct. Now: The modern version of the Greek objection is not philosophical but scientific: dead bodies do not rise. Paul’s answer is the same: the evidence of the witnesses. The question is not whether bodies normally rise but whether this specific body, on this specific morning, was raised by the God who created bodies in the first place.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I would remind you, brothers, of the gospel I preached to you, which you received, in which you stand, and by which you are being saved, if you hold fast to the word I preached to you—unless you believed in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fifteen chapters of correction are behind him — factions, immorality, lawsuits,marriage, idol meat, head coverings, the Supper, the gifts. Now Paul turns to the thing allof it rests on, and his tone changes completely.

Now I would remind you, brothers, of the gospel I preached to you, which you received,in which you stand, and by which you are being saved.

Four verbs, and together they are a small map of the Christian life. The gospel waspreached — it came from outside, as news; nobody worked it out. It wasreceived — taken, as a gift is taken, which is the only posture available to aman being given something. It is what they stand in — the present tense of it,the ground under their feet, and Paul chooses that verb for a congregation that had beenstanding on its gifts, its wisdom and its teachers. And it is what they are beingsaved by, which is a present continuous: salvation is not only something that happenedto them at a meeting years ago but something still going on.

Then the clause that stops some readers cold: if you hold fast to the word I preachedto you — unless you believed in vain.

It sounds, at first hearing, as though everything is conditional, and a Christian troubledabout his own perseverance can be badly frightened by it. So read what Paul actually says.He does not say you will lose what you have if you slip. He raises the possibilitythat some of them believed in vain — that is, believed to no purpose, withouteffect, a profession that never had anything living in it. That is a different thing from abeliever falling out of God’s hand, which this apostle elsewhere says is impossible(Rom 8:38–39).

Holding fast, in the New Testament, is never the cause of being kept; it is the evidence ofit. The people God keeps are the people who keep going, and he keeps them by making them keepgoing. So this clause is not a threat held over a frightened Christian; it is a question putto a comfortable one. And it has a searching form: not do you remember believing?but are you still holding on? The mark of a real faith is not the vividness of itsbeginning but the fact that it is still there (cf. Col 1:23; Heb 3:14).

There is one more thing in the opening line that is easy to walk past. I would remindyou. Paul is not about to tell this church anything new. Everything in this chapter, thelongest and greatest in the letter, is material they already had and had stopped standing on.

That is worth knowing, because Christians commonly assume that what they need is moreinformation. The Corinthians were drowning in information; they had been taught by Paul foreighteen months and by Apollos after him. What they needed was for somebody to walk them backto the first thing and make them look at it again.

Most of the Christian life is like that. Very little of what steadies a believer in a hardyear is new to him. It is the old thing, remembered at the right moment, by someone whotroubled to say it again.

verseByVerse.quote: For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ diedfor our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on thethird day in accordance with the Scriptures.

Two words in that sentence are worth more than they look. Received anddelivered are the standard vocabulary for handing on a fixed tradition, word forword, without adjustment — the same pair he used of the Lord’s Supper at 11:23.Paul is not composing here. He is reciting something he was given.

And that matters more for the historical question than almost anything else in the NewTestament. Paul is writing about twenty-five years after the crucifixion. But he did notinvent this formula; he received it — which means it was already in circulation andalready fixed when he was taught it, and he was taught it at his conversion or shortly after,within a very few years of the event. This is not a legend that grew over generations. It isa summary that was being recited by Christians while the people who buried Jesus were stillmiddle-aged.

Now the four clauses, and each is load-bearing.

Christ died for our sins. Not merely died. The little word for carriessubstitution: in our place, on our account. A death without that word is a tragedy; with it,it is an exchange.

In accordance with the Scriptures. The phrase appears twice, once for the deathand once for the rising, and it means this was not an emergency. Isaiah had described aservant pierced for our transgressions, who would see his offspring andprolong his days after making his soul an offering for guilt (Isa 53:5, 10). Thepsalmist had said God would not let his Holy One see corruption (Ps 16:10), whichPeter preached at Pentecost. Hosea had spoken of God raising his people up on the thirdday (Hos 6:2), and Jesus himself pointed to Jonah in the fish. The plan is older than thecrime.

He was buried. The oddest item on the list, and the one people skip. Why includeit in a summary this compressed? Two reasons. It settles that he was actually dead —there was a body, and men carried it, and it was heavy. And it puts the claim in a place whereit could be checked: a burial means a tomb, and a tomb has an address, and Jerusalem is asmall city.

He was raised on the third day. Note the passive. Not he rose, thoughthat is also true, but he was raised — the Father acting on the Son. Theresurrection is the Father’s answer to the cross, and his verdict on it.

verseByVerse.quote: and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve.

The witness list begins, and it begins with a scandal.

Cephas is Peter, and the last thing the reader knows about Peter is that he stood by a firein a courtyard and swore three times that he had never met the man. He is the one apostlewhose failure is recorded in all four Gospels. And he is first on the list.

Luke preserves the same detail: when the two from Emmaus got back to Jerusalem, the otherstold them the Lord has risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon (Lk 24:34). Nobodyrecords what was said in that meeting, which is a mercy; some conversations are not forpublication. But the fact of it is here, in the earliest Christian creed we possess: the risenChrist went first to the man who had denied him.

Then the twelve — and a careful reader stops, because at that point therewere not twelve. Judas was dead. Thomas was absent from the first appearance. So the number iswrong, and someone will say so.

The answer is that the Twelve had become a title rather than a headcount. It wasthe name of the group, the way a committee keeps its name when a seat is empty and a regimentkeeps its number after a bad year. John uses it the same way, calling Thomas one of thetwelve on an occasion when the room held ten (Jn 20:24).

And here is what to notice about that. A man polishing a story does not leave acountable discrepancy in the second line of his creed. He writes the eleven, which iswhat Luke writes when he is being precise (Lk 24:33), and nobody ever raises the question.The rough edge is the mark of a formula that was in use among people who were there and knewperfectly well what it meant.

Two men, then, at the head of the evidence: a denier, and a group with a hole in it where atraitor used to be. That is who the risen Christ chose to show himself to first. He did not goto the Sanhedrin, or to Pilate, or to the crowd. He went back to his friends, and the firstname on the list is the one who had let him down worst (cf. Mk 16:7; Jn 21:15–17).

The angel at the tomb had already signalled it. Go, tell his disciples and Peter(Mk 16:7) — and those two extra words are the gospel in miniature. Peter haddisqualified himself and would have said so. Somebody made sure his name was spokenseparately, in case he assumed the message was for the others and not for him.

Which is the shape of this chapter’s comfort for anyone who has failed badly enoughto believe he has forfeited his place. The risen Christ does not begin with the loyal. Hebegins with the man who has to be told twice that he is still wanted, and he goes and findshim first.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive, though some have fallen asleep. Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are stillalive, though some have fallen asleep. Then he appeared to James, then to all theapostles.

Two more entries, and both are doing work that is easy to miss.

The appearance to more than five hundred at once is recorded nowhere else in the NewTestament, which is itself striking — Paul knows more than the Gospels chose to writedown. But the clause to weigh is the parenthesis: most of whom are still alive.

That is not a devotional remark. It is an invitation, and its tone is almost brisk. Theletter is going to a port city with constant traffic to Palestine. Paul is saying: severalhundred people saw this at the same time, they are not hard to find, and you may go and askthem. A man inventing a story does not name a crowd of living witnesses and mention that theycan be interviewed. He locates his miracle somewhere quieter.

Then James, and this one is quietly devastating. This is James the brother of theLord, who ended up leading the church in Jerusalem and was killed for it. And the Gospelsrecord, without embarrassment, what he thought before that: not even his brothersbelieved in him (Jn 7:5). His family had at one point gone out to seize Jesus, saying hewas out of his mind (Mk 3:21).

Consider what it takes to change a brother’s mind. Nobody in the world is harder toconvince that a man is the Son of God than the man who grew up in the same house, ate at thesame table, and watched him be an ordinary older brother for thirty years. Scepticism about asibling is not a theory; it is a lifetime of evidence. James went from that to leading themother church of Christianity and dying rather than take it back, and this verse is the wholeexplanation: then he appeared to James.

One thing the list does not contain is worth explaining, since a modern reader will noticeit. The women are not here, though all four Gospels say the women found the tomb and saw himfirst. Paul is assembling something like a legal brief, and in that world a woman’stestimony carried no weight in a court — which is precisely why the fact that theGospels kept the women in is such powerful evidence of honesty. Nobody constructing a caseputs his least admissible witnesses at the front. They did it because that is what happened.

verseByVerse.quote: Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me. For I am the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me. For I am the least of theapostles, unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God.

The word translated untimely born is blunt in Greek: it means a miscarriage, abirth that came violently and out of season. It may have been a name his opponents used forhim — the runt, the one who arrived wrong — and if so, he has picked it up and putit in his own creed. Paul does that repeatedly. He takes the insult and keeps it.

Because it fits. The Twelve had three years of walking beside Jesus, being taught, beingcorrected, being prepared. Paul had none of it. He was on a road with warrants in his bag,travelling to arrest people, and the risen Christ intercepted him mid-journey. He was notraised into apostleship; he was seized into it.

Then the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecutedthe church of God. There is no performance in that sentence. Elsewhere he will callhimself the foremost of sinners (1 Tim 1:15) and, later still, less than the least of all thesaints (Eph 3:8) — and the striking thing is the direction of travel. The longer hewalked with Christ, the smaller his estimate of himself became. That is the normal arithmeticof grace, and it runs the opposite way from the arithmetic of religion.

Notice what he never does, though. He does not say he is not an apostle. He never tradeshis commission for the comfort of self-abasement, because the commission was not his toresign; it was given. A Christian can hold two things at once here: an honest low estimate ofhimself, and a settled certainty about what God has said about him. Losing either produces adistortion — arrogance on one side, false humility on the other, and both of them arefinally about the same subject.

And there is evidence in this verse as well as autobiography. Paul’s own conversionis one of the harder facts for a sceptic to place. Here is a trained, motivated, well-connectedopponent, actively destroying the movement, with everything to gain by continuing — andhe changes sides, loses his standing, and spends thirty years being beaten and imprisoned forthe thing he was suppressing. Something happened on that road. He says he knows what itwas.

And the persecution he names is not left in the abstract. Luke tells us what it lookedlike: young men laying their coats at his feet while a man was stoned to death (Acts 7:58);Saul ravaging the church, going house to house, dragging off men and women andcommitting them to prison (Acts 8:3); still breathing threats and murder as he setout for Damascus (Acts 9:1). There were widows in Jerusalem who knew his name.

That is the man who says he appeared also to me. Whatever else grace is, it is nota general kindliness. It is specific enough to walk out onto a road and stop a man who is onhis way to arrest more of the family (cf. 1 Tim 1:13–16).

verseByVerse.quote: But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain. On the contrary, I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me. Whether then it was I or they, so we preach and so you believed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain. On thecontrary, I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I, but the grace of God that iswith me.

One of the most compressed sentences in Paul, and it holds together two things that peopleare forever pulling apart.

By the grace of God I am what I am. Nothing about him is self-made. Not theapostleship, not the conversion, not the endurance, and not the letters. Everything tracesback to an unearned kindness that intercepted him when he was going the other way.

And then, immediately: I worked harder than any of them. Which sounds, on theface of it, like the boast he has just disowned — until the last clause takes it backwithout cancelling it: though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me.

Do not resolve that tension by choosing a side; Paul refuses to. Grace is not analternative to effort. Grace is what produces the effort. The man worked himself toexhaustion, and the working was itself the gift. It is the same grammar aswork out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you(Phil 2:12–13), and it is the answer to two opposite mistakes that Christians make withequal enthusiasm.

The first is the one that hears grace and concludes that effort is unspiritual— that a Christian should wait to be moved, that trying hard is a form of unbelief, thatthe disciplined believer is really relying on himself. Paul was the most exhausted man in theNew Testament and he did not think so.

The second is the one that hears work and quietly begins keeping score —that measures itself against other Christians, is pleased with its own diligence, and would beoffended to be told that all of it was a gift. Paul had a genuine claim to that comparisonand he made it in the same breath as its cancellation.

Then verse 11 puts the whole apostolic company back on one footing: whether then it wasI or they, so we preach and so you believed. After all that autobiography, it does notmatter which of them said it. The Corinthians had been dividing over exactly this —Paul, Apollos, Cephas — and here is the man himself waving the question away. Themessenger is not the point. What was preached is the point, and it was the same from all ofthem.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–19 — If Christ Has Not Been Raised
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now deploys the logical consequences of denying the resurrection with a series of devastating conditional arguments. If the dead are not raised, then Christ has not been raised. If Christ has not been raised, then the preaching is empty, the faith is empty, the apostolic witness is false, no one’s sins have been forgiven, those who have died in Christ have perished, and Christians are, of all people, most to be pitied.

The argument is a reductio ad absurdum of the Corinthian position. The Corinthians apparently wanted to accept Christ’s resurrection as a unique event while denying the general resurrection of the dead. Paul shows that this is incoherent: the two stand or fall together, because Christ’s resurrection is of the same kind as the general resurrection, not a different kind of event. If the general resurrection is impossible, then Christ’s resurrection is impossible; and if Christ’s resurrection is impossible, then everything the Corinthians claim to believe has no foundation.

“You are still in your sins” (v. 17) — this is the pastoral heart of the argument. The resurrection is not merely a fact about Jesus’s fate after death; it is the evidence that the atonement was accepted. If the Father accepted the Son’s sacrifice, the verdict is the resurrection. If there is no resurrection, there is no verdict; if there is no verdict, the atonement is unconfirmed; if the atonement is unconfirmed, sins are not forgiven. The resurrection is not a bonus feature of the gospel; it is the receipt that proves the transaction was completed.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Resurrection as the Confirmation of the Atonement

Paul’s logic in v. 17 — “if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins” — grounds the significance of the resurrection in its relationship to the atonement. The death of Christ atones; the resurrection of Christ confirms and declares the atonement accepted. This is why Romans 4:25 says Christ “was raised for our justification”: the resurrection is the Father’s “yes” to the Son’s atoning sacrifice. Without the resurrection, Good Friday is a tragedy; with the resurrection, Good Friday is the pivot of history.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian denial of bodily resurrection was probably influenced by Platonic body-soul dualism: if the soul is what matters, and it survives death, why would God re-attach it to a body? Paul’s argument is that this misunderstands both what salvation means (the redemption of the whole person, body and soul) and what happened to Christ (his body was raised, not merely his spirit). Now: The contemporary version of the Corinthian position often appears in Christian thinking that treats the soul’s going to heaven as the whole story and the resurrection as an afterthought. Paul’s insistence is that the resurrection body is the destination, and the intermediate state (soul in God’s presence before the resurrection) is the waiting room.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if Christ is proclaimed as raised from the dead, how can some of you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? But if there is no resurrection of the dead, then not even Christ has been raised. And if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now if Christ is proclaimed as raised from the dead, how can some of you say that thereis no resurrection of the dead?

At last the actual problem. Some in Corinth were denying the resurrection of the dead— not, apparently, the resurrection of Jesus, which they seem to have accepted, but theidea that the rest of us will be raised bodily.

It helps to know why that felt reasonable to them, because it was not stupidity. EducatedGreeks had a settled view of the body, and it was low. The soul was the real self; the bodywas its container and, for many, its prison. There was a well-worn play on words for it— sōma sēma, the body is a tomb. On that view, death is not theenemy but the release: the soul finally gets out. Immortality of the soul, yes, gladly. ButGod putting you back into a body? That is not salvation; that is being re-arrested.

So the Corinthian denial was not an attack on Christianity as they understood it. It was anattempt to keep the parts of it they liked and file the rest under the crude expectations ofJewish converts.

Paul’s reply is to show that the thing they wanted to keep cannot survive the thingthey wanted to drop. But if there is no resurrection of the dead, then not even Christ hasbeen raised. The reasoning is exact. Resurrection of the dead is the category. Christ’sresurrection is an instance of it. If the category is impossible in principle, no instance ofit happened, including that one. You cannot say such things do not occur, except once.

And if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is invain. The word means empty — hollow, with nothing inside. Not mistaken in a detail;containing nothing at all. An empty sermon and an empty faith, because faith is only ever asgood as the thing it is resting on, and if the thing is not there the sincerity of the restingchanges nothing.

That is worth sitting with, because it is the exact opposite of how faith is usually spokenabout today. Christianity does not claim that believing is good for you. It stakes everythingon an event, and it says so out loud, and it offers to be checked.

It is worth noticing what Paul does not do here, since it is what most of us woulddo. He does not tell the doubters that their faith can survive without the doctrine. He doesnot offer them a version of Christianity that keeps the ethics, the community and the comfortand quietly drops the miracle. There was an easier letter available to him and he did notwrite it.

That is a courtesy to the reader, though it does not always feel like one. A faith thatcan be adjusted to fit whatever a generation finds credible has no power to contradict thatgeneration, and therefore nothing to offer it. Paul puts the whole weight on one load-bearingclaim, and invites anyone who wishes to try to knock it down.

verseByVerse.quote: We are even found to be misrepresenting God, because we testified about God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise if it is true that the dead are not raised. For if the dead are not raised, not even Christ has been raised. And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We are even found to be misrepresenting God, because we testified about God that heraised Christ, whom he did not raise if it is true that the dead are not raised.

Paul follows the logic down and it gets worse at every step. If there was no resurrection,then the apostles have not merely been mistaken. They have been going round the Mediterraneantelling people that God did something he did not do — putting words in his mouth,attaching his name to a fiction. The Greek phrase means false witnesses against God.

Notice that Paul takes that possibility seriously enough to name it. He does not say thegospel is worth believing regardless. He says: if this did not happen, we are liars about theGod we claim to serve, and we deserve whatever that means.

Then he arrives at the worst consequence, and it is not the one most people would haveguessed. And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still inyour sins.

Why should that follow? He died, after all. If the death is what pays for sin, why does therising matter to the accounting?

Because a death, by itself, tells you nothing about whether it worked. Two men werecrucified beside him and their deaths paid for nobody. What the cross needed was a verdict— some public act by which the Father declared that the sacrifice had been received andthe debt cleared. That is what the resurrection is. Paul says it plainly elsewhere: Jesus wasdelivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification (Rom 4:25).

Think of it as a receipt. A man may pay an enormous debt and the payment does the work; butuntil the paper comes back stamped, the debtor has no way of knowing whether it went through.The empty tomb is the stamp. On Friday the price was paid. On Sunday the Father put it inwriting, in a form that could be walked into and looked at.

Which turns this into a chapter about assurance and not only about the afterlife. TheChristian troubled about whether his sins are really forgiven is being pointed, by this verse,away from his own feelings and toward a garden outside Jerusalem. The question is not whetheryou feel forgiven. It is whether the tomb is empty. If it is, the matter is settled, and it wassettled without consulting you.

And notice how carefully Paul distinguishes two states that people confuse. He does notsay that without the resurrection a Christian would feel unforgiven. He saysyou are still in your sins — a statement about the actual position, not theimpression of it. Which cuts both ways, and the second way is the comfort. If the objectivefact governs when the news is bad, it governs when the news is good. The believer who feelsnothing on a grey Tuesday is not less forgiven than he was on the day he wept at the front ofa church. The tomb did not become less empty overnight.

verseByVerse.quote: Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. If in Christ we have hope in this life only, we are of all people most to be pitied.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. If in Christ we havehope in this life only, we are of all people most to be pitied.

The argument stops being abstract. There were graves in Corinth with Christians in them— members of that congregation who had died in the few years since the church began, andwhose families were still in the room when this letter was read out.

Fallen asleep is the New Testament’s habitual word for the death of abeliever, and it is not a euphemism designed to avoid the subject. It says something: thatthis condition is temporary and that there will be a waking. But Paul now removes that, forthe sake of the argument, and states the alternative without softening it. If there is noresurrection, they have perished. Gone. Not asleep — finished. Every one ofthose funerals was a final parting and the words said over the grave were false.

That is what the clever position in Corinth actually cost, and Paul makes them look at it.A doctrine can be discussed as an idea in a room full of healthy people. Take it to agraveside and you find out what it is.

If in Christ we have hope in this life only, we are of all people most to bepitied.

Not we are still better off. Not at least the ethics are good and thecommunity is warm. Paul says that if this life is all there is, the Christian has madethe worst bargain of anyone alive, and deserves not respect but pity.

He had grounds for saying so. He had given up his standing, his safety, his prospects andhis comfort; he would shortly list the beatings, the shipwrecks, the hunger and the sleeplessnights (2 Cor 11:23–28). If there is no resurrection, that is not nobility. It is a manwho threw his one life away on a rumour.

And the verse quietly indicts a kind of Christianity that is very common and verycomfortable — the sort that values the faith for what it does now. It steadies afamily, gives a shape to the week, provides friends and a moral framework and a sense ofmeaning. All of that is real, and Paul’s point is that a religion which delivers thosethings and nothing else is a pitiable arrangement, whatever its members say about it. Thisfaith is not primarily a way to live. It is a claim that a dead man is alive, and everythingelse follows from that or falls with it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.” The “but in fact” (nyn de) is the most powerful two-word pivot in the chapter — possibly in the Bible. After the devastating catalogue of what follows if Christ is not raised, Paul turns the corner with the simplest assertion of the most important fact in history. He is raised. Firstfruits.

The firstfruits metaphor is drawn from the OT harvest liturgy: the first sheaf of grain, brought to the temple on the day after the Sabbath following Passover, was the pledge of the whole harvest to come. Christ’s resurrection is not an isolated miracle but the first instalment of a harvest that includes all who belong to him. His resurrection is not complete until theirs is complete; his rising is the beginning of a general rising in which all who are in him will participate.

The Adam/Christ typology of vv. 21–22 is one of the most compressed and profound theological arguments in the NT. As through one man (Adam) death came into the world and spread to all who are in him, so through one man (Christ) resurrection from the dead comes to those who are in him. The parallel is structural: two representative heads, two realms of existence, two destinies. Everyone is in one or the other — either in Adam (under death) or in Christ (under resurrection). The question is which solidarity defines you.

The section does not stop at Adam and Christ. Verses 23 to 28 lay out the sequence: Christ the firstfruits, then those who belong to him at his coming, then the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God the Father after destroying every rule and authority and power. What is handed over is not a ruin salvaged from a fire but a completed kingdom.

At the centre of it stands verse 26, and it is the sentence a grieving Christian most needs: the last enemy to be destroyed is death. Not a doorway, not a natural transition, not a friend at the end of a long day — an enemy, and the one still standing when everything else has fallen. Scripture gives the mourner permission to hate it; the Lord himself wept outside a tomb he was about to open. And verses 27 and 28 apply Psalm 8 to Christ as the true human being, doing at last what Adam was made for, and end with the goal of everything: that God may be all in all.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Adam/Christ Typology and the Scope of Redemption

The Adam/Christ typology here (cf. Rom 5:12–21) is the cornerstone of Paul’s understanding of both sin and salvation. Adam’s representative headship means that his sin brought death to all who are “in Adam” — which is every human being by natural birth. Christ’s representative headship means that his obedience, death, and resurrection bring life to all who are “in Christ” — which is every believer by the new birth. The scope is parallel but not identical: “in Christ shall all be made alive” refers to all who are in Christ, not to every human being universally. The typology demands that the domain of redemption be at least as real and significant as the domain of death.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians who had lost members to death needed to know that those deaths were not permanent losses but sleeps awaiting a harvest. The firstfruits language gave them a specific, liturgically resonant image: the resurrection of Christ is God’s pledge that the full harvest of resurrection is coming. Now: The Christian stands at the graveside of a believer with the same confidence: the firstfruits have already appeared; the rest of the harvest is as certain as the God who made the pledge. The resurrection is not a hope against hope but a certainty grounded in a historical event.

verseByVerse.quote: But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. For as by a man came death, by a man has come also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who havefallen asleep.

Two words in Greek, and they turn the whole chapter: but in fact. Paul has spenteight verses in a nightmare of his own construction — empty preaching, futile faith,unforgiven sin, dead friends gone for ever, a life thrown away. And then, without argument,he simply steps out of it. The corridor of horrors was hypothetical. He was never in any doubtabout the way out.

The firstfruits. The image is agricultural and liturgical at once, and every Jewishreader knew it. On the day after the Sabbath following Passover, a single sheaf of the newbarley was cut and brought to the priest and waved before the LORD (Lev 23:10–11). Onesheaf, in a field still standing. It was not the harvest; it was the promise of the harvest.The rest was coming, and the sheaf in the priest’s hands was the proof.

Consider the timing of that ceremony, and then consider on which morning Jesus came out ofthe tomb.

What the image does is change the category of the resurrection completely. It is not amiracle that happened to one exceptional person — a stand-alone wonder, best admiredfrom a distance. It is the first of a series. Nobody waves a sheaf over an empty field. Theresurrection of Jesus is God’s public statement that the harvest of the dead has begun,and it therefore says something about every Christian grave that has ever been dug.

For as by a man came death, by a man has come also the resurrection of the dead. Foras in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.

Paul’s way of thinking about the human race is one of representation. Two men standat the head of two humanities, and what each did counts for everyone belonging to him. Adamsinned, and death entered and spread to all who are in him — which is everybody, bybirth. Christ obeyed, died and rose, and life comes to all who are in him — which iseverybody who belongs to him, by new birth.

The two alls must be read in their own halves of the sentence, and one clausecontrols both: in Adam, and in Christ. The verse is not teaching that everyhuman being will finally be saved, since Paul spends the rest of his letters saying otherwiseand this same chapter speaks of enemies still to be subdued. It is saying that whichever manyou are joined to, his outcome is yours. Nobody is standing on his own.

Which is bad news read one way and the best news in the world read the other. You did notchoose to be in Adam and you cannot argue your way out of it; the evidence is that you aregoing to die. But the same principle that ruins you is the principle that saves you, becausebeing in Christ works exactly the same way — not by achievement, but by belonging(cf. Rom 5:17–19).

verseByVerse.quote: But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then at his coming those who belong to Christ. Then comes the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God the Father after destroying every rule and every authority and power.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then at his coming those who belongto Christ. Then comes the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God the Father after destroyingevery rule and every authority and power.
