Each in his own order is a military word — a rank, a division, troops movingin sequence. Paul is not being vague about the future; he is saying it has a shape and theshape has stages.

The first has happened. Christ, the firstfruits, is raised, and that is now a fixed pointin history behind us rather than in front of us.

The second is still to come: at his coming, those who belong to Christ. And noticethe definition of the group. Not those who achieved something, or understood something, orbelonged to the right party in Corinth. Those who belong to Christ — the solequalification is ownership, and it runs the right way round. They are his.

Then the end, and a picture that ought to be better known than it is. The Sondelivers the kingdom to God the Father. The whole long campaign — theincarnation, the cross, the empty tomb, the two thousand years of the church, the resurrectionof the dead — is a mission with a completion, and it ends with the Son handing thefinished work to his Father.

And before that, destroying every rule and every authority and power. Paul usesthose three words in this letter and elsewhere for more than parliaments and armies; theycover the spiritual forces behind the visible ones, the powers he says the Christian actuallywrestles with (Eph 6:12). Every one of them goes. Not reformed, not negotiated with,not accommodated. Abolished.

There is a steadiness in this for anyone reading the news. The powers that presently lookpermanent — the regimes, the ideologies, the interests that seem able to outlast anyopposition, and the darker things that stand behind them — are on a list, and the listhas a completion date. Nothing on it is going to survive the arrival of the King, and none ofit will require a second campaign (cf. Col 2:15; Rev 11:15).

The verb at the centre of the sequence deserves a moment: he delivers the kingdom toGod the Father. It is the language of a steward handing back an estate, or of acommander reporting to the one who sent him. And what is handed over is not a ruin salvagedfrom a fire. It is a kingdom — the whole thing, complete, every enemy dealt with andevery subject alive.

There is a quiet correction here for the way Christians often picture the end. It is notprincipally a rescue in which a remnant is snatched out of a world written off as a totalloss. It is a campaign that finishes, a work that is completed, and a Son with something topresent to his Father.

verseByVerse.quote: For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to bedestroyed is death.

Six words that a great many people need and have never been given: the last enemy to bedestroyed is death.

Look at what death is called. Not a doorway. Not a natural transition, not a part of thecircle of life, not a friend who comes at the end of a long day. An enemy — andthe last one standing, the one still on its feet after everything else has fallen.

That single word is worth more to a grieving Christian than a great deal of what is said atfunerals. There is a way of speaking about death in religious circles that tries to make peacewith it — that says it is only a change of address, that we should not be sad, that abeliever ought to be serene. The Bible does not do this. The Bible calls death an enemy, andit gives the mourner permission to hate it.

The Lord himself did. Standing outside the tomb of a friend he was about to raise, knowingexactly what would happen in ten minutes, Jesus wept (Jn 11:35) — and the word John usesof him a moment earlier suggests something closer to anger than sorrow, a snort of fury. Hewas not weeping about the outcome; he knew the outcome. He was standing in front of the thingitself, the enemy in a graveyard, doing to a family he loved what it does to everybody.

And be concrete about what it does, because vagueness here helps nobody. It takes a personwho was in the room and makes the room empty. It ends the conversation in the middle. It takesa hand that has been held for fifty years and makes it cold in an hour. It leaves a chair, acoat, a handwriting, a voice on an old recording that is now unbearable to play. It is nottidy and it is not gentle and it does not care what anyone was in the middle of.

So the Christian is not asked to pretend. He is asked to believe that the enemy is on aschedule. The last enemy to be destroyed — not tamed, not made bearable,destroyed — and last, because everything else goes first and this is the one that has tobe dealt with at the end.

The reigning Christ is at this moment putting his enemies under his feet, one after another,and he is working his way toward the grave. When he reaches it, it will not be a truce. Therewill come a day on which there is no death anywhere in the universe, and no one will everagain have to be told that someone has died.

verseByVerse.quote: For “God has put all things in subjection under his feet.” But when it says, “all things are put in subjection,” it is plain that he is excepted who put all things in subjection under him. When all things are subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who put all things in subjection under him, that God may be all in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For “God has put all things in subjection under his feet.” But when it says,“all things are put in subjection,” it is plain that he is excepted who put allthings in subjection under him.

The quotation is from Psalm 8, and the psalm is not, in the first place, about the Messiah.It is about human beings: what is man that you are mindful of him? — and yetGod has crowned him with glory and put all things under his feet (Ps 8:4–6). It iscreation’s job description for the human race, given in the garden and abandoned there.Adam was made to rule the world under God and instead handed it over.

Paul applies the psalm to Christ, and the logic is the one running through this wholechapter. Christ is the last Adam — the true human being, doing at last what humanity wasmade for. Psalm 8 has not been wrenched out of context; it has finally found a man it fits.

Then Paul stops to make a point so obvious it is almost comic, and yet it needs making:when Scripture says everything is put under him, that plainly does not include the One doingthe putting. Nobody subjects himself to somebody else by an act of his own authority. TheFather is not among the things subdued.

When all things are subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected tohim who put all things in subjection under him, that God may be all in all.

And here is a sentence that has troubled readers for centuries, because it appears to makethe Son permanently lesser. It does not, and the reason is the same one that answered thesame question at 11:3.

What is described here is not the Son’s nature but the completion of his mission. Hewas sent; he came; he obeyed; he died; he rose; he reigns; he subdues; and when the work isfinished he presents it all to the Father and takes his place in the order he has occupiedwillingly from the beginning. The Son who is the exact imprint of his nature(Heb 1:3) does not become less divine by handing over a completed kingdom. He is doing whathe has always done — and it is the same Son who said, in a garden, not my will, butyours, be done (Lk 22:42).

That God may be all in all. That is the end of the story, and it is worthrefusing to leave it as a phrase. It means a universe with nothing left in it that is notfilled with God — no corner where he is absent, no life he does not saturate, nothingbetween him and his people, and nobody anywhere having to go looking for him. Every placewhere a believer has felt God to be distant will have been abolished, along with distanceitself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–34 — The Logic of Resurrection Living
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now makes two arguments for the resurrection from the logic of Christian behaviour. First, an obscure and much-debated reference to baptism for the dead (v. 29): if the dead are not raised, why are people being baptised for them? Whatever the practice was, Paul uses it ad hominem — not endorsing it but pointing out that even by their own behaviour, the Corinthians reveal a belief in resurrection. Second, Paul’s own apostolic suffering: “I die every day!” (v. 31). If there is no resurrection, Paul’s life of constant danger, daily exposure to death, fighting with beasts at Ephesus — all of it is pointless self-destruction. If the dead are not raised, “let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.” The Epicurean counsel of hedonism is the only rational alternative to resurrection hope.

The section closes with a proverb borrowed from the playwright Menander: bad company ruins good morals (v. 33). It is a sentence about company, and that assumption matters — people rarely reason their way into abandoning the resurrection. They drift, in company, over time. Then the sharpest words in the chapter: wake up from your drunken stupor… for some have no knowledge of God. I say this to your shame (v. 34). Behind the denial lies not a difficulty with biology but a God too small to raise the dead.
verseByVerse.theology:
Resurrection and the Rational Grounds of Christian Ethics

Paul’s argument here anticipates the famous wager logic: if there is no resurrection, Christian ethics (self-denial, risk, suffering for others) is irrational. The person who lives as if the resurrection were true is either right (and has invested wisely) or wrong (and has lived a meaningful but ultimately futile life). The Epicurean is consistent: if there is no resurrection, maximise pleasure now. Paul’s whole life is a living argument for the resurrection: his willingness to face death daily makes no sense on any other hypothesis.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s reference to “fighting with beasts at Ephesus” may be literal (arena animals) or metaphorical (violent opponents); either way it describes the real mortal danger of apostolic ministry. The question is: for what purpose? If the dead are not raised, the purpose has no transcendent ground. Now: Every Christian who chooses a harder path for the sake of the gospel — the missionary in a dangerous field, the pastor who refuses to compromise his convictions, the layperson who sacrifices career advancement for integrity — is making an implicit resurrection bet. Their lives only make sense if the resurrection is true.

verseByVerse.quote: Otherwise, what do people mean by being baptized on behalf of the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why are people baptized on their behalf? Why are we in danger every hour?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Otherwise, what do people mean by being baptized on behalf of the dead? If the dead arenot raised at all, why are people baptized on their behalf? Why are we in danger everyhour?

Verse 29 is the most obscure sentence in the letter, and something like forty explanationsof it have been offered. It is worth being honest about that rather than pretending to acertainty nobody has.

Three readings are worth knowing. The plainest sense of the Greek is that some people atCorinth were being baptised as proxies for relatives or friends who had died unbaptised, inthe hope that it would do the dead some good. Early writers such as Chrysostom knew of such apractice and condemned it, and it is still practised today by the Latter-day Saints on thestrength of this verse. A second reading takes the small word for as meaningbecause of: people were coming to baptism because of the dead — moved to faithby the death of a believer whose hope had held to the end. A third takes it as baptism withone’s own coming death and resurrection in view.

What can be said with certainty is how Paul is using it, and that is the part that matters.He is not teaching it. Notice that he does not say you but they — heholds the practice at arm’s length, neither endorsing nor attacking it, and simplypoints out that whatever it is, it makes no sense at all unless the dead have a future. Hisargument is that the Corinthians’ own behaviour contradicts their stated theology.

That is worth noting as a method, because it is a fair one. People are often better thantheir opinions, and one honest way to answer a bad idea is to show the person that he does notactually live as though it were true. Nobody grieves as if the dead were nothing. Nobodyattends a funeral and behaves like a man who thinks a machine has stopped.

Why are we in danger every hour? The second argument is Paul’s own life, andit will run to the end of verse 32. It is the same question turned on himself: what am I doing,if there is nothing after this?

Two things are worth carrying away from a verse this obscure. The first is that it ispossible to hold a passage loosely without holding the Bible loosely. Not every sentence inScripture yields its meaning, and saying so is honesty rather than doubt. The doctrine of theresurrection does not rest on verse 29; verse 29 is a supporting argument, and Paul’sown case runs perfectly well without our knowing what the practice was.

The second is a caution about the opposite error, which is real and does damage. A wholeteaching has been built by one movement on this single obscure verse, against the plain senseof the rest of Scripture, which nowhere else suggests that anything can be done for the deadby the living. A doctrine erected on one difficult sentence, with nothing else in the Bible tosupport it, is a building on a very narrow footing.

verseByVerse.quote: I protest, brothers, by my pride in you, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord, I die every day! What do I gain if, humanly speaking, I fought with beasts at Ephesus? If the dead are not raised, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
I protest, brothers, by my pride in you, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord, I dieevery day! What do I gain if, humanly speaking, I fought with beasts at Ephesus? If the deadare not raised, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”

I die every day is not a devotional phrase about self-denial. Paul is describinghis working conditions. He lived where a violent end was a daily possibility, and he issaying that a man in that position needs a reason.

He swears to it, oddly, by my pride in you — he stakes the truthfulness ofthe claim on the one thing this difficult congregation would recognise as valuable: that he isproud of them. Even in the middle of an argument he tells them that.

I fought with beasts at Ephesus. Whether this is literal is disputed. A Romancitizen was not normally thrown to animals, and Luke does not record it; many take it as avivid description of the mob and the opposition that nearly cost him his life in that city(Acts 19:23–41). Either way the sense is the same: he had been in a place where he didnot expect to come out alive.

What do I gain? That is the honest question, and it deserves an honest answer.Nothing. If the dead are not raised, Paul has purchased absolutely nothing with his life, andhe says so without flinching.

Then the quotation, which is from Isaiah 22 and is not a joke. Isaiah described a city undersiege that ought to have been weeping and repenting, and instead threw a party — killingthe oxen, drinking the wine, saying let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die. It isthe exact philosophy that the ancient world had already worked out and that ours hasrediscovered: if this is all there is, get what you can before the lights go out.

And Paul does not sneer at it. That is the striking thing. He treats it as the rationalposition for a man with no resurrection. If death is the end, then a life of self-denial forother people’s benefit is not admirable, it is merely a waste, and the person eating anddrinking has understood the situation better than the martyr has.

Which puts a sharp question to any Christian, and it is not one anyone can answer forsomebody else. If you knew for certain there was nothing after death, what in your life wouldyou change? Whatever comes to mind is the part of your life currently being funded by theresurrection. And if nothing comes to mind, that is worth sitting with too.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be deceived: “Bad company ruins good morals.” Wake up from your drunken stupor, as is right, and do not go on sinning. For some have no knowledge of God. I say this to your shame.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be deceived: “Bad company ruins good morals.” Wake up from yourdrunken stupor, as is right, and do not go on sinning. For some have no knowledge of God. Isay this to your shame.

The proverb is a quotation from Menander, a Greek playwright, and it was probably a commonsaying by Paul’s day — the sort of line everybody knew without knowing where itcame from. Paul is not shy about using it. He does the same at Athens with the poets(Acts 17:28) and in Titus with a Cretan. Truth is truth wherever it turns up, and an apostle isfree to borrow a good sentence from a playwright.

But notice what the quotation is doing in an argument about the resurrection. It is asentence about company, and that tells us something Paul assumes and we often donot: that people do not usually reason their way into a false belief. They drift into it, incompany, over time.

That is worth taking seriously, because most Christians who abandon what they believed didnot do it in a library. It happened gradually, through friendship, through the desire to bethought reasonable by people they admired, through a slow adjustment of what could comfortablybe said aloud. Nobody sits down and decides to stop believing in the resurrection. He startsspending time where it is quietly assumed to be embarrassing, and after two years he finds hehas moved.

Paul is not commanding a retreat from the world; he has already ruled that out in thisletter (5:10). He is pointing at the particular company that is doing this particular damage— the confident deniers inside the church — and telling the congregation to stopfinding them impressive.

Wake up from your drunken stupor. The verb is what you say to a man sleeping itoff: sober up, come round. It is an extraordinary thing to say to a congregation that thoughtitself the most spiritually advanced in Greece. He does not tell them they are mistaken. Hetells them they are not properly conscious.

For some have no knowledge of God. That is the diagnosis under the error. Behindthe denial of the resurrection is not a difficulty with biology but an inadequate view of God— a God not big enough to raise the dead, which is to say not the God who made the worldout of nothing. And Paul says he is telling them this to your shame, which is thesecond time in the letter he has used that phrase (6:5). A church full of knowledge, and someof its members do not know God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The objection Paul now addresses is philosophical: “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?” He calls the questioner a fool — not for asking but for assuming the objection is unanswerable. The answer comes in two parts: the seed analogy (vv. 36–44) and the Adam/Christ typology applied to the body (vv. 45–49).

The seed analogy is brilliant in its simplicity and precision. When you plant a seed, you do not plant the body that will grow; you plant a bare seed, and God gives it a body as he wills. The same is true of the resurrection: what is buried is the seed; what is raised is the fruit of that seed — the same organism, transformed. The continuity is real (it is the same seed that becomes the same plant); the transformation is radical (no one looking at a wheat seed would predict the wheat stalk). So with the resurrection body: continuous with the buried body (it is the same person raised), but transformed into a glory undreamt of by the buried condition.

The contrast of vv. 42–44 is fourfold: perishable/imperishable, dishonour/glory, weakness/power, natural body/spiritual body. Each contrast is between a condition appropriate to the present age (subject to entropy, subject to sin, subject to mortality) and a condition appropriate to the age to come (freed from all these). The “spiritual body” is not an immaterial ghost; it is a body animated and organised by the Holy Spirit, as the present body is animated and organised by the natural life principle (psychē). It is more physical than the present body, not less — fully embodied, fully alive, fully free from everything that degrades the present embodiment.

The section ends where it began, with Adam. The first man Adam became a living being; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit (v. 45) — the first man was a vessel, the second is a spring. And verse 46 states the order God works in: it is not the spiritual that is first but the natural, and then the spiritual. The dust comes before the glory; there is no shortcut past the ordinary, and the Lord himself did not take one.

Then the promise the whole section has been building to: just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven (v. 49). Flat future, no condition attached. The man you have wanted to be and the man you are have never once been the same man. On that day the gap closes, and there will be nothing left in you that Christ would have to overlook.
verseByVerse.theology:
Continuity and Transformation in the Resurrection Body

The Reformed tradition has insisted, against all forms of Gnosticism and spiritual idealism, on the bodily nature of the resurrection. The creeds confess “the resurrection of the body” — not the survival of the soul. Paul’s seed analogy establishes both poles: continuity (the seed and the plant are the same organism in different stages) and transformation (the glory of the plant exceeds anything visible in the seed). The specific body that is buried — your body, with its particular history, its particular wounds, its particular scars — is the body that will be raised. This is why the bodily resurrection of Christ is the paradigm: the same body that was crucified was raised — still bearing the wounds (John 20:27), yet transformed into resurrection glory.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Greek objection to bodily resurrection was that the body is the problem, not the solution; the soul’s liberation from the body is the goal, not its resurrection. Paul refuses this framing entirely: the body is God’s creation, declared good, destined for resurrection. The problem is not embodiment but mortality, not physicality but corruption. The resurrection is the redemption of the body, not its abolition. Now: Every theology that treats the goal of salvation as the soul going to heaven (leaving the body behind) has the Corinthian problem. The goal is the new creation, the resurrection body, the renewed earth — the full embodied flourishing of redeemed humanity in the presence of God.

verseByVerse.quote: But someone will ask, “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?” You foolish person! What you sow does not come to life unless it dies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But someone will ask, “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do theycome?” You foolish person! What you sow does not come to life unless it dies.

Now the real objection, and Paul lets the sceptic put it in his own words, which is fair ofhim. It is not a stupid question. Bodies decay. Bodies burn. Bodies are lost at sea and eatenby animals and scattered so completely that not a molecule stays in place. The atoms that makeup a man are borrowed and returned. Where exactly is the body that is going to be raised?

You foolish person is sharper in English than in Greek, and Paul is not callinghim stupid for asking. The word describes someone reasoning without taking into account whathe already knows — a man who has the answer in his own back garden and has not looked atit.

Because here is the answer: what you sow does not come to life unless it dies.

Every farmer in the ancient world, and every gardener since, has watched this happen andnever found it strange. You take a hard dry seed and you bury it in the ground. That is afuneral. It goes into the dark, it is covered over, and if you dug it up a fortnight later youwould find it soft and rotting and finished. And out of that comes a green shoot, and then astalk taller than the seed ever was, carrying thirty seeds of its own.

The objection assumes that burial is the end of the story. The seed says otherwise, and itsays it in every field the objector has ever walked past. Death is not the obstacle to the newlife; in the only process any of us can actually observe, death is the doorway to it. Thething that looks like destruction is the mechanism.

And Jesus said exactly this about himself, days before it happened: unless a grain ofwheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears muchfruit (Jn 12:24). He was talking about his own burial, and about a harvest that wouldinclude the man asking this question.

There is something worth noticing in Paul’s choice of evidence. He could haveanswered a question about the resurrection body from revelation — he had been caught upinto the third heaven and had things he was not permitted to repeat (2 Cor 12:2–4). Heanswers it from a seed.

God has arranged the world so that the hardest thing a person has to believe is acted outevery spring in front of him, in mud, by vegetables. That is not an accident. Theresurrection is not an alien intrusion into a universe that runs on other principles; it isthe principle the universe has been running on since the beginning, applied at last to thething that matters most.

verseByVerse.quote: And what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare kernel, perhaps of wheat or of some other grain. But God gives it a body as he has chosen, and to each kind of seed its own body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare kernel, perhaps of wheat orof some other grain. But God gives it a body as he has chosen, and to each kind of seed itsown body.

Paul presses the picture, and the two halves of it answer the two halves of theobjection.

First: what you sow is not the body that is to be. Nobody who had never seen ithappen would predict a wheat stalk from a wheat grain. Hold a seed in your hand: it is small,brown, dry, hard, and entirely unremarkable. There is nothing in its appearance that suggestsa green stem, a head of grain, a field moving in the wind. If you had only ever seen the seed,you would consider the plant a wild story.

So the question with what kind of body do they come? has an answer, and part of theanswer is: not one you could work out from looking at what goes into the ground. Theresurrection body is not an improved corpse. It stands in the same relation to the buried bodyas harvest stands to seed-time.

Second: God gives it a body as he has chosen. That is where the question ofmolecules and dust and scattered atoms is quietly settled. The wheat plant is not built out ofthe material of the seed; the seed is spent, and the plant is made of soil and rain and air.Continuity is not a matter of the same particles being reassembled. It is a matter of the sameGod attending to the same person.

Which means that a Christian may lay to rest a body ruined by illness, or burned, or lostat sea, or long since gone to dust in a churchyard whose stones are unreadable, and none of itis an obstacle of any kind. The God who is going to do this made the original body out of theground in the first place and has never been short of material. He is not searching foranything. He knows exactly where every one of his people is.

And note the last clause, which is a promise of particularity: to each kind of seed itsown body. Not one generic glorified shape issued to everybody. Its own. Whatever else isuncertain, God is not planning to raise a crowd of interchangeable strangers.

That answers a fear people do not usually put into words: that whatever is raised will notreally be me — that eternity means being absorbed into something general, asoul among souls, a light among lights. Every seed in a field goes into the ground as itselfand comes up as itself. Barley does not come up wheat.

And the choosing is God’s, which is the last comfort in the verse. The body you willhave was designed by the same person who designed this one, and he has had a very long timeto think about it. He is not improvising at the graveside.

verseByVerse.quote: For not all flesh is the same, but there is one kind for humans, another for animals, another for birds, and another for fish. There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies, but the glory of the heavenly is of one kind, and the glory of the earthly is of another. There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For not all flesh is the same, but there is one kind for humans, another for animals,another for birds, and another for fish. There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies, but theglory of the heavenly is of one kind, and the glory of the earthly is of another. There is oneglory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for stardiffers from star in glory.

Paul now widens the lens, and the argument is doing something specific: it is dismantlingthe assumption that the word body can only mean one thing.

Look around, he says. A man’s flesh and a fish’s flesh are both flesh and theyare not remotely alike; the bird that can live in the air and the fish that would drown in itare both embodied creatures. Then lift your eyes: there are bodies down here and bodies upthere, and their glories are of different orders altogether. And even among the lights in thesky, no two are the same — the sun, the moon, and star differing from star.

The point is that God has never worked with one template. A God with this much range inwhat he has already made is not likely to be stuck for a design when he comes to raise thedead. The objector at verse 35 was assuming that a resurrection body would have to be the samesort of thing as the body he currently has, and that assumption is the whole of his difficulty.

There is also a note being sounded here that the Corinthians particularly needed, andPaul has been sounding it all letter. Star differs from star in glory. Difference isnot a defect in God’s workmanship; it is his habit. He made a universe in which nothingis standardised — a church of eyes and ears and feet (12:17), and a sky in which no twolights are matched. A congregation that had been ranking one another by a single measure isbeing shown a night sky.

And there is something to be simply enjoyed in the passage, which too many commentarieshurry past. This is a tentmaker writing to a quarrelling church about a difficult doctrine,and he stops in the middle of it to look up. He notices fish and birds. He notices that thestars are not alike. The man who wrote the hardest arguments in the New Testament had his eyesopen in the world, and thought God’s ordinary handiwork was worth putting into asentence about the last day (cf. Ps 19:1; Job 38:31–33).

verseByVerse.quote: So is it with the resurrection of the dead. What is sown is perishable; what is raised is imperishable. It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So is it with the resurrection of the dead. What is sown is perishable; what is raisedis imperishable. It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it israised in power.

The comparisons stop and the promises begin. Four contrasts follow; here are the firstthree, and each one names something a reader has felt.

Sown perishable; raised imperishable. The present body is on a schedule of decayand everyone knows it. It began wearing out at about twenty-five. The knee goes, the eyes go,the name of somebody you have known for forty years will not come. Whatever is done to slow it— and there is nothing wrong with slowing it — the direction is fixed. Theresurrection body will have no such direction. It will not be a body kept young by effort. Itwill be a body with nothing in it that can wear out.

Sown in dishonour; raised in glory. This is the honest one, and it should not besoftened, because anyone who has sat with the dying knows exactly what Paul means. There isvery little dignity available at the end. There is the indignity of being washed by strangers,of a body that will not obey, of a mind that says the wrong word, of a person who wasformidable and is now frightened of the stairs. Death does not merely end a life; it humiliatesit first. And into that Paul writes raised in glory — the same word used of thesplendour of God himself. The body that was carried out of a ward with a sheet over it comesback radiant.

Sown in weakness; raised in power. Weakness is the daily one. It is not only thesickbed; it is the ordinary ceiling every person lives under — wanting to help and beingtoo tired, wanting to stay and having to sleep, wanting to do the good thing and finding thatthe body will not carry the will that far. Every human being alive is limited by an instrumentthat cannot keep up with him. Raised in power means the instrument will be equal to theperson at last.

And notice the verb governing all three: sown. Not disposed of, not lost, notstored. Sown — which is a thing done by a farmer, on purpose, with a harvest in mind.Christians have buried their dead for two thousand years in that word’s shadow. A grave,on Paul’s account, is not a full stop but a planting.

verseByVerse.quote: It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. If there is a natural body,there is also a spiritual body.

The fourth contrast, and the one most often misunderstood, so it must be handledcarefully.

Spiritual body does not mean a body made of spirit. It does not mean a ghost, amist, a shining outline, or a soul that has escaped its container. The word does not describewhat a thing is made of; it describes what animates and governs it. The natural bodyis a body run by ordinary created life — breath, blood, appetite, sleep. Thespiritual body is a body wholly animated and directed by the Holy Spirit.

Which means the resurrection body is not less physical than the present one. If anything itis more so — more solid, more alive, more capable, because everything that currentlydrags at the body has been removed from it.

And we are not guessing, because one such body exists and was examined. The risen Christwas not a vision. He told them to touch him, and said that a spirit does not have fleshand bones as you see that I have (Lk 24:39). He ate a piece of grilled fish in front ofthem, which is a strange thing for a phantom to do, and which reads exactly like a man provinga point. And when Thomas needed evidence, he offered the wounds (Jn 20:27).

That last detail answers a question people carry and rarely ask. He kept thescars. The one resurrection body we have any information about is marked, permanently, bywhat was done to it. Glorification did not erase the history; it healed it and kept the record.Whatever that means for the rest of us, it means the risen life is not an amnesia.

Other questions crowd in here, and it is better to answer them plainly than to leave areader guessing. Will we know one another? The disciples knew him — sometimes at once,sometimes after a moment, and always in the end — and Paul assumes throughout hisletters that Christians will be reunited and will recognise each other (1 Thess 4:17–18;2 Cor 4:14). What about a body wrecked by disease, or a mind lost to dementia, or a life livedwith a disability? Verse 38 has already answered it: God gives it a body as he haschosen, and what is raised is imperishable, glorious, powerful. Nothing that thefall put into a body is going to be raised with it.

And what age? Scripture does not say, and it is better to admit that than to invent. Whatit does say is enough: the body will be like his (Phil 3:21). That is the whole promise, andit is a great deal more than a description.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus it is written, “The first man Adam became a living being”; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit. But it is not the spiritual that is first but the natural, and then the spiritual.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus it is written, “The first man Adam became a living being”; the lastAdam became a life-giving spirit. But it is not the spiritual that is first but the natural,and then the spiritual.

Paul goes back to Genesis, and the difference between the two halves of his sentence is oneword.

Of Adam, Genesis says he became a living being (Gen 2:7). He received life; Godbreathed it into him and he sat up. Everything about the first man is on the receiving end: hewas made from dust he did not gather, given breath he did not take, and put in a garden he didnot plant.

Of Christ, Paul says he became a life-giving spirit. Not merely alive — asource. The first Adam was a vessel; the last Adam is a spring. That is why the resurrectionof Jesus is not simply the best example of resurrection but its cause. He does not stand at thehead of the queue. He is the reason there is a queue.

Note also the title: the last Adam. Not the second, as though there might be athird. The human race has had two representatives and will have no more. Everything afterChrist is a matter of which of the two you belong to.

Then verse 46, which looks like a small logical aside and is doing real work: it is notthe spiritual that is first but the natural, and then the spiritual.

Paul is establishing the order of God’s working, and it runs against the instinct ofevery religious person who has ever wanted to skip a stage. The ordinary comes first. The dustcomes before the glory, the natural body before the spiritual one, the long unremarkable lifebefore the transformation. God does not begin with the finished thing.

That is a rebuke to the Corinthian error, which was to believe they had already arrived— already reigning, already filled, already beyond the ordinary business of bodies andpatience (4:8). And it is a comfort to anyone who suspects his own Christian life is tooplain to be real. The plainness is not a sign that something has gone wrong. It is theappointed order. Seed first. Harvest afterwards. Nobody gets the second without going throughthe first, and the Lord himself did not (cf. Heb 5:8; Phil 2:8–9).

It is a rule with a wide application. The long apprenticeship before the work. The years offaithfulness nobody notices before the door opens. The decades of an ordinary marriage, anordinary job, an ordinary congregation. Christians are forever looking for a shortcut past thenatural into the spiritual, and there is not one; there is only the appointed sequence, andGod is not in a hurry.

Thirty years in a carpenter’s shop came before three years of ministry. If the lastAdam took the natural first and did not complain about the ratio, nobody else is beingshort-changed.

verseByVerse.quote: The first man was from the earth, a man of dust; the second man is from heaven. As was the man of dust, so also are those who are of the dust, and as is the man of heaven, so also are those who are of heaven. Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first man was from the earth, a man of dust; the second man is from heaven. As wasthe man of dust, so also are those who are of the dust, and as is the man of heaven, so alsoare those who are of heaven. Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall alsobear the image of the man of heaven.

Two men, two origins, and two families that look like their heads.

A man of dust. Genesis says so and does not apologise for it: God formed the manof dust from the ground (Gen 2:7), and told him after the fall that to dust he would return(Gen 3:19). Every person carries the evidence. We are made of the same elements as the soilin the garden, we require constant maintenance from that soil in the form of food and water,and in the end we go back into it. There is a reason the funeral service says what it says overa grave.

The second man is from heaven. Not made of different material — he had areal body, born of a woman, that got tired and hungry and bled. He is from heaven in origin:he came from somewhere, which no other human being has ever done.

And then the promise in verse 49, and it is one of the great sentences of the Bible.Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of theman of heaven.

We have borne the first image all our lives, and we know its features intimately: mortality,weakness, the pull toward what we know is wrong, the face in the mirror getting older. Nobodyhad to be taught to bear that image. It came with the birth.

The second is as certain as the first. Note the tense — we shall bear, flatfuture, no condition attached. This is the same thing Paul says in Romans, that those Godforeknew he predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son (Rom 8:29), and whatJohn says in one line: we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is(1 Jn 3:2).

Measure that against what is actually broken. The man you have wanted to be and the man youare have never once been the same man; every Christian carries an internal record of the gap.On that day the gap closes. Not by lowering the standard, and not by a lifetime of gradualimprovement finally arriving — but because the likeness of Christ, which has been workedinto his people slowly and against resistance, will be completed in an instant and will hold.There will be nothing left in you that he would have to overlook.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“Behold! I tell you a mystery.” Paul announces a revelation: not all Christians will die before the Parousia, but all will be transformed. The change will be instantaneous — “in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet.” The dead will be raised imperishable; the living will be changed. This is not an optional upgrade but a necessary transformation: “flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable.” The present bodily condition, however good and however beloved of God, is not fitted for the new creation; it must be transformed into what God intends.

Then the doxology — the most triumphant sentences Paul ever wrote, perhaps the most triumphant sentences in Scripture. Death has been swallowed up in victory. The taunt against death: “O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?” The answer: nowhere. The sting of death is sin; the power of sin is the law; but God gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. Death has been robbed of its sting because sin has been atoned for; sin has been dealt with because the law’s demands have been met in Christ; Christ’s resurrection has declared the victory. The enemy still exists — the last enemy will be destroyed (v. 26) — but it has already been defeated in principle. The resurrection of Christ is the down payment on a victory that is as certain as God himself.

The conclusion drawn from the entire chapter (v. 58) is one of Paul’s most bracing practical statements: “Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labour is not in vain.” The resurrection is not an academic doctrine about the afterlife; it is the foundation of present, costly, patient, unstoppable labour for the Lord. Because the resurrection is certain, no act of faithfulness in this life is lost, no sacrifice is wasted, no patient endurance is pointless. In the Lord your labour is not in vain. This is the word the church has been waiting for throughout sixteen chapters of rebuke, correction, and instruction. It is the word that makes everything else possible.
verseByVerse.theology:
Resurrection as the Foundation of Present Labour

The practical conclusion of the resurrection argument — “your labour is not in vain” (v. 58) — is the most comprehensive positive statement about Christian ethics in the letter. The resurrection does not merely give hope for the future; it validates the present. Every act of love, faithfulness, service, and endurance that has been poured out for Christ is stored up in a creation that will be renewed, not discarded. Herman Bavinck stated it with characteristic precision: Grace restores nature. The resurrection does not annul creation — it redeems and glorifies it. Every act of love, faithfulness, and service done in Christ’s name is not lost but transformed into the fabric of the new creation.

Anthony Hoekema, in The Bible and the Future, makes the same point: the resurrection is the guarantee that present labour is not in vain, because the God who raised Christ will also raise and renew the creation in which that labour was performed. The resurrection does not make the present world irrelevant; it makes it eternally significant.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians needed to hear that the deaths of their beloved dead were not permanent losses, that their own present labour was not ultimately futile, and that the God who raised Christ had the power and the intention to complete what he had begun in them. The resurrection doctrine is not abstract comfort; it is the concrete ground of the community’s ability to bear all things, believe all things, hope all things, endure all things (ch. 13). Now: Every generation of the church faces the question that faces every human being: does my life mean anything beyond this brief span? Paul’s answer is the most radical possible: yes, because the God who raised Jesus from the dead is the God who inhabits your story, and he wastes nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you this, brothers: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable. Behold! I tell you a mystery. We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed,
verseByVerse.commentary:
I tell you this, brothers: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor doesthe perishable inherit the imperishable. Behold! I tell you a mystery. We shall not all sleep,but we shall all be changed.

Flesh and blood is a Jewish idiom for a human being in his present frail condition— not a slur on physical existence, which Paul has spent fifteen verses defending. He issaying that this body as it now is, mortal and running down, is not equipped for the worldthat is coming. It is not a moral judgment; it is a statement about fitness. You do not godeep-sea diving in a jacket.

Behold! I tell you a mystery. A mystery in Paul is never a puzzle; it is somethingthat could not have been worked out and has now been disclosed. He is about to say somethingthe church did not know.

We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed. There is the new information.The entire chapter so far has assumed the pattern of death and resurrection — sown, thenraised. But there will be a generation of Christians alive when Christ returns, who will neverbe buried at all. They will not miss out on the transformation; they will simply reach it by adifferent road.

This is where Paul’s teaching here joins hands with what he had already written toThessalonica: the Lord descending with a cry of command and the sound of the trumpet, the deadin Christ rising first, and then those who are alive being caught up together with them tomeet the Lord in the air (1 Thess 4:16–17).

Christians hold different convictions about the timing and sequence of these events, andmany of them are held by people who love the Scriptures and read them with great care. It isworth being clear about how much is shared before any of that is discussed, because the sharedpart is nearly all of it: that Jesus Christ will return personally, visibly and bodily; thatthe dead in Christ will be raised; that those alive will be transformed; that this will happenin an instant and at his initiative; and that no believer of any generation will be left outof it. That is what this passage teaches, and it is what Christians of every persuasion saytogether at a graveside.

Where they differ is on the arrangement of what follows, and this verse does not settle itone way or the other. What it settles is the fact and the certainty. It is a poor use of apromise this size to make it the occasion of a quarrel among people who are all waiting forthe same trumpet.

verseByVerse.quote: in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised imperishable, and we shall be changed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet willsound, and the dead will be raised imperishable, and we shall be changed.

Paul reaches for two measures of time and both of them mean the same thing: there will beno process.

In a moment translates en atomōi — in an uncuttable instant.It is the word from which we get atom, and it meant the smallest thing that cannot bedivided further. Paul is saying the change will happen in a slice of time too thin to haveparts.

In the twinkling of an eye is the homelier version of the same idea. Not the blink— the flicker, the involuntary movement of the eye that is over before it has beennoticed. It is the fastest thing a person can observe in himself.

Both images say the same thing and it is worth pausing on, because it is not what anyonewould have guessed. Everything else in the Christian life is slow. Sanctification takesdecades and moves backwards on many days. Grief takes years. Prayers are answered over thecourse of a lifetime, or not visibly at all. The whole of a believer’s experience trainshim to expect God to work at the pace of growing things.

And then this. No preparation, no ramp, no gradual improvement. A woman who has spenteleven years unable to leave her chair, and in the next instant she is not merely well butimperishable. A man in a churchyard since 1840 whose stone is illegible, and in the sameinstant he is standing. The slowest work God does and the fastest work God does are bothdirected at the same person.

At the last trumpet. A trumpet in Israel summoned the assembly, announced theking, and called the camp to move (Num 10). This one does all three at once. And there issomething worth noticing in the word last: there will never be another summons afterit, because there will never again be anyone who needs calling.

And note who is doing what in the sentence. The dead do not rise; they will beraised — the same passive that was used of Christ at verse 4. Nobody in that vastcompany contributes anything to his own resurrection. They are not straining at the lid. Theyare called, and they come, because the voice that calls them is the voice that called lightout of nothing and Lazarus out of a tomb.

Which means that the certainty of this does not depend in the least on the strength of thefaith of the person waiting for it. Everyone in the churchyard will be raised by the samevoice, at the same instant, with the same ease (cf. Jn 5:28–29; 1 Thess 4:16).

verseByVerse.quote: For this perishable body must put on the imperishable, and this mortal body must put on immortality. When the perishable puts on the imperishable, and the mortal puts on immortality, then shall come to pass the saying that is written: “Death is swallowed up in victory.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this perishable body must put on the imperishable, and this mortal body must put onimmortality. When the perishable puts on the imperishable, and the mortal puts on immortality,then shall come to pass the saying that is written: “Death is swallowed up invictory.”

Notice the verb: put on. It is the word for getting dressed — putting on acoat, a garment, clothing. Paul does not say the perishable body is discarded and a better oneissued. He says it is clothed, and the thing underneath is still there.

That matters, because it is the difference between resurrection and replacement. TheChristian is not going to be swapped for a superior model of person. The same man who hasstruggled and prayed and failed and hung on is going to be dressed in immortality, and it willbe him inside it.

And this perishable body, Paul writes, twice. He might have said theperishable. He says this, and one imagines him gesturing at himself as he dictated— a man in his fifties with a scarred back and failing eyes, saying: this one.

Then the quotation, from Isaiah 25. It is worth knowing what surrounds it there, becauseIsaiah is describing a feast. On his mountain the LORD will make a banquet of rich food forall peoples; he will destroy the covering that is cast over all nations, the veil spread overeverything — and then: He will swallow up death forever; and the Lord GOD will wipeaway tears from all faces (Isa 25:6–8).

The verb is worth having. Death is not defeated in a negotiated settlement. It isswallowed — taken in and gone, the way the sea takes something and closes overit. The thing that has swallowed every human being who ever lived is itself swallowed at last,and there is a rough justice in the image that Isaiah plainly intended.

And the detail that most people need is the one about the faces. God is not described asissuing a decree about grief. He is described as coming close enough to wipe tears offindividual faces with his own hand — which is what he is doing at the end of the Bibletoo (Rev 21:4). Whatever else that day contains, it contains a God who has come near enough totouch the people who have been crying.

One word in these verses is worth pressing, because Paul repeats it: must. Thisperishable body must put on the imperishable. That is the language of necessity —not what is likely, or hoped for, or reasonable to expect, but what has to happen.

Necessary to whom? Not to us; nobody here arranged anything. It is necessary because Godhas purposed a new creation and has determined that his people will live in it, and aperishable body cannot. The obligation sits on his side of the transaction. He has boundhimself, and the raising of the dead is now something he must do in order to be theGod he has said he is.

verseByVerse.quote: “O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?” The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?” The sting ofdeath is sin, and the power of sin is the law.

Paul turns and speaks to death directly, and the tone is not respectful. He is quotingHosea, and the two questions are a taunt — the sort of thing shouted after an enemy whohas been beaten and is being watched off the field.

Where is your victory? Death has had a total record. It has never lost a singleengagement in the history of the world; every person it has come for, it has taken. And Paulstands in front of it and asks what it has won.

Then the word to concentrate on: sting. It is the word for the barb of a scorpionor a bee — not the size of the creature but the part that can actually kill you.

The old illustration is still the best one, and it is worth stating properly. A bee thathas stung has left its sting behind. It can still come at you; it can still fly at your faceand make a grown man leave a picnic. What it cannot do is hurt you, because the thing thatmade it dangerous is gone. And a child who knows that will stand perfectly still while itbuzzes round his head.

That is precisely the Christian’s position, and Paul explains the mechanism in thenext clause rather than leaving it as a picture. The sting of death is sin. What makesdeath terrible is not that it ends the body; animals die and it is sad and it is notfrightening in this way. What makes death terrible is that it is the doorway to judgment for aguilty person — it is sin that gives death its barb.

And the power of sin is the law. The law is not the villain here; Paul sayselsewhere it is holy, righteous and good (Rom 7:12). But the law is what turns wrongdoing intoa documented offence. It names it, measures it, and pronounces the sentence, and so it is thelaw that gives sin its legal force.

So follow the chain backwards to see what has actually happened. Death is fearful because ofsin. Sin has its power from the law. And Christ has dealt with both — he kept the lawwe broke and bore the sentence it pronounced. Pull those two out and death is a bee with nosting. It is still an enemy. It can still frighten. It cannot kill a Christian, and it neverwill again.

verseByVerse.quote: But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.

The argument stops. The proofs are finished, the objections are answered, and Paul does theonly thing left to do.

Read the verbs. Nobody in the sentence wins anything. The victory is given —handed over, made a present of — and it is given to people who were not on the field.This is not the language of a struggle in which the believer participated and finallyprevailed. Every Christian who will ever be raised was, at the decisive moment, dead intrespasses and sins, and had contributed nothing to the outcome except the problem.

And notice the tense: gives. Present. Not will give, though theresurrection is future. The giving is already going on. The victory is being handed over now,to people still in perishable bodies, still burying their friends, still afraid of thediagnosis. The thing has been settled and the settlement is in force.

And the channel is named, as it always is in Paul: through our Lord Jesus Christ.Not through our grasp of the doctrine, our steadiness under pressure, or the quality of ourdying. Christians have died well and Christians have died badly — frightened, confused,heavily medicated, saying nothing memorable at all — and it makes no difference whateverto the outcome, because the victory was won by somebody else and is handed over as a gift topeople who were not in a position to receive anything.

The word victory has been in the air since verse 54, and it is a battlefield term:the outcome, the thing carried off the field. Paul uses it again in Romans and puts an evenstranger word in front of it — in all these things we are more than conquerorsthrough him who loved us (Rom 8:37). More than conquerors. Not merely surviving theengagement, but coming out of it with more than was taken in.

So there is nothing left but thanks, and it is worth letting the sentence be what it israther than pressing on to the application in the next verse.

He was dead. Properly dead, taken down by men who did this for a living and knew when a jobwas finished, wrapped and weighted with spices and shut behind a stone by people with noexpectation whatever of seeing him again. Everything that has ever terrified the human race haddone its complete work on him, and had done it with the full cooperation of the authorities,the crowd, and his own friends.

And on the first morning of the week he got up and folded the cloth that had been on hishead and left it lying in the place where it had been, and went out into a garden where a womanwas crying, and said her name.

Thanks be to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work ofthe Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain.

Fifty-seven verses of the highest doctrine in the letter, and the conclusion is aboutMonday.

That therefore is doing all the work, and it should stop anybody who has everthought the resurrection is a subject for funerals. Paul does not say: therefore look forwardto heaven. He says: therefore get on with it.

Steadfast, immovable. Two words meaning much the same thing, laid one on the otherfor weight — seated, settled, not to be shifted. This is the answer to a church that hadbeen blown about by every teacher, every fashion and every clever argument for sixteenchapters.

Always abounding in the work of the Lord. Abounding is an overflow word. Notmanaging, not maintaining, not doing one’s bit — more than is required, spillingover the edge. And note that a man is being told to spend himself in a body he has just beentold is perishable, on the ground that the body is going to be raised. The doctrine does notproduce detachment from this life. It produces recklessness in it.

Then the clause the whole chapter has been travelling toward: knowing that in the Lordyour labor is not in vain.

The word in vain has been haunting this chapter. If Christ is not raised, thepreaching is in vain, the faith is in vain (v. 14); Paul’s grace was not in vain (v. 10).Now it lands where the reader lives. Because Christ is raised, nothing done for him is wasted.

And that needs to be made concrete, because it is exactly the sort of promise thatevaporates when it is left general. Consider the mother who has prayed for a son for thirtyyears and has watched him get worse. The man who taught a Sunday class of eight children for adecade and has no idea what became of any of them. The woman who nursed a husband throughseven years of dementia, doing everything, thanked by nobody, remembered by a man who did notknow her name. The believer who has held a difficult marriage together in private for alifetime and will never be commended for it. The missionary who gave forty years to a placeand left it with three converts and a small building.

Every one of them has looked at what they have to show for it and thought: that wasnothing. And every one of them has been wrong, on the authority of this verse. Notyour labour will probably bear fruit eventually. Not God sees your effort evenif it failed. Your labour is not in vain — the work itself is not lost,because it was done in the Lord, and what is done in the Lord belongs to a world that is notgoing to be thrown away but raised.

That is what the empty tomb finally means for an ordinary Tuesday. The God who did not lethis Son’s body stay in the ground is not going to let his people’s work stay thereeither. He wastes nothing, he forgets nothing, and he is going to raise all of it.

If the dead are not raised at all, why are people baptized on their behalf?<sup>30</sup>Why are we in danger every hour?<sup>31</sup>I protest, brothers, by my pride in you, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord, I die every day!<sup>32</sup>What do I gain if, humanly speaking, I fought with beasts at Ephesus?
